source: Neurology Board and RITE Practice Examinations

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with a single episode of optic neuritis. MRI shows periventricular, juxtacortical, and infratentorial T2 lesions, none enhancing. CSF shows oligoclonal bands not present in serum. Under the 2017 McDonald criteria, what is the diagnosis?

options.text: Multiple sclerosis; CSF-specific oligoclonal bands substitute for dissemination in time
Clinically isolated syndrome; MS cannot be diagnosed until a second attack

questions.explanation: The 2017 revision allows CSF-specific oligoclonal bands to fulfill dissemination in time after a single attack when dissemination in space is met (≥2 of 4 CNS regions), permitting earlier treatment. Symptomatic and asymptomatic lesions count, and cortical lesions are included. (The 2024 revision proposes adding the optic nerve as a fifth region and central vein sign/paramagnetic rim lesions.)

questions.stem: The sagittal T1 image shows a destructive, lobulated midline mass centred on the clivus with posterior displacement of the brainstem. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chordoma. A midline, destructive, lobulated clival mass that is markedly T2 bright and erodes bone is a chordoma until proven otherwise. Chordomas arise from notochordal remnants and occur at the clivus, sacrococcyx and vertebral bodies. The main mimic is chondrosarcoma, which is typically off-midline at the petro-occipital fissure. A clival meningioma is dural-based and causes hyperostosis rather than destruction; a macroadenoma is centred on the sella, not the clivus; nasopharyngeal carcinoma arises from the mucosa below and invades upward.
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal T1: destructive, lobulated mass centered on the clivus with posterior displacement of the brainstem. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 130)
questions.salient: Midline clivus + bone destruction + very bright T2 = chordoma. Off-midline at the petro-occipital fissure = chondrosarcoma.
questions.learning: Confirmed histologically by physaliphorous (bubble-bearing) cells and nuclear brachyury (TBXT) immunostaining. Locally aggressive with a high recurrence rate; treated with maximal resection plus proton beam radiotherapy.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis develops back pain; the MRI shown involves L2, L3 and the intervening disc. What feature distinguishes this process from metastatic disease?

options.text: Involvement of two adjacent vertebral bodies with the intervening disc

questions.explanation: Involvement of two adjacent vertebral bodies with the intervening disc. Tumor spares the disc; infection crosses it. In children infection starts in the vascularized disc; in adults at the endplate. Back pain >90%, fever <20%; bacteremia (endocarditis, IVDU) is the usual setting. In children infection begins in the still-vascularized disc; in adults it begins at the endplate and crosses the disc to the neighboring body. The two-vertebrae-one-disc pattern separates infection from tumor, which spares the disc. TB (Pott disease) spares the disc longer and produces large paraspinal abscesses.
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal T1 lumbar spine: loss of the L2-L3 disc space with destruction and low signal of the adjacent endplates and vertebral bodies; ring enhancement on the post-contrast study. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 35)

questions.stem: A 9-year-old with ataxia has the post-contrast images shown, with an enhancing mural nodule and a non-enhancing cyst wall. Which molecular alteration is most likely?
questions.explanation: KIAA1549-BRAF fusion. Posterior fossa pilocytic astrocytomas carry the BRAF fusion; the non-enhancing cyst wall lacks tumor, so nodule resection is curative. WHO grade 1, most common pediatric glioma and the histology of 80-85% of cerebellar astrocytomas (the deck\'s phrasing, 80-85% of cerebellar tumors, overstates it; medulloblastoma is comparably common), peak 5-14 years; does not typically progress in grade. Posterior fossa tumors carry the KIAA1549-BRAF fusion; NF1-associated optic pathway gliomas are the same histology. Non-enhancing cyst wall lacks tumor, so nodule resection is curative; gross total resection is possible in >70%.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal and axial post-contrast T1: cerebellar hemispheric cyst with a brightly enhancing mural nodule; the cyst wall does not enhance. (RITE Review deck, slide 6)

questions.stem: Histology of a suprasellar mass shows nodules of anucleate keratinized cells. The term and tumor are:
questions.explanation: Craniopharyngioma: wet keratin. Wet keratin is pathognomonic of adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma.
questions.imageAlt: H&E: nodules of anucleate eosinophilic keratinized cells (wet keratin) with calcification and cholesterol clefts; peripheral palisading epithelium.
questions.salient: Calcification in ~90%; CTNNB1; Papillary variant: adults, BRAF V600E, no calcification
questions.learning: Compare Exam 309 histology. Calcification in ~90% of adamantinomatous cases; papillary adults lack it. Endocrine deficits (growth failure, DI) and visual loss; hypothalamic injury after surgery.

questions.stem: H&E shows a neuron with a round pale cytoplasmic inclusion; silver stain shows a dense round argyrophilic inclusion. Highest on the differential?
questions.explanation: Pick body versus other round neuronal inclusions. Round, argyrophilic (Bielschowsky positive, Gallyas negative), tau-positive inclusions in dentate and frontotemporal neurons are Pick bodies; Lewy bodies are not argyrophilic.
questions.imageAlt: Left (H&E): a neuron with a rounded, pale eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion displacing the nucleus. Right (silver stain): a dense, round, argyrophilic cytoplasmic inclusion.
questions.salient: Pick: 3R tau; NFT: flame/globose, Gallyas positive; Balloon (achromatic) neurons in CBD and Pick
questions.learning: Pick bodies: round, argyrophilic (Bielschowsky positive, Gallyas negative), tau-positive, in dentate gyrus granule cells and frontotemporal cortex. Lewy bodies: eosinophilic with halo, alpha-synuclein positive, not argyrophilic. Neurofibrillary tangles: flame-shaped or globose, Gallyas positive. Balloon neurons: swollen, achromatic (CBD, Pick).
questions.note: Two adjacent exams; identity of each inclusion is inferred.

questions.stem: Which descending motor pathway decussates in the caudal midbrain and activates flexor motor neurons of the upper extremities?
questions.explanation: The rubrospinal tract originates in the red nucleus, decussates in the ventral tegmental decussation of the midbrain, and facilitates flexor tone in the contralateral upper limb.

questions.stem: The CT images shown demonstrate a calcified intraocular mass and a calcified pineal mass in a young child. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Pineal calcification is normal at this age
This combination is termed trilateral retinoblastoma and implies germline RB1 disease
The pineal lesion is likely a germinoma

questions.explanation: This combination is termed trilateral retinoblastoma and implies germline RB1 disease. Pineal calcification before age 2 is abnormal; germline carriers face lifelong second-cancer risk, especially after radiation. Calcification is the key discriminator of retinoblastoma from other leukocoria causes (Coats disease, PHPV, toxocariasis). Bilateral or multifocal disease implies a germline RB1 variant (13q14); a pineoblastoma in a germline carrier is trilateral retinoblastoma. Knudson\'s two-hit hypothesis derived from this tumor. Germline carriers are at lifelong risk of osteosarcoma and other second cancers, especially after radiation. The deck\'s point: pineal calcification before age 2 is abnormal.
questions.imageAlt: Axial CT orbits (A): calcified intraocular mass(es) arising from the retina. Axial CT brain (B): calcified pineal region mass. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 141)

questions.stem: A 17-year-old presents with dysarthria, drooling, dystonia, and a wing-beating tremor; MRI shows T2 hyperintensity of the midbrain tegmentum with relative sparing of the red nuclei ("face of the giant panda"). Serum ceruloplasmin is 8 mg/dL. What genetic defect and first-line management apply?

options.text: ATP7B; chelation (trientine or penicillamine) or zinc, with awareness that chelation can transiently worsen neurologic symptoms

questions.explanation: Wilson disease (autosomal recessive ATP7B) impairs biliary copper excretion and ceruloplasmin incorporation; Kayser-Fleischer rings are present in nearly all neurologic cases. Diagnosis: low ceruloplasmin, elevated 24-hour urine copper, Leipzig score, sequencing. Neurologic worsening occurs in up to 20–30% starting penicillamine; trientine or zinc are often preferred initially. Liver transplant cures the hepatic phenotype.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with cough-induced occipital headache and cape-like loss of pain sensation has the imaging shown. What is the preferred initial surgical treatment?
questions.explanation: Posterior fossa decompression. Chiari I with syrinx is treated by addressing the foramen magnum obstruction; shunting the syrinx directly is reserved for failures. Tonsillar descent >5 mm below the basion-opisthion line. Presents with tussive occipital headache, dissociated (cape) sensory loss from the syrinx, scoliosis in children. Chiari I is the most common cause of syrinx; other causes are trauma, tumor (look for enhancement), arachnoiditis. Posterior fossa decompression treats the syrinx; do not shunt the syrinx first.
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal T1 (A) and T2 (B) cervical spine and axial T2 (C): cerebellar tonsils herniated below the foramen magnum with a central CSF-signal cavity expanding the cervical cord. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 38)

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman of Han Chinese ancestry is diagnosed with focal epilepsy. Before starting carbamazepine, what pharmacogenomic test is recommended?
questions.explanation: HLA-B15:02 strongly predicts carbamazepine (and phenytoin/oxcarbazepine) Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN in Han Chinese, Thai, Malaysian, and other Southeast Asian populations; FDA labeling recommends screening before use. HLA-A31:01 predicts hypersensitivity across broader ancestries but with weaker effect.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man from rural Central America presents with a new-onset seizure. MRI shows several small cystic lesions, one containing an eccentric dot (scolex), with surrounding edema, plus scattered calcified nodules. Ophthalmologic examination is normal. What is the treatment?

options.text: Albendazole (with or without praziquantel) plus corticosteroids and antiseizure medication for viable cysts; calcified lesions need no antiparasitic therapy

questions.explanation: Neurocysticercosis (Taenia solium) is the leading cause of acquired epilepsy worldwide. Antiparasitic therapy accelerates cyst resolution and reduces seizure recurrence but induces inflammation, so steroids are given concurrently; ocular and subarachnoid disease and hydrocephalus require special handling. Calcified lesions can still seed seizures via perilesional edema.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old grandfather presents with progressive gait ataxia and action tremor. His grandson has fragile X syndrome with severe cognitive impairment and macroorchidism. What genetic state underlies the grandfather's condition?

options.text: Full mutation (>200 CGG repeats) in FMR1

questions.explanation: Fragile X–associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS) occurs in premutation carriers (55–200 CGG repeats) of FMR1; full mutations cause methylation-silencing and fragile X syndrome, not FXTAS.

questions.stem: A patient presents with acute bilateral lower motor neuron facial paralysis (facial diplegia), paresthesias, and generalized hyporeflexia. CSF demonstrates marked albuminocytological dissociation (protein 180 mg/dL, WBC 2). What Guillain-Barré variant is this?

options.text: Bifacial weakness with paresthesias variant of GBS

questions.explanation: Facial diplegia with distal paresthesias is a localized variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome with bilateral CN VII palsies, preserved limb strength, areflexia, and cytoalbuminologic dissociation. Miller Fisher (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia) is associated with anti-GQ1b.

questions.stem: FLAIR, T1 pre, and T1 post images of a large left basal ganglia lesion with ring enhancement. Which sequence best discriminates abscess from necrotic tumor?
questions.explanation: Ring-enhancing lesion with mass effect. Central restricted diffusion indicates pus; necrotic tumor centers do not restrict.
questions.imageAlt: A: FLAIR extensive left basal ganglia/insular hyperintensity with mass effect. B: precontrast T1 hypointense center. C: coronal post-contrast: ring enhancement with central non-enhancement.
questions.salient: Thin smooth rim thinner toward ventricle = abscess; thick nodular rim = tumor; MRS: amino acids/succinate in abscess versus choline in tumor
questions.learning: Abscess: central restricted diffusion (bright DWI, low ADC), smooth thin rim thinner on the ventricular side. Necrotic tumor: non-restricting center, irregular thick nodular rim. MRS: abscess shows amino acid, acetate, succinate peaks; tumor shows choline peak.

questions.stem: A neonate with hypotonia, poor feeding, respiratory distress, and cardiomegaly is found to have massive lysosomal glycogen accumulation in skeletal muscle and cardiac myocytes. What enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: Infantile Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II) is caused by acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency, leading to intralysosomal glycogen storage, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and hypotonia. Enzyme replacement (alglucosidase alfa) is standard and is on many state newborn screening panels.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old with ataxia and polycythemia has the imaging shown. Which systemic condition should be considered?
questions.explanation: von Hippel-Lindau disease. Cerebellar hemangioblastoma with erythropoietin-driven polycythemia; a quarter to a third are VHL (3p25). Most common primary intra-axial posterior fossa tumor in adults. Cyst-with-nodule in an adult cerebellum = hemangioblastoma; in a child = pilocytic astrocytoma. WHO grade 1, highly vascular (flow voids), may cause secondary polycythemia via erythropoietin. About a quarter to a third occur in VHL (3p25); screen young patients or those with multiple/spinal lesions for retinal hemangioblastoma, RCC, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic and endolymphatic sac tumors.
questions.imageAlt: Axial T2 and post-contrast T1: cerebellar hemispheric cyst with an intensely enhancing mural nodule abutting the pial surface. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 133)

questions.stem: An intraparenchymal haematoma is bright on T1 and bright on T2. Which stage of haemorrhage does this signal pattern represent?
questions.explanation: Late subacute, roughly 1 to 2 weeks old. Red cells lyse and methaemoglobin spills into the extracellular space. Methaemoglobin keeps the blood T1 bright, and the loss of red-cell compartmentalisation removes the susceptibility effect that had been darkening T2 — so T2 turns bright while T1 stays bright. Bright-on-both is the only stage with that combination.
questions.imageAlt: Axial T1 bright, T2 bright, GRE bright center with dark rim, DWI bright. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 10)
questions.salient: Work the T1/T2 pair in order — Iso-Bright, Iso-Dark, Bright-Dark, Bright-Bright, Dark-Dark (IB, ID, BD, BB, DD) — for hyperacute, acute, early subacute, late subacute, chronic.
questions.learning: Hyperacute (oxyhaemoglobin, <24 h): T1 iso, T2 bright. Acute (deoxyhaemoglobin, 1-3 d): T1 iso, T2 dark. Early subacute (intracellular methaemoglobin, 3-7 d): T1 bright, T2 dark. Late subacute (extracellular methaemoglobin, 1-2 wk): T1 bright, T2 bright. Chronic (haemosiderin, >1 mo): T1 dark, T2 dark. The T1 change tracks the appearance of methaemoglobin; the T2 change tracks whether that methaemoglobin is still inside intact red cells. GRE/SWI stays dark at the rim once haemosiderin forms, and DWI can appear bright here from T2 shine-through rather than true restriction.

questions.stem: Two hours after repair of a thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm, a patient has flaccid paraplegia, urinary retention, and loss of pain and temperature sensation below T10, with preserved vibration and proprioception. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Anterior spinal artery syndrome (infarction in the territory of the artery of Adamkiewicz)

questions.explanation: The single anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord; the great radicular artery of Adamkiewicz (usually T9–L2, left) is vulnerable during aortic surgery, dissection, or hypotension. Dorsal columns (paired posterior spinal arteries) are spared. CSF drainage and MAP augmentation are used perioperatively. Fibrocartilaginous embolism and surfer's myelopathy are other vascular etiologies in young patients.

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing Parkinson disease develops severe peak-dose choreiform dyskinesias while on carbidopa/levodopa. What medication has proven efficacy in reducing levodopa-induced dyskinesias?
questions.explanation: Amantadine acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist; it is the established oral agent for reducing peak-dose dyskinesias in Parkinson disease. Entacapone prolongs levodopa half-life and may worsen dyskinesia.

questions.stem: NADH-TR stain shows central unstained zones in nearly all fibers. Diagnosis and associated risk?
questions.explanation: Central core disease. Cores devoid of oxidative activity in type 1 fibers indicate RYR1 central core disease with MH susceptibility.
questions.imageAlt: NADH-TR stain: well-demarcated central pale zones (cores) devoid of oxidative enzyme activity in nearly every fiber, with type 1 fiber predominance.
questions.salient: Cores are invisible on H&E; oxidative stains required; RYR1 dominant; avoid volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine
questions.learning: Cores lack mitochondria and sarcoplasmic reticulum; autosomal dominant RYR1; malignant hyperthermia susceptibility. Multiminicore disease (SEPN1, RYR1) shows multiple short cores. Cores are invisible on H&E; oxidative stains are required.

questions.stem: During polysomnography, what EEG waveform marks Stage N2 non-REM sleep and is generated by rhythmic burst discharges of the thalamic reticular nucleus?
questions.explanation: Stage N2 sleep is characterized by sleep spindles (11–16 Hz, typically 12–14) and K-complexes. Spindles are paced by the thalamic reticular nucleus.

questions.stem: The paired PET and MRI images shown contrast AD and FTD. When FDG-PET is ambiguous, which test best separates the two?
questions.explanation: Amyloid PET. Amyloid PET is negative in FTD; tau PET adds staging in AD. Same patient triad on two modalities. Frontal-predominant atrophy and hypometabolism with posterior sparing = bvFTD; parietal-predominant = AD. When FDG-PET is ambiguous, amyloid PET (negative in FTD) settles it. Right temporal predominant atrophy suggests the right temporal variant of FTD (prosopagnosia, behavioral change); left = semantic variant PPA.
questions.imageAlt: Top: axial FDG-PET normal, AD (temporoparietal hypometabolism, yellow arrows) and FTD (frontal hypometabolism, red arrows). Bottom: corresponding axial FLAIR showing frontal atrophy in FTD. (RITE Review deck, slide 109)

questions.stem: The coronal brain slice shown demonstrates firm pale gyri and nodules protruding into the lateral ventricle. Which first-line treatment is indicated for infantile spasms in this condition?
questions.explanation: Vigabatrin. Tuberous sclerosis (TSC1 9q34, TSC2 16p13.3): vigabatrin is first line for TSC-related spasms; everolimus for SEGA. TSC1 (9q34, hamartin) and TSC2 (16p13.3, tuberin), AD, \~2/3 de novo; mTORC1 hyperactivation. Tubers cause the epilepsy; subependymal nodules near the foramen of Monro can transform into SEGA (obstructive hydrocephalus; everolimus). Vogt triad (seizures, intellectual disability, facial angiofibromas) is present in a minority. Other criteria: hypomelanotic macules, shagreen patch, ungual fibromas, cardiac rhabdomyoma, renal angiomyolipoma, LAM. Vigabatrin is first line for TSC-related infantile spasms.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal brain slice: firm, pale, expanded gyri (cortical tubers) with blurring of the gray-white junction, and nodules protruding into the lateral ventricle (subependymal nodules, candle guttering). (Neuroradiology deck, slide 127)

questions.stem: Alpha-synuclein immunostain of cortex from a 74-year-old with fluctuating cognition and visual hallucinations. What is shown?

options.text: Cortical Lewy body with Lewy neurites

questions.explanation: Lewy body and Lewy neurites, alpha-synuclein immunostain. A dense round cytoplasmic inclusion with abundant immunoreactive neurites is a cortical Lewy body.

questions.stem: Which medication is most dangerous in this patient?
questions.explanation: Typical neuroleptics provoke severe sensitivity reactions (rigidity, autonomic instability) in DLB.
questions.imageAlt: Cortical section with a neuron containing a dense round intracytoplasmic inclusion and abundant thread-like immunoreactive neurites in the neuropil.
questions.context: Alpha-synuclein immunostain of cortex from a 74-year-old with fluctuating cognition and visual hallucinations. What is shown?
questions.salient: Cortical Lewy bodies lack the halo seen in brainstem Lewy bodies and need immunostaining; Braak: dorsal motor nucleus of X and olfactory bulb first; GCIs in oligodendrocytes define MSA
questions.learning: Brainstem Lewy bodies on H&E: eosinophilic core with pale halo. Cortical Lewy bodies lack the halo and require immunostaining. Braak staging: dorsal motor nucleus of X and olfactory bulb first, then locus coeruleus, substantia nigra, then cortex. Glial cytoplasmic inclusions in oligodendrocytes define MSA.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer disease (positive amyloid PET) is APOE ε4 homozygous and is considering lecanemab. What is the most important counseling point regarding risk?

options.text: Risk of severe hypotension during infusion
Risk of hepatotoxicity requiring LFT monitoring
Substantially increased risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA-E edema and ARIA-H hemorrhage), requiring MRI surveillance; anticoagulation increases hemorrhage risk

questions.explanation: Anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies (lecanemab, CLARITY-AD; donanemab, TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2) slow cognitive decline by roughly 25–35% over 18 months in early symptomatic AD. ARIA is most frequent in APOE ε4 homozygotes (lecanemab ARIA-E ~33% vs ~5% in non-carriers), most cases asymptomatic; baseline MRI with >4 microbleeds, CAA, or anticoagulation are exclusions. Plasma p-tau217 is emerging as a screening biomarker.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl with Down syndrome develops recurrent transient left hemiparesis provoked by crying and hyperventilation. Angiography shows bilateral stenosis of the terminal internal carotid arteries with a "puff of smoke" collateral network. What is the most effective treatment to prevent further ischemia?

options.text: Surgical revascularization (direct or indirect bypass such as EDAS)

questions.explanation: Moyamoya (Japanese for "puff of smoke") is a progressive occlusive arteriopathy of the circle of Willis; associations include Down syndrome, NF1, sickle cell disease, prior cranial irradiation, and RNF213 variants in East Asians. Hyperventilation-induced hypocapnic vasoconstriction provokes ischemia. Revascularization surgery reduces stroke recurrence; avoid hypotension and hyperventilation perioperatively.

questions.stem: Bilateral symmetric hemorrhagic necrosis of the putamen is the characteristic autopsy finding in poisoning with which toxin?
questions.explanation: Methanol is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase to toxic formic acid, which selectively targets the bilateral putamina and retinal ganglion cells. Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase.

questions.stem: A newborn is flagged on state newborn screening with homozygous deletion of SMN1 exon 7 and two copies of SMN2. He is currently asymptomatic. What is the appropriate management?

options.text: Serial examination and treat at symptom onset
Immediate initiation of disease-modifying therapy (onasemnogene abeparvovec, nusinersen, or risdiplam)

questions.explanation: SMN2 copy number inversely predicts severity (2 copies = expected type 1). Presymptomatic treatment (NURTURE, SPR1NT) yields near-normal motor milestones, so infants with ≤3 copies should be treated immediately. Onasemnogene is an AAV9 gene replacement (single IV dose, hepatotoxicity risk); nusinersen is an intrathecal splice-switching ASO; risdiplam is an oral splicing modifier.

questions.stem: The drawing shown demonstrates scapular winging with preserved deltoids. Which molecular mechanism underlies the most common form of this dystrophy?
questions.explanation: D4Z4 repeat contraction derepressing DUX4. FSHD1 is 4q35 D4Z4 contraction on a permissive 4qA haplotype; FSHD2 is SMCHD1; extraocular and bulbar muscles are spared. AD; FSHD1 is contraction of the 4q35 D4Z4 repeat (1-10 units) on a permissive 4qA haplotype, FSHD2 is SMCHD1 with hypomethylation; both derepress DUX4. Facial weakness (cannot whistle, sleeps with eyes open), asymmetric scapular winging, biceps/triceps wasting with spared deltoid (Popeye arm), Beevor sign, foot drop; retinal telangiectasia (Coats) and hearing loss in early-onset cases. Extraocular, bulbar and cardiac muscles are spared.
questions.imageAlt: Line drawing of a patient from behind with arms abducted: the scapulae wing and ride up laterally, with atrophy of the periscapular muscles and preservation of the deltoids. (RITE Review deck, slide 254)

questions.stem: Enhancing pineal mass in a 14-year-old boy with Parinaud syndrome; histology shows large clear cells and small lymphocytes. Best initial therapy after diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Germinoma. Germinomas are exquisitely radiosensitive; surgery is limited to biopsy/CSF diversion.
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal T1 post-contrast: enhancing pineal region mass. H&E: two-cell population of large polygonal neoplastic cells with clear cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli mixed with small mature lymphocytes.
questions.salient: PLAP, OCT4, c-KIT; AFP indicates nongerminomatous elements; Suprasellar site: DI, hypopituitarism; bifocal disease
questions.learning: Most common pineal tumor; also suprasellar (DI, visual loss, hypopituitarism); adolescent males; bifocal disease. Markers: PLAP, OCT4, c-KIT (CD117); beta-hCG mildly elevated in syncytiotrophoblastic variant; AFP indicates nongerminomatous elements. Exquisitely radiosensitive; Parinaud syndrome from tectal compression.

questions.stem: The lateral MR venogram labels four venous structures. Which labeled structure is the straight sinus?
questions.explanation: Cerebral venous anatomy on MR venography, lateral view. D marks the straight sinus at its junction with the vein of Galen; C is the superior sagittal sinus, F the sigmoid sinus/jugular bulb, and G the internal cerebral vein.

questions.stem: Thrombosis of the structure labeled G would most characteristically produce which imaging finding?
questions.explanation: Deep venous (internal cerebral vein/vein of Galen/straight sinus) thrombosis produces bilateral thalamic and basal ganglia venous congestion; the empty delta sign and parasagittal infarcts belong to superior sagittal sinus thrombosis; temporal hemorrhage to Labbe/transverse sinus.
questions.imageAlt: Lateral MRV. C: superior sagittal sinus. D: straight sinus at its junction with the vein of Galen. E: deep venous drainage in the region of the internal cerebral vein/basal vein. F: sigmoid sinus continuing to the jugular bulb. Second image, G: internal cerebral vein running posteriorly to join the vein of Galen.
questions.context: The lateral MR venogram labels four venous structures. Which labeled structure is the straight sinus?
questions.salient: Deep system: internal cerebral veins to vein of Galen to straight sinus; thrombosis causes bilateral thalamic edema; Labbe drains to the transverse sinus; Trolard to the SSS
questions.learning: Deep system (internal cerebral veins to vein of Galen to straight sinus) drains thalami and basal ganglia; deep venous thrombosis produces bilateral thalamic edema. Superficial system drains via SSS to torcular, transverse, sigmoid. Vein of Labbe (inferior anastomotic) to transverse sinus, vein of Trolard (superior anastomotic) to SSS.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy presents with progressive spastic paraparesis, cognitive impairment, and cutaneous bronzing (hyperpigmentation). Laboratory testing shows elevated plasma very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs). What is the defective transporter?
questions.explanation: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD) is caused by variants in ABCD1, impairing peroxisomal beta-oxidation of VLCFAs, which accumulate and destroy parieto-occipital myelin and adrenal cortical cells.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old has clumsiness, declining school performance, splenomegaly, and sudden loss of muscle tone when laughing. Examination shows inability to generate vertical saccades with preserved vestibulo-ocular reflex. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: NPC (NPC1 95%, NPC2) is a lysosomal cholesterol-trafficking disorder; vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (initially saccades) with gelastic cataplexy, dystonia, and neonatal cholestasis history is characteristic. Plasma oxysterols and lysosphingomyelin-509 have replaced filipin staining. Miglustat is used in Europe; arimoclomol and levacetylleucine received FDA approval in 2024. Gaucher type 3 also causes horizontal saccade initiation failure.

questions.stem: What visual field deficit is produced by a lesion of Meyer loop in the right temporal lobe?

options.text: Left homonymous superior quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky")
Left homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing
Left homonymous inferior quadrantanopia ("pie on the floor")

questions.explanation: Meyer loop courses through the temporal white matter around the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle, carrying fibers representing the superior visual field; lesions produce a contralateral superior quadrantanopia.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male with sudden severe "thunderclap" headache has a normal non-contrast head CT performed 9 hours after symptom onset. What is the mandatory next step in management?

options.text: Lumbar puncture for opening pressure, cell count, and spectrophotometric xanthochromia

questions.explanation: Modern-scanner CT within 6 hours of onset is ~99–100% sensitive for SAH and can reasonably exclude it in that window (Perry 2011); beyond 6 hours sensitivity falls and lumbar puncture is required to evaluate for persistent red cells across tubes and xanthochromia.

questions.stem: An infant with macrocephaly presents with severe motor regression. Brain MRI demonstrates diffuse megalencephaly with spongiform leukodystrophy involving subcortical U-fibers and deep white matter. What biochemical abnormality is diagnostic?

options.text: Elevated urine and brain N-acetylaspartic acid (NAA)

questions.explanation: Canavan disease is an autosomal recessive leukodystrophy caused by aspartoacylase deficiency (ASPA), resulting in NAA accumulation, macrocephaly, and spongiform degeneration.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a left hemispheric TIA has the carotid angiogram shown, which demonstrates an ulcerated plaque with occlusion of the proximal ICA. What is the appropriate management of the occluded vessel?

options.text: Medical management; complete occlusion is not a revascularization indication

questions.explanation: Medical management; complete occlusion is not a revascularization indication. Endarterectomy benefits symptomatic 70-99% stenosis; a chronically occluded ICA is managed medically. Deck teaching point: distinguish plaque-related occlusion from dissection (tapered flame-shaped occlusion, intramural hematoma on fat-sat T1) and note that a complete occlusion is not an endarterectomy indication. Symptomatic 70-99% stenosis benefits from CEA within 2 weeks of the event.
questions.imageAlt: Carotid angiograms (A, lateral; B, magnified): irregular ulcerated plaque at the ICA origin with occlusion of the proximal ICA; distal vessels fill via collaterals. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 73)

questions.stem: A 5-year-old from an endemic region has hydrocephalus; post-contrast MRI shows multiple small enhancing nodules along the ventricles and parenchyma, and CT shows calcified nodules and subcortical cysts. Highest on the differential?
questions.explanation: Neurocysticercosis with hydrocephalus in a 5-year-old. Multiple cystic, ring-enhancing, and calcified lesions with hydrocephalus in an endemic-region child indicate neurocysticercosis across colloidal to calcified stages.

questions.stem: Before starting albendazole, which examination is mandatory?
questions.explanation: Antiparasitic-induced inflammation of an intraocular cyst can cause blindness.
questions.imageAlt: A, B: post-contrast axial T1 with dilated lateral ventricles and multiple small enhancing nodules along the ventricular walls and in the parenchyma. C: CT with ventriculomegaly, calcified subependymal nodules, and subcortical hypodense lesions.
questions.context: A 5-year-old from an endemic region has hydrocephalus; post-contrast MRI shows multiple small enhancing nodules along the ventricles and parenchyma, and CT shows calcified nodules and subcortical cysts. Highest on the differential?
questions.salient: Stages: vesicular (scolex), colloidal (ring), granular-nodular, calcified; Albendazole plus steroids for viable cysts; intraventricular cysts need endoscopic removal; exclude ocular disease
questions.learning: Stages: vesicular (scolex, no edema), colloidal vesicular (ring enhancement, edema, seizures), granular nodular, calcified. Albendazole with corticosteroids for viable parenchymal cysts; calcified lesions need no antiparasitic therapy but can still seed seizures. Intraventricular and subarachnoid (racemose) disease: endoscopic removal or prolonged therapy, shunting for hydrocephalus. Ophthalmologic examination before treatment.
questions.note: Low confidence; no clinical data beyond age.

questions.stem: Inferior view of a brain from a motor vehicle collision victim. The lesion distribution reflects:

options.text: Coup/contrecoup contusions against the skull base

questions.explanation: Orbitofrontal and temporal pole contusions, gross. Orbitofrontal and temporal pole contusions occur where the brain impacts the rough anterior and middle fossa floors.
questions.imageAlt: Inferior surface of the brain with hemorrhagic discoloration of the orbitofrontal gyri and temporal poles.
questions.salient: Contusions involve gyral crests; infarcts involve sulcal depths; Old contusions: golden-brown plaques jaunes
questions.learning: Brain impacts the rough anterior and middle fossa floors; contrecoup contusions are typically larger than coup. Contusions involve the crests of gyri (versus infarcts, which involve depths). Old contusions become golden-brown plaques jaunes.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes has stepwise cognitive decline, executive dysfunction, gait apraxia, and pseudobulbar affect. MRI shows confluent periventricular white matter disease with multiple lacunes. What is the diagnosis, and what most effectively slows progression?

options.text: Vascular cognitive impairment (subcortical ischemic/Binswanger type); aggressive vascular risk factor control

questions.explanation: Vascular cognitive impairment is the second most common dementia and commonly coexists with AD pathology. Executive slowing predominates over amnesia; the hippocampus is relatively spared. SPRINT-MIND showed intensive BP control reduces MCI. Cholinesterase inhibitors have marginal benefit. Consider CADASIL in early-onset cases without risk factors.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with severe bilateral optic neuritis and a longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis spanning C2–T4, with intractable hiccups. She was previously started on interferon-beta for presumed MS and worsened. What test is most likely positive, and which therapy is appropriate for relapse prevention?

options.text: Anti-AQP4 IgG (cell-based assay); eculizumab, inebilizumab, satralizumab, or rituximab

questions.explanation: NMOSD is an astrocytopathy driven by AQP4-IgG; area postrema syndrome (hiccups/vomiting) is a core feature. Interferon-beta, natalizumab, fingolimod, and alemtuzumab worsen NMOSD. Acute attacks receive IV methylprednisolone and early plasma exchange; approved maintenance agents target complement (eculizumab, ravulizumab), CD19 (inebilizumab), or IL-6R (satralizumab).

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man arrives in convulsive status epilepticus that persists after adequate benzodiazepine dosing. According to the ESETT trial, how do intravenous levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, and valproate compare as second-line agents?

options.text: All three are similarly effective (~45–47% seizure cessation at 60 minutes) with similar safety
Fosphenytoin is superior in seizure cessation
Levetiracetam is superior with fewer adverse events

questions.explanation: ESETT (Kapur 2019) randomized benzodiazepine-refractory status to levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, or valproate 40 mg/kg; each stopped seizures with improved responsiveness in roughly half of patients with no significant difference in efficacy or safety across ages. Underdosing of first-line benzodiazepines remains the most common error.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old child presents with diabetes insipidus, bitemporal visual field loss, and growth deceleration. Head CT demonstrates a cystic suprasellar mass with prominent rim calcification. Pathology reveals "wet keratin" nodules. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Adamantinomatous craniopharyngiomas are suprasellar, calcified cystic tumors of childhood containing "machine-oil" fluid and wet keratin; they carry CTNNB1 mutations, whereas adult papillary craniopharyngiomas carry BRAF V600E.

questions.stem: Which feature favors a conus medullaris lesion over a cauda equina lesion?

options.text: Strictly lower motor neuron signs with late bladder involvement
Early and symmetric saddle anesthesia with early sphincter dysfunction and mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs
Asymmetric, severe radicular leg pain with early onset

questions.explanation: The conus (L1–L2 vertebral level) contains sacral segments, so lesions cause early, symmetric saddle anesthesia and sphincter failure, sparing leg strength but adding Babinski signs. Cauda equina lesions compress lumbosacral roots asymmetrically with prominent radicular pain, areflexia, and later sphincter dysfunction. Both are surgical emergencies; decompression within 48 hours improves bladder outcome.

questions.stem: A man with HIV (CD4 60 cells/µL) presents with 2 weeks of headache and diplopia; CSF opening pressure is 380 mm H2O with cryptococcal antigen positive. What are the key management steps?

options.text: Liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine induction; serial therapeutic lumbar punctures for elevated pressure; defer ART 4–6 weeks to avoid IRIS

questions.explanation: Cryptococcal meningitis mortality is driven by intracranial hypertension; LP to reduce pressure is therapeutic. Single high-dose liposomal amphotericin with flucytosine and fluconazole (AMBITION) is now WHO-preferred. Early ART increases mortality via IRIS (COAT trial), so ART is deferred 4–6 weeks. Serum CrAg screening at CD4 <100 identifies preclinical infection.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with progressive spastic paraparesis has the thoracic MRI shown. The subarachnoid space is widened above and below the lesion and the cord is displaced. In which compartment is the lesion?
questions.explanation: Intradural extramedullary. Widening of the SAS adjacent to the mass is the classic sign of an intradural extramedullary lesion; intramedullary lesions expand the cord, extradural lesions efface the SAS. Localization is the question: intramedullary (ependymoma, astrocytoma, hemangioblastoma) expands the cord; extradural lesions efface the SAS. Not lipoma, which would be T1 bright. Spinal meningiomas: 90% intradural extramedullary, \~80% thoracic, strong female predominance, 98% solitary; multiple lesions or a pediatric case implies NF2.
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal T1 thoracic spine: well-circumscribed intradural mass (arrow) displacing and compressing the cord with widening of the subarachnoid space above and below the lesion, the classic sign of an intradural extramedullary location. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 17)

questions.stem: The FDG-PET shown demonstrates temporoparietal hypometabolism. Which pattern would suggest frontotemporal dementia instead?
questions.explanation: Frontal and anterior temporal hypometabolism. AD temporoparietal/posterior cingulate; FTD frontal; DLB occipital. Temporoparietal and posterior cingulate hypometabolism precedes atrophy and correlates with tau burden. Compare FTD (frontal/anterior temporal) and DLB (occipital with cingulate island sign).
questions.imageAlt: Axial FDG-PET, control versus AD: reduced tracer uptake in bilateral temporoparietal cortex with relatively preserved frontal, sensorimotor and occipital metabolism. (RITE Review deck, slide 74)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man wakes unable to move his legs. MRI shows restricted diffusion in the anterior cord and the axial T2 sign shown. Which sensory modality is expected to be preserved?
questions.explanation: Vibration and proprioception. Anterior spinal artery infarct spares the dorsal columns (posterior spinal arteries); pain/temperature and motor function are lost bilaterally. Anterior cord syndrome: acute bilateral paralysis, loss of pain/temperature, sparing of proprioception/vibration (dorsal columns), sphincter dysfunction. Causes: aortic dissection/surgery, atherosclerosis, cholesterol embolus, hypotension, vasculitis, fibrocartilaginous embolism. The ASA is a single midline vessel fed by the artery of Adamkiewicz (T9-L2, left side in 75%); the paired PSAs protect the dorsal columns.
questions.imageAlt: Axial DWI (restricted diffusion in the anterior cord), axial T2 (bilateral anterior-horn hyperintensity, the snake-eyes or owl\'s-eyes sign), and sagittal T2 (long-segment anterior cord signal). (Neuroradiology deck, slide 43)

questions.stem: Coronal brain slice with a variegated hemorrhagic necrotic infiltrative mass. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hemorrhagic necrotic glioblastoma, gross. Variegated necrotic hemorrhagic mass with infiltrative margins is GBM; melanoma metastases are usually multiple and well circumscribed.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal slice with a large, poorly circumscribed variegated mass in the frontotemporal white matter with hemorrhage, yellow necrosis, and mass effect.
questions.salient: Pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation; IDH-wildtype by definition; MGMT methylation predicts temozolomide response
questions.learning: Grossly infiltrative, crosses the corpus callosum. Microscopy: pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation. Metastatic melanoma, choriocarcinoma, renal cell, and thyroid are the classically hemorrhagic metastases.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old with headache, encephalopathy and multifocal infarcts has the angiogram shown. Which statement about this finding is correct?

options.text: It excludes reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome
Brain and leptomeningeal biopsy remains the reference standard
MRA is more sensitive than catheter angiography for distal disease
It is specific for primary CNS angiitis

questions.explanation: Brain and leptomeningeal biopsy remains the reference standard. Beading is seen in RCVS, atherosclerosis and infection; small-vessel vasculitis is often angiographically occult. Beading is not specific: RCVS (thunderclap headache, normalizes within 12 weeks), intracranial atherosclerosis, infection and moyamoya can look identical. Angiography sensitivity for primary CNS angiitis is only moderate because small vessels are below resolution; brain-leptomeningeal biopsy remains the reference standard. MRA/CTA miss distal disease.
questions.imageAlt: Lateral carotid angiogram: multifocal segmental narrowing and dilatation (beading) of medium and small intracranial arteries with distal irregularity. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 55)

questions.stem: The plaque shown has a dense core and halo with dystrophic neurites. Which scoring system counts this plaque type?
questions.explanation: CERAD. Neuritic plaques are scored by CERAD; diffuse plaques occur in normal aging. Neuritic plaques (with tau-positive dystrophic neurites) are the ones counted in CERAD scoring; diffuse plaques lack neurites and occur in normal aging. Plaque core is A-beta 1-42 derived from APP cleavage by beta and gamma secretase; APP triplication in Down syndrome produces early AD pathology universally by age 40.
questions.imageAlt: Cortex (silver-type stain): extracellular spherical plaque 60-120 microns across with a dense amyloid core, a clear halo, and a corona of swollen, distorted dystrophic neurites. (RITE Review deck, slide 92)

questions.stem: Cerebellar vermis tumor in a 6-year-old. Histology with Homer Wright rosettes. Which molecular group carries the best prognosis?
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma. WNT-activated medulloblastoma (CTNNB1) has >90% survival; group 3 (MYC) is worst.
questions.imageAlt: Densely packed small round blue cells with scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei; Homer Wright rosettes (cells around a central neuropil core).
questions.salient: Small round blue cells, synaptophysin positive, CSF drop metastases; Hyperdense on CT; taurine peak on MRS
questions.learning: Synaptophysin positive. Molecular groups: WNT (best prognosis, CTNNB1), SHH (infants and adults, PTCH1/SUFU, desmoplastic/nodular), group 3 (MYC, worst), group 4 (most common). Midline vermis in children, hyperdense on CT, CSF dissemination; MRS shows taurine peak.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with brief flexor spasms in clusters. EEG shows high-voltage, chaotic, disorganized background activity with multifocal spikes (hypsarrhythmia). What is the first-line medical therapy?

options.text: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), high-dose oral prednisolone, or vigabatrin

questions.explanation: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (West syndrome) features spasms, developmental regression, and hypsarrhythmia. ACTH or high-dose prednisolone are first-line; vigabatrin is first-line when tuberous sclerosis is the cause.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old male presents with right wrist drop and weakness of finger extension. Forearm supination is weak with the elbow extended, and the brachioradialis reflex is absent. Triceps strength and the triceps reflex are normal. Where is the radial nerve injured?

options.text: Superficial radial sensory branch at the wrist
Posterior interosseous nerve at the arcade of Frohse

questions.explanation: Radial nerve compression in the spiral groove ("Saturday night palsy") spares the triceps branch (which arises proximally in the axilla) but paralyzes the brachioradialis, supinator, and wrist/finger extensors. Posterior interosseous neuropathy spares brachioradialis and sensation.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child presents with spasticity, gait unsteadiness, and peripheral neuropathy. MRI demonstrates symmetric cerebral demyelination sparing the subcortical U-fibers. Peripheral nerve biopsy shows metachromatic storage granules on toluidine blue staining. What enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: Metachromatic leukodystrophy (MLD) is caused by arylsulfatase A deficiency, resulting in sulfatide accumulation that spares subcortical U-fibers and causes a demyelinating peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with asymmetric limb weakness, fasciculations, and brisk reflexes has a sister with similar disease and a father who died with behavioral-variant FTD. What is the most likely genetic cause, and which approved therapy targets a different familial ALS gene?

options.text: C9orf72 GGGGCC hexanucleotide expansion; tofersen for SOD1-ALS

questions.explanation: C9orf72 repeat expansion is the most common cause of familial ALS and FTD (~40% of familial ALS in European populations); it is missed by exome sequencing. Tofersen, an intrathecal ASO against SOD1, received accelerated approval in 2023 based on neurofilament reduction. Riluzole extends survival by ~3 months; edaravone and sodium phenylbutyrate-taurursodiol have modest or contested benefit (the latter was withdrawn in 2024 after PHOENIX failed).

questions.stem: An infant with severe hypotonia, poor feeding requiring gavage, hypogonadism, and almond-shaped eyes develops hyperphagia and obesity by age 3. What single test detects the causative mechanisms with the highest yield?

options.text: DNA methylation analysis of the 15q11-q13 imprinting center

questions.explanation: Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of paternally expressed genes at 15q11-q13 (paternal deletion ~65%, maternal uniparental disomy ~30%, imprinting defect ~2–5%). Methylation testing detects >99% regardless of mechanism; microarray detects only deletion. Growth hormone improves body composition and development. Maternal UPD carries higher psychosis risk. The mirror-image disorder of Q25 (Angelman) reflects the parent-of-origin logic of imprinted loci.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has a 10-year history of bilateral 6–8 Hz postural and kinetic hand tremor that improves with alcohol; his mother and grandfather were affected. What are the first-line pharmacologic options?
questions.explanation: Essential tremor is the most common adult movement disorder; propranolol and primidone have level A evidence (each reduces tremor ~50%). Topiramate and gabapentin are second-line. VIM thalamic DBS or MR-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy is used for refractory cases. Cerebellar Purkinje cell pathology is implicated; ET may carry modest increased PD risk.

questions.stem: Brainstem sections from a patient who died after a large supratentorial hemorrhage. What are the lesions?
questions.explanation: Duret hemorrhages of the brainstem, gross. Midline and paramedian hemorrhages in the midbrain and pons after herniation are Duret hemorrhages from stretched basilar perforators.
questions.imageAlt: Transverse sections of the midbrain and rostral pons with multiple midline and paramedian hemorrhages in the tegmentum and base.
questions.salient: Ventral paramedian location distinguishes Duret from primary pontine hemorrhage (lateral tegmental); Marks downward herniation; usually fatal
questions.learning: Caudal displacement stretches and tears paramedian perforating branches of the basilar artery; ventral pontine and midbrain location. Distinguish from primary pontine hypertensive hemorrhage (lateral tegmental, larger, single) and hemorrhagic cavernoma.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old with a single seizure. CT, sagittal T2 gradient echo, and T2 spin echo are shown. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Cavernous malformation on gradient echo. A round lesion with marked GRE blooming and a hemosiderin rim on spin echo (popcorn) is a cavernoma; AVMs show flow voids.
questions.imageAlt: A: noncontrast CT with subtle hyperdensity in the right temporal lobe. B: sagittal T2 gradient echo: round markedly hypointense lesion with blooming. C: T2 spin echo showing a small mixed-signal lesion with a dark rim.
questions.salient: GRE/SWI far more sensitive than spin echo; angiographically occult; Familial CCM1/KRIT1 (Hispanic founder), CCM2, CCM3/PDCD10 (most aggressive)
questions.learning: Angiographically occult; GRE/SWI far more sensitive than spin echo. Familial forms (CCM1/KRIT1, CCM2, CCM3/PDCD10) are multiple, especially Hispanic-American CCM1 founder mutation. Annual hemorrhage risk ~1 to 3%, higher after prior bleed and in brainstem.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl develops subacute generalized chorea, emotional lability, and hypotonia 6 weeks after pharyngitis; ASO titer is elevated. What is the diagnosis and what is required in management beyond symptomatic chorea therapy?

options.text: Sydenham chorea; echocardiography and secondary penicillin prophylaxis to prevent rheumatic carditis

questions.explanation: Sydenham chorea is a major Jones criterion of acute rheumatic fever, mediated by antibodies cross-reacting with basal ganglia antigens (dopamine D2 receptor, lysoganglioside); chorea alone establishes the diagnosis. It is usually self-limited over months, with recurrence in ~20%. Chorea is treated with valproate, carbamazepine, or dopamine blockers; steroids or IVIG for severe cases. Prophylactic penicillin continues at least until age 21.

questions.stem: The imaging shown is from a patient whose hemorrhage occurred 3 years ago. Which finding is expected to persist indefinitely?

options.text: A hypointense rim on gradient-echo imaging

questions.explanation: A hypointense rim on gradient-echo imaging. Hemosiderin-laden macrophages remain at the margin permanently; the cavity itself follows fluid signal and edema resolves. Ferritin/hemosiderin are superparamagnetic (10\^3-10\^4 unpaired electrons per aggregate) and remain in macrophages indefinitely; the GRE/SWI rim is permanent. Mnemonic: Die Die for the rim. Full sequence: I Bleed, I Die, Bleed Die, Bleed Bleed, Die Die.
questions.imageAlt: Axial T1, T2, GRE, DWI: cavity is T1 dark / T2 bright (hemichromes and fluid, no paramagnetism); rim is dark on all sequences, most conspicuous on GRE. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 11)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man after massive intracerebral hemorrhage is unresponsive with absent brainstem reflexes 24 hours after admission. Core temperature is 36.5°C, systolic BP 110, no sedatives for 5 half-lives, and no confounding metabolic derangement. During the apnea test, what arterial blood gas result supports the determination of death by neurologic criteria?

options.text: PaCO2 ≥60 mm Hg (or ≥20 mm Hg above baseline) with pH <7.30 and no respiratory effort

questions.explanation: The 2023 AAN/AAP/CNS/SCCM consensus requires a known catastrophic irreversible cause, exclusion of confounders (hypothermia, drugs, severe metabolic derangement), coma, absent brainstem reflexes, and apnea with adequate hypercapnic stimulus. Ancillary tests (catheter angiography, nuclear perfusion, TCD) are reserved for when clinical examination or apnea testing cannot be completed; EEG is no longer recommended.

questions.stem: The electron micrograph shown demonstrates concentric Schwann cell lamellae around an axon. Which nerve conduction pattern is expected in the most common hereditary cause?

options.text: Uniform slowing below 38 m/s without conduction block
Absent sensory responses with normal motor studies

questions.explanation: Uniform slowing below 38 m/s without conduction block. Onion bulbs indicate demyelination/remyelination; CMT1A (PMP22 duplication) shows uniform slowing, CIDP non-uniform slowing with block. Onion bulbs indicate repeated demyelination and remyelination: CMT1A (PMP22 duplication, most common), Dejerine-Sottas (CMT3, PMP22/MPZ point mutations, CV <10 m/s), CIDP, Refsum disease and hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies (tomacula). CMT1 shows uniformly slow conduction velocities (<38 m/s ulnar) without conduction block; CIDP shows non-uniform slowing, block and temporal dispersion.
questions.imageAlt: Electron micrograph: a myelinated axon encircled by concentric lamellae of Schwann cell processes and collagen (onion bulb). (RITE Review deck, slide 256)

questions.stem: Ubiquitin/TDP-43 immunostain of frontal cortex from a 62-year-old with disinhibition and loss of empathy. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration, ubiquitin/TDP-43 immunostain. Neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions positive for ubiquitin/TDP-43 with loss of nuclear TDP-43 define FTLD-TDP.

questions.stem: Which gene is most likely if the patient's brother had ALS?
questions.explanation: C9orf72 hexanucleotide expansion is the commonest cause of familial FTD-ALS.
questions.imageAlt: Cortical neurons with brown granular cytoplasmic immunoreactivity and dense compact cytoplasmic inclusions; some neurons show loss of normal nuclear staining. Marginal notes: 62-year-old with behavioral disorder and inappropriate social behavior; anti-ubiquitin staining, tau negative, TDP-43.
questions.context: Ubiquitin/TDP-43 immunostain of frontal cortex from a 62-year-old with disinhibition and loss of empathy. Diagnosis?
questions.salient: FTLD-TDP types A (GRN), B (C9orf72, with ALS), C (semantic), D (VCP); FTLD-tau: Pick (3R), PSP and CBD (4R), MAPT
questions.learning: FTLD-TDP is characterized by neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions and loss of nuclear TDP-43. Subtypes A (GRN), B (C9orf72, with ALS), C (semantic variant, long dystrophic neurites), D (VCP). FTLD-tau: Pick disease (3R), CBD and PSP (4R), MAPT mutations. FTLD-FUS: young onset, severe caudate atrophy.

questions.stem: A patient presents with subacute painful sensorimotor polyneuropathy, abdominal cramping, and transverse white lines across the fingernails (Mees lines). What heavy metal toxicity is this?
questions.explanation: Arsenic poisoning presents with gastrointestinal distress, painful sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy, hyperkeratosis, and Mees lines (also seen in thallium, which adds alopecia). Lead causes a motor-predominant neuropathy (wrist drop).

questions.stem: Axial T1 and sagittal T2 in an infant with infantile spasms. What is the malformation?
questions.explanation: Agenesis of the corpus callosum. Parallel lateral ventricles with colpocephaly and radiating medial sulci define callosal agenesis.

questions.stem: This infant is a girl with chorioretinal lacunae. Which inheritance pattern and mechanism apply?
questions.explanation: Aicardi syndrome occurs almost exclusively in females (and XXY males), consistent with X-linked dominance with male lethality.
questions.imageAlt: Axial T1: parallel, widely separated lateral ventricles with disproportionate dilation of the occipital horns (colpocephaly). Sagittal T2: absent corpus callosum with medial hemispheric sulci radiating toward the third ventricle (sunburst pattern) and high-riding third ventricle.
questions.context: Axial T1 and sagittal T2 in an infant with infantile spasms. What is the malformation?
questions.salient: Colpocephaly, high-riding third ventricle, Probst bundles, sunburst medial sulci; Aicardi syndrome: girls, spasms, chorioretinal lacunae
questions.learning: Associations: Aicardi syndrome (girls, infantile spasms, chorioretinal lacunae), Chiari II, Dandy-Walker, inborn errors (nonketotic hyperglycinemia, PDH deficiency), >200 genetic syndromes. Probst bundles run longitudinally along the medial ventricular walls.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with disinhibition and loss of empathy has the imaging shown. Which protein is most likely to be found in the inclusions at autopsy if this is Pick disease?
questions.explanation: 3-repeat tau. Pick bodies are 3R tau; PSP and CBD are 4R; most non-tau FTLD is TDP-43. Lobar atrophy with a sharp anterior-posterior gradient is the imaging correlate of bvFTD and semantic variant PPA. Pick disease is now the FTLD-tau (3R) subtype with Pick bodies; TDP-43 (progranulin, C9orf72) and FUS account for most of the rest. Onset typically 45-65, roughly equal to AD in prevalence in that age range.
questions.imageAlt: Axial CT and sagittal T1 images: severe, disproportionate atrophy of the frontal and anterior temporal lobes with knife-edge gyri and widened sylvian fissures; posterior cortex relatively preserved. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 95)

questions.stem: Cerebellar cyst with mural nodule in a 35-year-old; histology shows vacuolated stromal cells among capillaries. What systemic condition must be excluded?
questions.explanation: Hemangioblastoma. Hemangioblastoma in a young patient or with multiple lesions suggests VHL (3p25).
questions.imageAlt: Abundant thin-walled capillary vessels interspersed with large stromal cells having clear, lipid-laden vacuolated cytoplasm.
questions.salient: Stromal cell is neoplastic (inhibin-alpha); polycythemia from EPO; VHL: renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, retinal angiomas
questions.learning: Cerebellar cyst with mural nodule in adults; the stromal cell is the neoplastic element (inhibin-alpha positive). von Hippel-Lindau (VHL, 3p25) when multiple, spinal, retinal, or young; VHL also causes renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic cysts. Secondary polycythemia from erythropoietin production.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old with headache that resolves when lying flat has the post-contrast MRI shown. Which additional finding would be expected?

options.text: Sagging of the brainstem with tonsillar descent

questions.explanation: Sagging of the brainstem with tonsillar descent. SEEPS: subdural collections, pachymeningeal enhancement, venous engorgement, pituitary hyperemia, sagging brain; enhancement is smooth and dural, not leptomeningeal. Monro-Kellie: CSF loss is compensated by venous and dural engorgement. SEEPS: subdural fluid collections, enhancement of pachymeninges, engorgement of veins, pituitary hyperemia, sagging brain (tonsillar descent, flattened pons, narrowed prepontine cistern). Orthostatic headache; opening pressure low but can be normal. Enhancement is dural and smooth, not leptomeningeal and nodular as in meningitis or carcinomatosis. Treat with epidural blood patch; look for a spinal leak or CSF-venous fistula.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal post-contrast T1: smooth, diffuse, thick pachymeningeal (dural) enhancement with engorged venous sinuses. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 84)

questions.stem: Panels show small angular fibers, ATPase fiber type grouping, and group atrophy. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Denervation atrophy. Angular atrophic fibers (acute denervation), fiber type grouping (reinnervation), and group atrophy (loss of reinnervated units) indicate chronic denervation.
questions.imageAlt: H&E: small angular atrophic fibers scattered among normal fibers. ATPase: large groups of uniform fiber type (fiber type grouping). H&E: group atrophy of contiguous fibers.
questions.salient: Target fibers = denervation; type 2 atrophy alone is nonspecific; Seen in ALS, SMA, chronic polyneuropathy
questions.learning: Angular atrophic fibers and target fibers indicate acute denervation; fiber type grouping indicates collateral reinnervation; group atrophy indicates loss of a reinnervated motor unit (chronic, e.g., ALS, SMA). Type 2 atrophy alone is nonspecific (disuse, steroids, cachexia).

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman reports 3 weeks of new temporal headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and polymyalgia; ESR is 92 mm/h. What is the correct sequence of management?

options.text: Temporal artery biopsy first, then start prednisone if positive
Obtain ophthalmology consultation and defer treatment until vision changes occur
Start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately and obtain temporal artery biopsy within 1–2 weeks

questions.explanation: Giant cell arteritis threatens permanent vision loss (arteritic AION); steroids must not be delayed for biopsy, which remains diagnostic for at least 1–2 weeks after treatment starts. Temporal artery ultrasound (halo sign) is an alternative. Tocilizumab (IL-6R) is approved as a steroid-sparing agent (GiACTA).

questions.stem: The histology shown demonstrates serpiginous necrosis rimmed by palisading nuclei. Which growth factor is upregulated by the palisading cells?
questions.explanation: VEGF. Hypoxic pseudopalisading cells express VEGF, driving neovascularization and the rationale for bevacizumab. Pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular (endothelial) proliferation are the two features that define grade 4 histologically in diffuse astrocytic tumors. The palisading cells are hypoxic, migrating tumor cells around a vaso-occlusive focus, which drives VEGF expression (basis for bevacizumab).
questions.imageAlt: H&E: serpiginous zones of necrosis bordered by densely packed, hyperchromatic tumor nuclei arranged in a palisade. (RITE Review deck, slide 23)

questions.stem: Coronal post-contrast T1 with linear enhancement following sulci and cerebellar folia in a woman with breast cancer. Highest on the differential?
questions.explanation: Diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement. Sulcal (pial) enhancement in a cancer patient indicates leptomeningeal metastasis; hypotension gives sulcus-sparing dural enhancement.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal post-gadolinium T1: linear enhancement following the sulci and cerebellar folia, extending along pial surfaces, with no parenchymal mass.
questions.salient: Leptomeningeal versus pachymeningeal pattern; CSF cytology ~50% sensitive on first tap; repeat large-volume taps
questions.learning: Leptomeningeal (pial/sulcal) enhancement versus pachymeningeal (dural, smooth, spares sulci: intracranial hypotension, post-surgical, IgG4, dural mets). CSF cytology sensitivity ~50% on first tap; repeat large-volume taps.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old female presents with progressive behavioral changes: uninhibited social spending, loss of empathy, hyperorality, and compulsive hoarding. Neuroimaging shows circumscribed frontal and anterior temporal lobar atrophy. Pathology reveals argyrophilic tau inclusions (Pick bodies). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pick disease is a 3-repeat (3R) tauopathy producing focal "knife-edge" frontotemporal atrophy, behavioral disinhibition, and round silver-staining Pick bodies. bvFTD overall is roughly half tau and half TDP-43 pathology; C9orf72, GRN, and MAPT are the major genes.

questions.stem: A patient with a ventricular drain develops fever; the post-contrast image shown demonstrates linear ependymal enhancement. Which additional finding supports ventriculitis over tumor dissemination?

options.text: Layering intraventricular debris with restricted diffusion

questions.explanation: Layering intraventricular debris with restricted diffusion. Pyogenic ventriculitis produces smooth ependymal enhancement with DWI-bright pus; nodular enhancement suggests CSF tumor spread. Ependymal enhancement with intraventricular debris (DWI-bright layering) is the picture of pyogenic ventriculitis, typically after shunt/EVD infection or rupture of an abscess into the ventricle. Deck\'s differential for ependymal enhancement: CSF dissemination of tumor (medulloblastoma, choroid plexus papilloma, ependymoma, lymphoma), TS subependymal nodules, and transependymal CSF flow (which is FLAIR signal, not enhancement).
questions.imageAlt: Axial post-contrast T1: smooth linear enhancement of the ependymal lining of the lateral ventricles (arrow) with ventricular enlargement. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 131)

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with progressive limb ataxia, pigmentary retinopathy, acanthocytes on a peripheral blood smear, and undetectable serum LDL and VLDL. What is the primary therapy to halt progression?
questions.explanation: Abetalipoproteinemia (Bassen-Kornzweig disease) impairs fat-soluble vitamin absorption due to microsomal triglyceride transfer protein deficiency; massive oral vitamin E prevents sensory ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant presents with macrocephaly, regression of developmental milestones, and prominent bilateral frontal white matter T2 hyperintensity. Brain biopsy demonstrates Rosenthal fibers within astrocyte cytoplasm. What gene is mutated?
questions.explanation: Alexander disease is caused by de novo dominant toxic gain-of-function variants in GFAP, resulting in macrocephaly, frontal-predominant leukodystrophy, and diagnostic intracytoplasmic Rosenthal fibers in astrocytes.

questions.stem: Occlusion of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) produces the lateral pontine syndrome. What clinical deficit distinguishes lateral pontine infarction from lateral medullary (Wallenberg) infarction?

options.text: Ipsilateral peripheral facial paralysis and sensorineural hearing loss
Contralateral loss of pain and temperature on the body

questions.explanation: AICA supplies the lateral caudal pons and gives rise to the labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery; occlusion damages the CN VII nucleus/fascicle and CN VIII root/cochlear nuclei, causing ipsilateral facial palsy and deafness.

questions.stem: Noncontrast CT with dense blood in the anterior interhemispheric fissure and gyrus rectus. Most likely source?
questions.explanation: Ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm with gyrus rectus hematoma. Interhemispheric and gyrus rectus blood localizes to ACoA.

questions.stem: Which trial finding governs prevention of delayed cerebral ischemia here?
questions.explanation: Nimodipine improves outcome without reliably reducing angiographic vasospasm; magnesium, statins, and prophylactic triple-H failed.
questions.imageAlt: Noncontrast CT: dense hemorrhage in the anterior interhemispheric fissure and inferior frontal region (gyrus rectus) with surrounding hypodensity and intraventricular extension. Marginal differential: amyloid, AVM, met, berry aneurysm, contusion.
questions.context: Noncontrast CT with dense blood in the anterior interhemispheric fissure and gyrus rectus. Most likely source?
questions.salient: Sylvian = MCA; medial temporal = PCoA (with CN III palsy); Nimodipine 21 days; secure within 24 to 72 hours
questions.learning: Location predicts the aneurysm: interhemispheric/gyrus rectus = ACoA; sylvian fissure = MCA; medial temporal = PCoM (also CN III palsy). CTA is first line; catheter angiography if negative with diffuse SAH. Nimodipine for 21 days; secure within 24 to 72 hours.

questions.stem: The MRI shown demonstrates a conus extending into the sacrum and adherent to the dorsal canal. Why is prophylactic untethering usually recommended even in asymptomatic children?

options.text: Deficits from traction are poorly reversible once established

questions.explanation: Deficits from traction are poorly reversible once established. Retethering after prior repair is diagnosed clinically because a low conus is expected postoperatively. Prophylactic untethering is generally offered even in asymptomatic children because deficits are poorly reversible once established. Retethering after myelomeningocele repair presents the same way and is diagnosed clinically; a low conus is expected postoperatively and is not itself diagnostic.
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal T1 (A), T2 (B) and axial (C) lumbosacral spine: the conus is dragged into the sacrum and adheres to the posterior aspect of the canal. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 53)

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with learning difficulties, macrocephaly, multiple café-au-lait spots, and axillary freckling. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy reveals pigmented iris hamartomas (Lisch nodules). What gene is mutated?
questions.explanation: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is caused by loss-of-function variants in NF1 on chromosome 17q11.2, encoding the Ras-GAP neurofibromin. Learning disability is common; frank intellectual disability is uncommon.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with migraine with aura, mood disturbance, and two lacunar strokes has a mother and uncle with early-onset dementia. MRI shows confluent white matter hyperintensities involving the anterior temporal poles and external capsules. What gene and diagnostic tissue finding confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: NOTCH3; granular osmiophilic material in vascular smooth muscle on skin biopsy

questions.explanation: CADASIL is the most common monogenic small-vessel disease, caused by cysteine-altering NOTCH3 variants in EGF-like repeats. Anterior temporal pole involvement is highly specific. Genetic testing has largely replaced skin biopsy. Biallelic HTRA1 causes CARASIL (alopecia, spondylosis).

questions.stem: Biopsy of a destructive sacral mass in a patient with leg weakness and incontinence. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chordoma of the sacrum, H&E. Physaliphorous (bubbly vacuolated) cells in myxoid matrix define chordoma.
questions.imageAlt: Cords and nests of large vacuolated (physaliphorous, bubbly) cells in an abundant basophilic myxoid matrix. Marginal note: lower-extremity weakness, sensory loss, bowel and bladder dysfunction, bony destruction of the sacrum.
questions.salient: Brachyury (TBXT) nuclear positivity is diagnostic; keratin and S100 positive (chondrosarcoma is keratin negative); Sacrum and clivus; en bloc resection plus proton therapy
questions.learning: Notochordal remnant tumor: sacrococcygeal (50%), clivus (35%), vertebral bodies. Brachyury (TBXT) nuclear positivity is diagnostic; also cytokeratin and S100 positive (versus chondrosarcoma, keratin negative). Locally destructive, radioresistant; en bloc resection plus proton therapy.

questions.stem: Six days after aneurysmal SAH, a patient's serum sodium falls to 126 mEq/L with urine sodium 90 mEq/L and urine osmolality 500 mOsm/kg. She is clinically hypovolemic with negative fluid balance and rising hematocrit. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

options.text: Cerebral salt wasting; isotonic or hypertonic saline replacement and fludrocortisone

questions.explanation: SIADH and cerebral salt wasting both produce hyponatremia with high urine sodium and osmolality; volume status is the discriminator. Fluid restriction in SAH-associated CSW precipitates delayed cerebral ischemia, so euvolemia with salt repletion is mandatory. SIADH is treated with fluid restriction, salt tablets, or urea; hypertonic saline for symptomatic severe hyponatremia in either.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with developmental delay, headache, and a 4 cm lateral ventricular mass. Histology is shown. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, H&E. Large ganglion-like cells with glassy eosinophilic cytoplasm at the foramen of Monro in a child indicate SEGA (tuberous sclerosis).

questions.stem: Which is the most common cause of death in tuberous sclerosis in adulthood?
questions.explanation: Renal complications lead adult mortality; SUDEP and SEGA follow.
questions.imageAlt: Large polygonal and ganglion-like cells with abundant glassy eosinophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli in a fibrillary background. Marginal note: 7-year-old with developmental delay, headache, vomiting, 4 cm lateral ventricular mass.
questions.context: A 7-year-old with developmental delay, headache, and a 4 cm lateral ventricular mass. Histology is shown. Diagnosis?
questions.salient: WHO grade 1, mixed glial-neuronal immunophenotype; mTOR inhibitor for growing asymptomatic SEGA; surgery for acute hydrocephalus
questions.learning: WHO grade 1, arises at the foramen of Monro from a subependymal nodule; enhances avidly; causes obstructive hydrocephalus. mTOR inhibitors (everolimus) shrink SEGA; surgery for acute hydrocephalus. Mixed glial/neuronal immunophenotype (GFAP, S100, synaptophysin).

questions.stem: An HIV-positive patient with a CD4 count of 40 presents with seizures; imaging is shown. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Empiric pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine with reimaging in 10-14 days

questions.explanation: Empiric pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine with reimaging in 10-14 days. Multiple ring-enhancing lesions with disproportionate edema at low CD4 are treated empirically for toxoplasmosis; failure to respond prompts biopsy for lymphoma. Most common mass lesion in AIDS at CD4 <100; reactivation of latent Toxoplasma gondii (cat is the definitive host). Multiple lesions at the gray-white junction and basal ganglia; eccentric target sign on contrast, concentric target sign on T2. Differential is primary CNS lymphoma (usually solitary, periventricular, subependymal spread, thallium-SPECT/FDG avid, EBV DNA in CSF). Standard approach: empiric pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine plus leucovorin and re-image at 10-14 days; failure to improve prompts biopsy. Healed lesions calcify at the gray-white junction.
questions.imageAlt: Post-contrast T1 (A): ring-enhancing basal ganglia and hemispheric lesions. T2 (B): edema grossly out of proportion to lesion size. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 91)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male with diabetes presents with sudden, severe, lancinating pain in the right anterior thigh, followed weeks later by profound wasting of the right quadriceps and an absent patellar reflex. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Diabetic amyotrophy is an ischemic radiculoplexopathy (mediated by microvasculitis) targeting the lumbosacral plexus, causing asymmetric thigh pain, quadriceps atrophy, weight loss, and loss of the knee jerk.

questions.stem: Episodic Ataxia Type 2 (EA2) is an autosomal dominant channelopathy characterized by stress- or exertion-triggered bouts of cerebellar ataxia lasting hours. What medication reduces the frequency and severity of attacks?
questions.explanation: EA2 is caused by loss-of-function variants in CACNA1A encoding the alpha-1A subunit of P/Q-type calcium channels. Attacks respond to acetazolamide; 4-aminopyridine is an alternative.

questions.stem: The gross specimen shown demonstrates bilateral parasagittal hemorrhagic infarcts and hemorrhagic necrosis of both thalami. Which vascular event explains the thalamic findings?

options.text: Deep cerebral venous (internal cerebral vein/straight sinus) thrombosis

questions.explanation: Deep cerebral venous (internal cerebral vein/straight sinus) thrombosis. Bilateral thalamic edema/hemorrhage with parasagittal infarcts is venous; artery of Percheron is the main arterial mimic. Bilateral symmetric parasagittal hemorrhage is the signature of SSS thrombosis; bilateral thalamic edema/hemorrhage is the signature of deep venous (internal cerebral vein/straight sinus) thrombosis, which presents with coma and is easily mistaken for artery of Percheron infarct or a thalamic glioma.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal brain slice: bilateral parasagittal hemorrhagic cortical/subcortical infarcts plus hemorrhagic necrosis of the thalami and basal ganglia, and thrombus in the sagittal sinus. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 82)

questions.stem: A newborn screen shows elevated C26:0-lysophosphatidylcholine; confirmatory testing identifies a pathogenic ABCD1 variant in a male infant. What is the appropriate surveillance and treatment strategy?

options.text: Brain MRI every 6 months beginning by ~12–18 months of age, adrenal function monitoring, and allogeneic HSCT or gene therapy at the earliest sign of cerebral disease
Lorenzo's oil to prevent cerebral disease; no imaging needed

questions.explanation: ~35% of boys develop childhood cerebral ALD (peak onset 4–10 years); HSCT halts progression only when performed early (Loes ≤9, limited gadolinium enhancement, preserved function). Elivaldogene autotemcel (lentiviral gene therapy) was approved in 2022, with subsequent reports of hematologic malignancy prompting label restriction. Adrenal insufficiency affects ~80% of males and is treated with hydrocortisone. Adrenomyeloneuropathy affects adults of both sexes. Lorenzo's oil does not prevent cerebral disease.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl with short stature, sensorineural hearing loss, and migraine develops acute right hemianopia and aphasia during a febrile illness.
