MRI shows a left occipitotemporal cortical lesion crossing vascular territories with elevated lactate on MR spectroscopy. What is the most common causative variant?
questions.explanation: MELAS is caused by m.3243A>G in the tRNA-Leu(UUR) gene in ~80% of cases. Stroke-like episodes reflect metabolic and endothelial dysfunction, not embolism; lesions migrate and are not confined to arterial territories. IV L-arginine is used acutely; valproate and metformin are avoided. The same variant causes maternally inherited diabetes and deafness at lower heteroplasmy.

questions.stem: Coronal section from a 55-year-old with chorea and dementia. What is the characteristic finding?
questions.explanation: Huntington disease, gross. Flattened, concave caudate nuclei producing boxcar frontal horns are the hallmark of Huntington disease.

questions.stem: What CAG repeat length in HTT is fully penetrant?
questions.explanation: 40+ is fully penetrant; 36 to 39 has reduced penetrance; 27 to 35 is intermediate (unstable, not disease-causing).
questions.imageAlt: Coronal section with marked atrophy of the caudate nuclei producing flattened, concave ventricular walls (boxcar ventricles) and generalized cortical atrophy.
questions.context: Coronal section from a 55-year-old with chorea and dementia. What is the characteristic finding?
questions.salient: Indirect-pathway enkephalin medium spiny neurons lost first (chorea), direct pathway later (rigidity); Intranuclear ubiquitin/huntingtin inclusions; Vonsattel grades
questions.learning: Medium spiny GABAergic neurons of the striatum are lost first (enkephalin-positive indirect pathway neurons before substance P-positive direct pathway), explaining early chorea and later rigidity. Intranuclear polyglutamine inclusions (ubiquitin/huntingtin positive). Vonsattel grades 0 to 4.

questions.stem: Fourth ventricle tumor in a child with perivascular pseudorosettes. Which is the strongest prognostic factor?
questions.explanation: Ependymoma. Gross total resection is the dominant prognostic factor in ependymoma.
questions.imageAlt: Perivascular pseudorosettes: tumor cells radially arranged around vessels with anuclear fibrillary zones; true ependymal rosettes with central lumen; GFAP highlights the perivascular processes.
questions.salient: Posterior fossa group A worse than B; supratentorial ZFTA::RELA fusion; Myxopapillary at the filum in adults
questions.learning: Fourth ventricle in children (posterior fossa group A, worse; group B), supratentorial ZFTA::RELA fusion, spinal cord in adults (myxopapillary at the filum, MPNST-like mucin). EMA dot-like positivity. Drop metastases; gross total resection is the main prognostic factor.

questions.stem: Which deep brain stimulation target and indication are correctly paired?

options.text: Ventral intermediate (VIM) thalamus; tremor-predominant essential tremor
Anterior nucleus of thalamus; Parkinson disease motor fluctuations
Globus pallidus interna; medication-refractory cluster headache

questions.explanation: VIM DBS treats tremor (ET, PD tremor). STN and GPi are both effective for PD motor fluctuations and dyskinesia (STN allows greater medication reduction; GPi has fewer mood/cognitive effects). GPi is the target for generalized/segmental dystonia, with TOR1A-positive patients among the best responders. Anterior thalamic nucleus DBS is approved for refractory focal epilepsy (SANTE). DBS does not help axial symptoms, freezing, or dementia in PD.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with new urinary incontinence and a hairy patch over the low back has the MRI shown. Which finding is diagnostic of the underlying condition?

options.text: Thickened filum with a low-lying conus and dorsal lipoma

questions.explanation: Thickened filum with a low-lying conus and dorsal lipoma. Tethered cord: conus below L2-L3 with a thick filum or lipoma; traction produces progressive bladder, gait and orthopedic deficits. The conus should lie at or above L2-L3 by about 3 months of age. Tethering produces progressive, traction-related deficits: gait change, bladder dysfunction, foot deformity, scoliosis, back pain. Cutaneous stigmata (sacral dimple above the gluteal cleft, hair tuft, hemangioma, lipoma) warrant imaging. Diastematomyelia and dermal sinus are associated.
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal T1/T2 (A-C) and axial (D) lumbosacral spine: low-lying conus extending into the sacrum, thickened filum, dorsal lipoma contiguous with subcutaneous fat, and a widened canal. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 51)

questions.stem: A child presents with severe intellectual disability, microcephaly, jerky ataxia, paroxysms of inappropriate laughter, and an interictal EEG with notched delta-theta runs. What genetic lesion is most common?

options.text: Deletion of the maternally derived 15q11-q13 chromosomal region
Deletion of the paternally derived 15q11-q13 chromosomal region

questions.explanation: Angelman syndrome is caused by loss of maternally expressed UBE3A in neurons, most commonly (~70%) via de novo deletion of the maternal 15q11-q13 region. Paternal deletion of the same region causes Prader-Willi syndrome.

questions.stem: Non-calcified suprasellar cyst, T1-bright, non-enhancing; wall lined by ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Rathke cleft cyst. Rathke cleft cysts are intrasellar/suprasellar, lack calcification, and have ciliated epithelium with goblet cells.
questions.imageAlt: CT: non-calcified hypodense suprasellar cyst. Sagittal T1: intrinsically T1-bright intrasellar/suprasellar cyst without solid enhancing component. H&E: cyst wall of ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells over a thin fibrous stroma.
questions.salient: Intracystic nodule on MRI; usually incidental; Squamous metaplasia can mimic craniopharyngioma
questions.learning: Intrasellar/suprasellar nonenhancing cyst derived from Rathke pouch; intracystic nodule is characteristic on MRI. Usually incidental; drain if headache, visual loss, or hypopituitarism. Squamous metaplasia can mimic craniopharyngioma.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with prominent bulbar, neck extensor, and respiratory weakness, tongue atrophy, and negative AChR antibodies worsens with pyridostigmine. What antibody is likely, and which treatment is most effective?
questions.explanation: MuSK-MG (IgG4-mediated, blocks agrin-LRP4-MuSK clustering) affects mainly women with bulbar-predominant disease, poor cholinesterase-inhibitor response (fasciculations, cholinergic crisis), and excellent response to rituximab; plasma exchange outperforms IVIG acutely. Drugs to avoid in all MG: aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, telithromycin, magnesium, botulinum toxin, D-penicillamine, beta-blockers (caution), and immune checkpoint inhibitors.

questions.stem: On the MR venogram shown, which structure is labeled D?
questions.explanation: Straight sinus. The straight sinus runs obliquely from the vein of Galen to the torcular on the lateral view. Use the labeled companion image to name the remaining structures. The straight sinus is identified on the lateral view as the oblique channel running from the vein of Galen/inferior sagittal sinus junction posteriorly and inferiorly to the torcular; it is a common RITE anatomy target along with the vein of Labbe, the basal vein of Rosenthal and the superior ophthalmic vein.
questions.imageAlt: AP and lateral MRV with structures A-F labeled. The deck\'s question asks for D; the answer is the straight sinus. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 75)

questions.stem: Sagittal lumbar T1 pre and post gadolinium in a 32-year-old immigrant with gait failure and incontinence: enhancing destruction of adjacent vertebral bodies crossing the disc with epidural extension. Highest on the differential?
questions.explanation: Destructive vertebral lesion with epidural extension. Contiguous involvement across the disc space with epidural/paraspinal extension in a young patient favors Pott disease.
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal lumbar T1 pre and post gadolinium: enhancing tissue replacing and destroying vertebral bodies with anterior epidural extension and a large enhancing sacral mass. Marginal note: 32-year-old with gait impairment and incontinence.
questions.salient: Metastases spare the disc; pyogenic osteomyelitis destroys disc early; Gibbus deformity; decompression for deficit
questions.learning: Pott disease: contiguous involvement crossing the disc space with paraspinal abscess, thoracolumbar predominance, gibbus deformity. Metastases typically spare the disc. Pyogenic osteomyelitis destroys disc early. Surgical decompression for neurologic deficit.

questions.stem: A hospitalized 80-year-old develops fluctuating inattention, disorganized thinking, and nighttime agitation 2 days after hip surgery. Which management is appropriate?

options.text: Physical restraints and diphenhydramine for sleep
Identify precipitants (infection, drugs, retention, pain), nonpharmacologic reorientation and sleep hygiene, and low-dose antipsychotic only for dangerous agitation

questions.explanation: Delirium (CAM criteria) is a marker of underlying illness and increases mortality and subsequent dementia. Benzodiazepines and anticholinergics worsen it except in alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal. Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium (MIND-USA) and are reserved for safety. Multicomponent prevention (HELP) reduces incidence by ~30%.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female presents with headache, vision changes, and bilateral optic disc swelling. Lumbar puncture reveals an opening pressure of 340 mm H2O with normal CSF cytology and protein. Brain MRI and MR venography are normal. What medication is a recognized risk factor?
questions.explanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is associated with obesity, excess vitamin A/retinoids, tetracyclines, and growth hormone therapy. Acetazolamide plus weight loss is first-line (IIHTT); GLP-1 agonists are emerging.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old with parkinsonism and psychiatric symptoms has the CT shown. Which is the most common gene in familial cases after metabolic causes are excluded?
questions.explanation: SLC20A2. Primary familial brain calcification: SLC20A2 most common (AD); PDGFB, PDGFRB, XPR1 AD; MYORG AR. Exclude hypoparathyroidism first. Diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out hypoparathyroidism/pseudohypoparathyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, mitochondrial disease, congenital infection, radiation and lead. Familial forms are AD: SLC20A2 (most common), PDGFB, PDGFRB, XPR1; AR MYORG. Parkinsonism, dystonia, chorea, psychiatric symptoms and dementia in mid-adulthood; calcification burden correlates poorly with symptoms. Deck\'s contrast with Leigh: necrotic basal ganglia are hypodense on CT and T2 bright.
questions.imageAlt: Axial non-contrast CT: dense symmetric calcification of the basal ganglia and cerebellar dentate nuclei; axial T2 shows corresponding low signal. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 137)

questions.stem: Trichrome and SDH stains with the accompanying electron micrograph. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial myopathy: ragged red fibers. Ragged red fibers, ragged blue on SDH, and paracrystalline mitochondrial inclusions indicate mitochondrial myopathy.

questions.stem: Ragged red fibers plus myoclonus, ataxia, and cervical lipomas most suggest which variant?
questions.explanation: MERRF: tRNA-Lys m.8344A>G; multiple lipomas are a clue.
questions.imageAlt: Modified Gomori trichrome: fibers with irregular subsarcolemmal red accumulations (ragged red fibers); SDH stain shows ragged blue fibers; electron micrograph shows paracrystalline (parking lot) inclusions in mitochondria.
questions.context: Trichrome and SDH stains with the accompanying electron micrograph. Diagnosis?
questions.salient: COX-negative/SDH-positive fibers imply mtDNA-encoded defects; MERRF, MELAS, CPEO/Kearns-Sayre, POLG
questions.learning: Ragged red fibers reflect compensatory proliferation of abnormal mitochondria; COX-negative/SDH-positive fibers indicate mtDNA-encoded defects. Seen in MERRF (m.8344A>G), MELAS, CPEO/Kearns-Sayre (single large deletions), and POLG-related disease. Paracrystalline inclusions on EM are characteristic.

questions.stem: A patient presents with fluent paraphasic speech, normal auditory comprehension, but severe impairment of repetition. Where is the structural lesion?
questions.explanation: Conduction aphasia is characterized by intact comprehension and fluent output with severely degraded repetition, typically localized to the arcuate fasciculus or peri-Sylvian superior temporal/inferior parietal cortex.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy develops encephalopathy, ataxia, and hemiparesis 10 days after a viral illness. MRI shows multiple large, poorly demarcated, bilateral asymmetric T2/FLAIR white matter and deep gray lesions. CSF has mild pleocytosis without oligoclonal bands. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: ADEM is a monophasic post-infectious demyelinating encephalopathy; encephalopathy is required for diagnosis. IV methylprednisolone (20–30 mg/kg/day for 3–5 days) is first-line, with IVIG or plasma exchange for refractory cases. MOG-IgG is positive in roughly half of pediatric ADEM; empiric acyclovir is reasonable until HSV is excluded.

questions.stem: Noncontrast CT with right hemispheric hypodensity, sulcal effacement, and midline shift 2 days after stroke onset in a 55-year-old. Which intervention reduces mortality?
questions.explanation: Malignant middle cerebral artery infarction. Pooled DECIMAL/DESTINY/HAMLET data show hemicraniectomy within 48 hours reduces mortality in malignant MCA infarction under 60.
questions.imageAlt: Noncontrast CT: extensive right hemispheric hypodensity with loss of gray-white differentiation, sulcal effacement, ventricular compression, and midline shift.
questions.salient: Edema peaks day 3 to 5; DESTINY II: survival benefit over 60 with worse function; steroids harmful
questions.learning: Edema peaks day 3 to 5. Decompressive hemicraniectomy within 48 hours in patients ≤60 reduces mortality (DECIMAL, DESTINY, HAMLET pooled analysis); benefit in >60 with worse functional outcomes (DESTINY II). Early CT signs: hyperdense MCA, insular ribbon loss, obscured lentiform nucleus.

questions.stem: After a stab wound to the back, a patient has right leg weakness with hyperreflexia and Babinski sign, loss of vibration and position sense in the right leg, and loss of pain and temperature in the left leg beginning two segments below the lesion. What is the syndrome?
questions.explanation: Hemisection interrupts the ipsilateral corticospinal tract and dorsal columns and the crossed spinothalamic tract; spinothalamic fibers ascend 1–2 segments before decussating, hence the contralateral sensory level lies slightly below the lesion. A band of ipsilateral pain/temperature loss and LMN weakness occurs at the lesion level.

questions.stem: In Graves ophthalmopathy (thyroid eye disease), what is the correct predilection order of extraocular muscle enlargement from most common to least common?

options.text: Inferior > Medial > Superior > Lateral > Oblique ("I'M SLOW")

questions.explanation: Graves ophthalmopathy affects muscles in the sequence "I'M SLOW": Inferior rectus > Medial rectus > Superior rectus > Lateral rectus > Oblique muscles, with tendon sparing.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presents with lancinating leg pains, sensory ataxia, absent knee jerks, and small irregular pupils that accommodate but do not react to light. What CSF test is most specific, and what is the treatment?

options.text: Serum RPR alone; single dose benzathine penicillin
CSF VDRL; intravenous aqueous penicillin G for 10–14 days

questions.explanation: Tabes dorsalis and Argyll Robertson pupils reflect late neurosyphilis. CSF VDRL is highly specific but only ~50–70% sensitive; a negative CSF FTA-ABS effectively excludes neurosyphilis. Treatment is IV penicillin G 18–24 million units/day; the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction may occur. Neurosyphilis can occur at any stage; ocular and otic syphilis are treated identically.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old with a port-wine stain involving the forehead and upper eyelid develops focal seizures and left hemiparesis. What is the genetic basis and a recommended screening measure?

options.text: Germline KRIT1 variant; annual brain MRI for cavernomas
Somatic mosaic GNAQ p.R183Q variant; ophthalmologic screening for glaucoma

questions.explanation: Sturge-Weber syndrome is caused by a post-zygotic activating GNAQ variant (also found in isolated port-wine stains); the same gene causes uveal melanoma. Leptomeningeal angiomatosis produces venous hypoperfusion, seizures, hemiparesis, stroke-like episodes, and "tram-track" gyriform calcification. Glaucoma occurs in ~50% (mostly with V1 and V2 involvement). Low-dose aspirin is often used to reduce stroke-like episodes; hemispherectomy is considered for refractory epilepsy.

questions.stem: The coronal MRI shown demonstrates hippocampal atrophy. Which pathologic staging system does this atrophy pattern follow?
questions.explanation: Braak neurofibrillary staging. Medial temporal atrophy tracks Braak tau stages; it is not specific to AD (hippocampal sclerosis, LATE). Medial temporal atrophy (Scheltens MTA score) is the structural biomarker of AD neurodegeneration and follows Braak staging (transentorhinal, limbic, isocortical). It is not specific (also hippocampal sclerosis, FTLD-TDP, LATE). The slide series pairs this with FDG-PET (hypometabolism) and amyloid PET (pathology) as the three levels of imaging biomarkers.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal T1 sections, control (left) versus AD (right): marked atrophy of the hippocampi and entorhinal cortex with dilated temporal horns and widened choroidal fissures. (RITE Review deck, slide 73)

questions.stem: What antiseizure medication is strongly associated with an increased incidence of neural tube defects (spina bifida in ~1–2% of exposed fetuses) when taken during the first trimester of pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Valproic acid carries the highest rate of major congenital malformations (dose-dependent, ~10% at >1500 mg/day) and neurodevelopmental impairment; lamotrigine and levetiracetam carry the lowest rates. Topiramate is also teratogenic (oral clefts).

questions.stem: A 62-year-old male presents with the triad of magnetic gait apraxia, urinary urgency/incontinence, and subcortical dementia. Brain MRI demonstrates ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal enlargement. What procedure best predicts responsiveness to shunting?

options.text: High-volume lumbar puncture (spinal tap test) or extended lumbar drainage

questions.explanation: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is managed by identifying gait improvement following high-volume (30–50 mL) lumbar CSF removal or 72-hour lumbar drainage, predicting successful ventriculoperitoneal shunting. Gait responds best; cognition least.

questions.stem: The histology shown demonstrates a delicate branching capillary network. Which clinical complication does this vasculature predispose to?
questions.explanation: Intratumoral hemorrhage. Chicken-wire vessels are fragile; oligodendrogliomas may present with hemorrhage. The fine capillary network predisposes to intratumoral hemorrhage. Together with fried-egg cytology and calcification this triad is the histologic signature; molecular confirmation (IDH plus 1p/19q) is now required for the diagnosis.
questions.imageAlt: H&E: delicate, acutely branching capillary-sized vessels forming an anastomosing network among tumor cells. (RITE Review deck, slide 30)

questions.stem: A 62-year-old hypertensive man presents 6 hours after sudden headache and left visual field loss. The lesion shown is isointense on T1, mildly hyperintense on T2 and restricts diffusion centrally. Which hemoglobin species dominates this lesion?
questions.explanation: Oxyhemoglobin. Deoxy-Hb would make T2 dark; either methemoglobin form would make T1 bright; hemosiderin gives a dark rim on all sequences. Oxy-Hb has no unpaired electrons (diamagnetic), so signal reflects clot water content, not iron. Mnemonic stage 1: I Bleed (iso T1 / bright T2). A hyperacute bleed can mimic a non-hemorrhagic lesion on conventional sequences; GRE/SWI is the sensitive sequence.
questions.imageAlt: Axial T1, T2, GRE and DWI of a posterior (parieto-occipital) hematoma. T1 isointense, T2 mildly hyperintense, central restricted diffusion; GRE variable (thin dark rim as deoxy-Hb forms at the periphery). (Neuroradiology deck, slide 7)

questions.stem: The EMG recording shown demonstrates discharges that wax and wane in frequency and amplitude. Which condition produces this finding in the paraspinal muscles as a clue to diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acid maltase deficiency (Pompe disease). Myotonic discharges in paraspinals with proximal weakness suggest late-onset Pompe; CRDs have abrupt onset/offset, neuromyotonia is very high frequency. Muscle fiber membrane hyperexcitability; provoked by needle movement or percussion. Causes: myotonic dystrophy types 1 (DMPK CTG) and 2 (CNBP CCTG, proximal), myotonia congenita (CLCN1), paramyotonia congenita and hyperkalemic periodic paralysis (SCN4A), acid maltase deficiency (paraspinals), colchicine and statin myopathy. Contrast: complex repetitive discharges are abrupt-onset/offset with constant frequency; neuromyotonia is very high frequency with a decrementing pinging sound; myokymia is grouped bursts.
questions.imageAlt: Two-channel EMG recording from the right deltoid: repetitive single-fiber discharges that wax and wane in amplitude and frequency (dive-bomber sound). (RITE Review deck, slide 276)

questions.stem: The coronal image shown demonstrates bilateral gray-matter-lined clefts with an absent septum pellucidum. Which endocrine complication should be anticipated?

options.text: Hypopituitarism as part of septo-optic dysplasia

questions.explanation: Hypopituitarism as part of septo-optic dysplasia. Schizencephaly with septal absence and optic nerve hypoplasia falls in the septo-optic dysplasia spectrum. Open-lip (CSF-filled) versus closed-lip (walls apposed) clefts; bilateral clefts predict worse motor and cognitive outcome. Gray-matter lining is the differentiator from porencephaly. Frequently coexists with septal absence and optic nerve hypoplasia (septo-optic dysplasia, hypopituitarism). Sporadic in most, with in utero vascular disruption favored; the early EMX2 association was not confirmed in later series, whereas COL4A1 is an established cause.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal T1: bilateral full-thickness clefts extending from the cortical surface to the ventricle, lined by dysplastic (polymicrogyric) gray matter, with absent septum pellucidum and small optic nerves. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 119)

questions.stem: Median motor study in a 74-year-old: distal latency 9.5 ms, CMAP 1.8 mV, forearm CV 30 m/s. Interpretation?

options.text: Severe carpal tunnel syndrome with axon loss

questions.explanation: Severe median neuropathy at the wrist. Marked distal latency prolongation with reduced amplitude indicates severe median neuropathy at the wrist with secondary axon loss.
questions.imageAlt: Median motor study recording abductor pollicis brevis: distal latency 9.5 ms (normal <4.4), amplitude 1.84 mV (reduced), forearm conduction velocity 30.2 m/s. Marginal note: 74-year-old with weakness.
questions.salient: Forearm slowing can reflect loss of fastest fibers, not a proximal lesion; Palmar mixed comparison studies most sensitive for mild CTS
questions.learning: Markedly prolonged distal motor latency with reduced CMAP amplitude indicates demyelination at the wrist plus secondary axon loss; forearm slowing can reflect loss of the fastest fibers rather than a proximal lesion. Compare median and ulnar sensory latencies (palmar mixed study) for sensitivity. Martin-Gruber anastomosis can produce a spuriously larger proximal CMAP.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old male presents with progressive generalized chorea, depression, and executive cognitive decline. His father developed identical symptoms at age 62. What genetic mechanism accounts for this earlier generational onset?

options.text: Anticipation via CAG repeat expansion during spermatogenesis

questions.explanation: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant CAG repeat disorder in HTT on chromosome 4p16 (≥40 repeats fully penetrant; 36–39 reduced penetrance). Paternal transmission involves meiotic instability and expansion, producing anticipation.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with sickle cell disease undergoes screening transcranial Doppler showing a time-averaged mean maximum velocity of 215 cm/s in the middle cerebral artery. What intervention reduces his stroke risk?

options.text: Chronic monthly transfusion to keep HbS below 30%
Observation with repeat TCD in one year

questions.explanation: The STOP trial showed chronic transfusion reduces first stroke by ~90% in children with abnormal TCD (≥200 cm/s). TWiTCH later showed hydroxyurea can substitute after a transfusion period in those without vasculopathy. Silent cerebral infarcts affect roughly a third of children with HbSS by age 14.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with well-controlled epilepsy on lamotrigine monotherapy starts a combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive and develops breakthrough seizures 3 weeks later. What is the mechanism?

options.text: Ethinyl estradiol induces glucuronidation (UGT1A4), lowering lamotrigine levels by roughly half
Lamotrigine induces CYP3A4, reducing contraceptive efficacy
Estrogen directly antagonizes sodium channel blockade
Progestin displaces lamotrigine from plasma proteins

questions.explanation: Estrogen-containing contraceptives induce lamotrigine glucuronidation, dropping levels ~50% (with rebound toxicity during the pill-free week). Conversely, valproate inhibits UGT and roughly doubles lamotrigine levels, mandating slow titration to limit rash risk. Enzyme-inducing ASMs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, topiramate >200 mg) reduce contraceptive efficacy.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with relapsing MS has been on natalizumab for 3 years. What combination most strongly increases her risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy?

options.text: Positive JC virus antibody with high index, prior immunosuppressant use, and treatment duration beyond 2 years
Female sex, age under 40, and low EDSS
Negative JC virus antibody and prior interferon use

questions.explanation: Natalizumab (anti-alpha4 integrin) PML risk stratifies by JCV serostatus/index (>1.5 highest), prior immunosuppression, and duration >24 months, reaching >1% in the highest-risk stratum. Extended-interval dosing lowers risk. PML presents with subacute cognitive, visual, or motor decline with non-enhancing subcortical U-fiber lesions and CSF JCV PCR.

questions.stem: A patient with a large right subdural hematoma develops a fixed dilated right pupil and right-sided hemiparesis. What explains the ipsilateral weakness?

options.text: Ipsilateral corticospinal involvement above the decussation is impossible; the imaging must be mislabeled
Kernohan notch phenomenon: compression of the contralateral cerebral peduncle against the tentorial edge produces a false localizing ipsilateral hemiparesis

questions.explanation: Uncal herniation classically produces an ipsilateral CN III palsy (pupil first, from peripheral parasympathetic fiber compression) and contralateral hemiparesis; when the midline shift compresses the opposite peduncle, hemiparesis becomes ipsilateral to the lesion. Central herniation produces progressive rostral-caudal deterioration with Cheyne-Stokes respiration and Duret hemorrhages.

questions.stem: A newborn has a lumbosacral myelomeningocele. What intracranial malformation is expected, and what maternal intervention reduces the risk of this condition in future pregnancies?

options.text: Chiari II malformation with hydrocephalus; folic acid 4 mg daily preconception and through the first trimester

questions.explanation: Chiari II (hindbrain herniation, beaked tectum, small posterior fossa, hydrocephalus) accompanies nearly all open myelomeningoceles. Standard-risk women take 0.4 mg folate; those with a prior affected pregnancy take 4 mg. Valproate and carbamazepine exposure raise NTD risk. The MOMS trial showed fetal surgery reduces shunt requirement and improves motor outcome at the cost of prematurity. Latex allergy and tethered cord are long-term concerns.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old female presents with progressive sensorineural hearing loss, limb ataxia, and spastic paraparesis. Gradient-echo and susceptibility-weighted MRI scans reveal extensive hypointense rim deposition outlining the cerebellar folia, brainstem, and spinal cord. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Superficial siderosis is caused by chronic, low-grade subarachnoid hemorrhage resulting in hemosiderin deposition along the leptomeningeal surfaces of the cerebellum, cranial nerves (especially CN VIII), and spinal cord.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female presents with acute painful vision loss in the left eye and decreased color perception. Pupillary exam reveals that when a flashlight is swung from the right eye to the left eye, both pupils paradoxically dilate. What is this sign?

options.text: Relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil)

questions.explanation: A relative afferent pupillary defect indicates asymmetric optic nerve conduction (as in demyelinating optic neuritis); light in the affected eye generates less pupillomotor drive, causing bilateral dilation.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has calf pseudohypertrophy, Gowers sign, and CK of 15,000 U/L. Deletion of DMD exons 45–50 is found. Why is his phenotype predicted to be Duchenne rather than Becker?

options.text: The deletion disrupts the open reading frame, producing no functional dystrophin
The deletion involves the actin-binding domain
The deletion is larger than 5 exons

questions.explanation: The reading-frame rule holds in >90% of cases: frameshifting deletions abolish dystrophin (Duchenne); in-frame deletions yield truncated but partially functional protein (Becker). Exons 45–50 deletion is out of frame and amenable to exon 51 skipping (eteplirsen). Corticosteroids (prednisone, deflazacort, vamorolone) prolong ambulation; cardiomyopathy and respiratory failure dominate later course. Delandistrogene moxeparvovec (micro-dystrophin gene therapy) received accelerated approval in 2023.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old immigrant presents with 3 weeks of headache, low-grade fever, a sixth nerve palsy, and lethargy. CSF shows 250 WBC (lymphocytic), protein 180 mg/dL, glucose 25 mg/dL. MRI shows basilar meningeal enhancement and hydrocephalus. What is the treatment?

options.text: Four-drug antituberculous therapy plus adjunctive dexamethasone

questions.explanation: Tuberculous meningitis produces basilar exudates causing cranial neuropathies, hydrocephalus, and vasculitic infarcts of perforating arteries. CSF AFB smear is insensitive; Xpert MTB/RIF and culture improve yield. Adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality (Thwaites 2004). Treatment lasts 9–12 months; hydrocephalus may need shunting.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man presents with progressive myoclonus, generalized seizures, ataxia, and multiple lipomas; muscle biopsy shows ragged red fibers. What is the most common genetic cause?
questions.explanation: MERRF is a progressive myoclonus epilepsy; m.8344A>G accounts for ~80% of cases. Cervical lipomatosis is a useful clue. Unverricht-Lundborg (CSTB) and Lafora disease (EPM2A/NHLRC1, with skin biopsy polyglucosan bodies) are the other core PME differentials.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with cafe-au-lait macules has the spine MRI shown. Which imaging feature should prompt evaluation for malignant transformation of one of these lesions?

options.text: Rapid interval growth with loss of the target sign and new pain

questions.explanation: Rapid interval growth with loss of the target sign and new pain. Target sign, foraminal extension, multiplicity and T2 brightness are all typical of benign neurofibromas; growth, pain, heterogeneity and loss of the target sign suggest MPNST and warrant FDG-PET. Neurofibromas are T1 dark, T2 bright, often with a central low-signal target sign (collagenous core; also seen in schwannoma and MPNST), heterogeneous enhancement. Usually asymptomatic or radicular pain; myelopathy only when large. Rapid growth, pain or loss of the target sign should prompt MPNST evaluation (FDG-PET).
questions.imageAlt: Coronal STIR/T2 (A, B) and axial T2 (C): innumerable bilateral, multilevel, hyperintense fusiform and dumbbell-shaped nerve-root and paraspinal masses extending through and widening the neural foramina. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 22)

questions.stem: The imaging and gross specimen shown demonstrate a CSF-filled cavity communicating with the ventricle. Which feature distinguishes this lesion from schizencephaly?

options.text: Lining of gliotic white matter rather than heterotopic gray matter

questions.explanation: Lining of gliotic white matter rather than heterotopic gray matter. Porencephaly is a destructive cavity lined by white matter; schizencephaly is a malformation lined by gray matter. Familial porencephaly suggests COL4A1. Encephaloclastic (destructive) lesion from a perinatal or fetal insult (arterial infarct, hemorrhage), lined by gliotic white matter. Familial porencephaly and infantile hemiparesis point to COL4A1/COL4A2 (also cataracts, retinal arterial tortuosity, adult ICH). The deck\'s contrast: a schizencephalic cleft is lined by heterotopic gray matter, a porencephalic cyst is not.
questions.imageAlt: Axial T1 and gross specimen: smooth-walled CSF-density cavity in the cerebral hemisphere communicating with the ventricle and subarachnoid space. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 112)

questions.stem: Transverse and longitudinal muscle sections show chains of internal nuclei. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Myotonic dystrophy. Numerous internal nuclei aligned in chains on longitudinal section characterize myotonic dystrophy.

questions.stem: Which is the leading cause of death in DM1 requiring routine surveillance?
questions.explanation: Conduction disease and sudden death mandate annual ECG and low threshold for pacing.
questions.imageAlt: Transverse H&E: numerous internal (central) nuclei in most fibers with fiber size variation and increased connective tissue. Longitudinal section: internal nuclei aligned in chains.
questions.context: Transverse and longitudinal muscle sections show chains of internal nuclei. Diagnosis?
questions.salient: Ring fibers, sarcoplasmic masses, type 1 atrophy (DM1); Single central nucleus per fiber = centronuclear myopathy, not DM
questions.learning: Additional features: ring fibers, sarcoplasmic masses, type 1 fiber atrophy (DM1) versus type 2 atrophy with nuclear clumps (DM2). Internal nuclei chains are the key discriminator from centronuclear myopathy, which shows a single central nucleus per fiber.

questions.stem: SWI in a 78-year-old shows a dominant frontal susceptibility lesion with scattered smaller foci. Highest on the differential?
questions.explanation: Lobar microbleeds on susceptibility-weighted imaging. Lobar/cortical susceptibility lesions in an elderly patient favor CAA; hypertensive bleeds are deep.
questions.imageAlt: SWI shows a dominant round hypointense left frontal lesion with scattered smaller susceptibility foci; T2 shows minimal corresponding signal. Marginal note: 78-year-old man.
questions.salient: Boston 2.0: lobar bleeds, cortical superficial siderosis; Microbleed burden matters for lysis and anti-amyloid therapy
questions.learning: CAA microbleeds are lobar; hypertensive microbleeds are deep (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum). Boston criteria 2.0 add cortical superficial siderosis and white matter features. Microbleed burden matters for thrombolysis and anti-amyloid antibody eligibility.
questions.note: Low-moderate confidence; the number of true microbleeds is hard to judge on this reproduction.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old female presents with bilateral gradual sensorineural hearing loss and imbalance. High-resolution internal auditory canal MRI demonstrates bilateral enhancing vestibular schwannomas. What protein is abnormal?
questions.explanation: NF2-related schwannomatosis is caused by variants in the NF2 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 22q12, which encodes merlin (schwannomin).

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has progressive parkinsonism with poor levodopa response, early falls, stridor, severe orthostatic hypotension, and urinary retention. MRI shows putaminal atrophy with a hyperintense lateral putaminal rim and a "hot cross bun" sign in the pons. What is the pathologic hallmark?

options.text: Neuronal tau tangles in the substantia nigra
Alpha-synuclein glial cytoplasmic inclusions in oligodendrocytes

questions.explanation: Multiple system atrophy (MSA-P and MSA-C) is an oligodendroglial synucleinopathy; autonomic failure (orthostatic drop ≥20/10 mm Hg, urogenital dysfunction) is required. RBD, stridor, and anterocollis are supportive. Alpha-synuclein seed amplification assays in CSF and skin biopsy are emerging biomarkers. Median survival is ~6–10 years.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female presents with the triad of simultanagnosia (inability to perceive more than one visual item at once), optic ataxia (impaired visual guidance of reaching), and ocular apraxia (inability to voluntarily guide saccades). What is the syndrome and localization?

options.text: Bálint syndrome; Bilateral parieto-occipital watershed regions
Korsakoff syndrome; Mammillary bodies and medial thalamus
Anton syndrome; Bilateral primary visual cortex

questions.explanation: Bálint syndrome results from bilateral injury (often watershed infarctions) to the posterior parietal and parieto-occipital cortices, disrupting the dorsal "where" visual stream.

questions.stem: The amyloid PET images shown include a cognitively normal amyloid-positive scan. What proportion of cognitively normal adults over 70 are amyloid positive?
questions.explanation: About 20-30%. Positive amyloid PET establishes pathology, not diagnosis; a negative scan effectively excludes AD as the cause. Florbetapir, flutemetamol and florbetaben image fibrillar amyloid; a negative scan effectively excludes AD as the cause of dementia, but a positive scan is present in 20-30% of cognitively normal people over 70, so it establishes pathology, not diagnosis. Appropriate-use criteria restrict it to atypical or early-onset presentations; it is required for anti-amyloid antibody therapy (lecanemab, donanemab) eligibility, and tau PET now stages neurodegeneration.
questions.imageAlt: Axial amyloid PET: AD (diffuse cortical retention, loss of gray-white contrast), cognitively normal amyloid-positive, and amyloid-negative (tracer confined to white matter). (RITE Review deck, slide 75)

questions.stem: A term neonate is born after placental abruption with Apgar scores of 1 and 3, cord pH 6.9, and moderate encephalopathy on Sarnat staging at 2 hours of life. What intervention improves survival without disability?

options.text: Therapeutic hypothermia to 33.5°C for 72 hours initiated within 6 hours of birth

questions.explanation: Whole-body or selective head cooling reduces death or major disability (NNT ~7) in infants ≥36 weeks with moderate-severe HIE (CoolCap, NICHD, TOBY). Deeper or longer cooling (NICHD optimizing trial) and adjunctive erythropoietin (HEAL) did not add benefit; cooling of mild HIE or preterm infants is unproven. MRI at day 4–7 (basal ganglia/thalamus and watershed patterns) guides prognosis; seizures are treated with phenobarbital first-line.

questions.stem: The histology shown demonstrates uniform round nuclei with clear perinuclear halos. What causes the halo?
questions.explanation: Formalin fixation artifact. The fried-egg appearance is an artifact absent on frozen section; look also for chicken-wire vessels and microcalcification. The perinuclear halo is a formalin-fixation artifact (absent on frozen section). Also look for perineuronal satellitosis, microcalcifications and the branching chicken-wire capillaries. Minigemistocytes are acceptable; frank astrocytic differentiation with mitoses and necrosis moves the tumor to grade 3.
questions.imageAlt: H&E (main panel) with normal white matter inset: monotonous sheets of cells with uniform round nuclei, fine chromatin and a clear perinuclear halo (fried-egg or honeycomb appearance). (RITE Review deck, slide 28)

questions.stem: The putamen histology shown demonstrates loss of small neurons with sparing of large neurons. Which neuronal population is lost first?

options.text: Medium spiny GABAergic neurons of the indirect pathway

questions.explanation: Medium spiny GABAergic neurons of the indirect pathway. Early loss of enkephalin/D2 indirect-pathway neurons explains chorea; CAG >=40 is fully penetrant. Selective loss of medium spiny GABAergic projection neurons (enkephalin/D2 indirect pathway first, explaining chorea) with sparing of large cholinergic interneurons until late. Caudate atrophy (boxcar ventricles) precedes putamen; Vonsattel grades 0-4. HTT CAG repeat >=40 fully penetrant, 36-39 reduced penetrance, 27-35 intermediate with paternal anticipation. Intranuclear huntingtin/ubiquitin inclusions on IHC.
questions.imageAlt: H&E of putamen: rarefaction of the neuropil with gliosis and loss of small neurons; a spared large neuron is arrowed. (RITE Review deck, slide 158)

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with headaches has the contrast CT shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma. Cyst with enhancing mural nodule in a child is pilocytic astrocytoma regardless of location; hemangioblastoma is an adult posterior fossa lesion; abscess is a complete ring with restricted diffusion. Cyst-with-nodule morphology in a child is pilocytic astrocytoma until proven otherwise; supratentorial location does not change that. Deck\'s exclusions: hemangioblastoma would be in the posterior fossa of an adult; an abscess enhances as a complete ring with restricted diffusion. Enhancing nodule plus non-enhancing cyst wall means resection of the nodule alone suffices.
questions.imageAlt: Axial contrast CT: large hypodense cyst occupying much of the hemisphere with an enhancing solid mural nodule. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 128)

questions.stem: GFAP-positive tumor of large eosinophilic cells at the foramen of Monro. Which gene pair is implicated?
questions.explanation: Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma. SEGA is a tuberous sclerosis tumor from TSC1/TSC2 loss with mTORC1 activation.
questions.imageAlt: Large polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli; GFAP immunopositivity; perivascular pseudorosette-like arrangements.
questions.salient: Surveillance MRI every 1 to 3 years to age 25 in TSC; Everolimus for growing SEGA
questions.learning: Foramen of Monro location; surveillance MRI every 1 to 3 years until age 25 in TSC; everolimus for growing lesions. Other TSC lesions: cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, cardiac rhabdomyoma, renal angiomyolipoma, facial angiofibroma, ash-leaf spots.

questions.stem: Mesial temporal biopsy from a patient with fever and aphasia. Panels A and B show:

options.text: Microglial nodule and perivascular lymphocytic cuffing of viral encephalitis

questions.explanation: Viral encephalitis: microglial nodule and perivascular cuffing. A microglial nodule (A) and perivascular lymphocytic cuff (B) in mesial temporal cortex indicate HSV encephalitis.
questions.imageAlt: A: cortical section with a focal cluster of microglia and lymphocytes (microglial nodule). B: perivascular lymphocytic cuff around a small vessel. Marginal note: mesial temporal lobe.
questions.salient: HSV-1: hemorrhagic necrosis of medial temporal, insular, orbitofrontal cortex; Cowdry A inclusions; Empiric acyclovir; CSF PCR may be negative in the first 72 hours
questions.learning: HSV-1: hemorrhagic necrotizing encephalitis of medial temporal, orbitofrontal, and insular cortex; Cowdry A intranuclear inclusions in neurons and glia. Microglial nodules and neuronophagia are generic to viral encephalitides (arboviral, rabies, HIV). Treat empirically with acyclovir.

questions.stem: The trichrome stain shown demonstrates rimmed vacuoles in a 68-year-old with quadriceps and finger flexor weakness. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Anti-cN1A antibodies are present in about a third
CK is typically over 50 times normal

questions.explanation: Anti-cN1A antibodies are present in about a third. Inclusion body myositis: steroid refractory, mild CK elevation, asymmetric distal/quadriceps pattern, vacuoles with amyloid, tau and TDP-43. Most common acquired myopathy after 50; slowly progressive, asymmetric, with early quadriceps and finger/wrist flexor weakness (versus DM/PM proximal pattern), dysphagia, and mild CK elevation. Vacuoles contain amyloid (Congo red), phosphorylated tau and TDP-43; COX-negative fibers and endomysial CD8 invasion accompany. Anti-cN1A (NT5C1A) antibodies in about a third. Refractory to steroids and immunosuppression, which helps distinguish it from PM misdiagnoses.
questions.imageAlt: H&E and modified Gomori trichrome: endomysial inflammation with fibers containing rimmed vacuoles (red-rimmed on trichrome, arrows). (RITE Review deck, slide 205)

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has bilateral leg pain with walking that resolves when he sits or leans forward. The myelogram shown is consistent with which diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lumbar spinal stenosis. Multilevel narrowing of the contrast column with an hourglass contour plus positional (neurogenic) claudication is degenerative stenosis. Degenerative stenosis (disc bulge, ligamentum flavum hypertrophy, facet arthropathy) produces neurogenic claudication: leg pain with standing and walking, relieved by sitting or flexion, in contrast to vascular claudication. Myelography is now reserved for patients who cannot undergo MRI or with hardware.
questions.imageAlt: AP (A) and lateral (B) contrast myelogram: multilevel narrowing of the contrast-filled dural sac with a washboard/hourglass contour at the disc levels. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 47)

questions.stem: Bilateral subdural collections are hyperintense on FLAIR; the left collection is also hyperintense on unenhanced T1. What is the most likely age of the left collection?

options.text: The signal cannot date a subdural collection

questions.explanation: Approximately 3 weeks. T1 and T2/FLAIR bright indicates extracellular methemoglobin, late subacute; subdural blood evolves more slowly than parenchymal blood, but the stage still dates it to weeks. T1 bright plus T2/FLAIR bright = extracellular methemoglobin, i.e. late subacute; the deck\'s answer is roughly 20 days. Hemosiderin margins (gray T1, dark T2) appear in weeks 2-3. Subdural blood evolves more slowly than parenchymal blood (higher oxygen tension, less macrophage access), so intervals are approximate.
questions.imageAlt: Axial FLAIR (top row) shows bilateral hyperintense subdural collections, larger on the left; coronal non-contrast T1 (bottom) shows the left collection to be T1 bright. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 13)

questions.stem: FLAIR and T2 show irregular ventricular margins with CSF-isointense periventricular cavities in a child born at 27 weeks. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Cystic periventricular leukomalacia / porencephaly. Gliotic, irregular, non-gray-matter-lined periventricular cavities in a preterm survivor are cystic PVL, a destructive lesion.
questions.imageAlt: A: FLAIR with irregular, angulated lateral ventricular margins and periventricular signal change with CSF-isointense cavities merging with the ventricles. B: T2 with a large confluent CSF-intensity region contiguous with both ventricles and thinned overlying white matter.
questions.salient: Spastic diplegia; oligodendrocyte precursor vulnerability; Malformations (schizencephaly) have gray-matter-lined clefts
questions.learning: Destructive lesions (PVL, porencephaly, hydranencephaly, multicystic encephalomalacia) are distinguished from malformations (schizencephaly, holoprosencephaly) by the absence of gray matter lining and by irregular, gliotic margins. PVL: preterm white matter injury of oligodendrocyte precursors, spastic diplegia, later periventricular gliosis with wavy ventricular contours.
questions.note: Revised after review; original draft misread this as a butterfly glioma/lymphoma. Distinction from open-lip schizencephaly (Exam 269) rests on the absence of a gray-matter-lined cleft.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with thunderclap headache has the CT shown. Following aneurysm repair she develops amnesia and confabulation. Injury to which structure explains this?

options.text: Basal forebrain and fornix via ACom perforators
Dorsomedial thalamus via artery of Percheron

questions.explanation: Basal forebrain and fornix via ACom perforators. ACom aneurysms and their treatment can injure basal forebrain/fornix perforators, producing an amnestic-confabulatory syndrome. ACom is the most common site of ruptured aneurysm. Blood distribution predicts location: interhemispheric/gyrus rectus for ACom, sylvian fissure for MCA, prepontine for basilar. ACom rupture or clipping can injure the perforators to the fornix and basal forebrain, producing amnesia and confabulation. Complications: rebleeding (highest in first 24 h), vasospasm (days 3-14, nimodipine), hydrocephalus, hyponatremia (cerebral salt wasting).
questions.imageAlt: Axial non-contrast CT: subarachnoid hemorrhage filling the basal cisterns and interhemispheric fissure with a rounded density at the ACom region (arrow). (Neuroradiology deck, slide 72)

questions.stem: A 65-year-old patient presents with rapidly progressive dementia and prominent myoclonic startle. EEG reveals periodic, synchronous, biphasic and triphasic sharp-wave complexes repeating at ~1 Hz. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sporadic CJD presents with rapid neurocognitive decline, myoclonus, and generalized periodic discharges at ~1 Hz. SSPE produces periodic complexes at much longer intervals (4–15 seconds).

questions.stem: Two pituitary adenoma panels: chromophobic and acidophilic. The acidophilic (GH-producing) variant with fibrous bodies predicts:

options.text: Poorer somatostatin analog response and more aggressive behavior

questions.explanation: Pituitary adenoma subtypes. Sparsely granulated somatotroph adenomas (cytokeratin fibrous bodies) respond less to somatostatin analogs.
questions.imageAlt: Left: chromophobic adenoma with pale cells in sheets. Right: acidophilic (GH-producing) adenoma with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm.
questions.salient: Tinctorial classes are historical; lineage by PIT1, TPIT, SF1; Reticulin loss separates adenoma from hyperplasia
questions.learning: Tinctorial classification is historical; current classification uses hormone and transcription factor immunostains (PIT1: GH, PRL, TSH; TPIT: ACTH; SF1: gonadotroph). Sparsely granulated somatotroph adenomas carry fibrous bodies (cytokeratin dot) and respond less to somatostatin analogs. Loss of reticulin acinar pattern separates adenoma from hyperplasia.

questions.stem: Temporal lobectomy specimen from a 30-year-old with intracerebral hemorrhage whose sister had a similar bleed. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Cavernous malformation, histology. Back-to-back thin-walled sinusoidal channels without intervening brain are a cavernoma; familial clustering suggests CCM genes.
questions.imageAlt: A: low-power section of temporal lobe with a hemorrhagic vascular lesion. B: closely apposed, dilated, thin-walled vascular channels lined by endothelium without intervening brain parenchyma, with adjacent hemosiderin. Marginal note: intracerebral hemorrhage, sister with similar problem.
questions.salient: No intervening neural tissue, no elastic lamina: cavernoma; AVM has intervening gliotic brain; CCM1/KRIT1, CCM2, CCM3/PDCD10 autosomal dominant
questions.learning: Cavernoma: back-to-back sinusoidal channels, no elastic lamina or smooth muscle, no intervening neural tissue (versus AVM, which has intervening gliotic brain and arterialized veins). Familial cavernomatosis: CCM1/KRIT1, CCM2, CCM3/PDCD10, autosomal dominant, multiple lesions; CCM3 is most aggressive.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man has slowly progressive spastic gait since his twenties with hyperreflexia, mild vibratory loss at the toes, and urinary urgency, but preserved arm function and cognition; his father and sister are affected. What is the most common genetic cause?
questions.explanation: SPAST accounts for ~40% of autosomal dominant hereditary spastic paraplegia (>80 loci overall); ATL1 is the leading childhood-onset AD form. SPG11 is the most common AR complicated HSP, with thin corpus callosum, cognitive impairment, and neuropathy. Adrenomyeloneuropathy must be excluded in males (VLCFA). Treatment is symptomatic (baclofen, intrathecal baclofen, botulinum toxin, physiotherapy).

questions.stem: A 26-year-old with 5 days of severe headache. DWI, T1 pre, T1 post, and FLAIR are shown. The best next step is:

options.text: Empiric antibiotics and aspiration for culture

questions.explanation: Brain abscess with central restricted diffusion. Central diffusion restriction within a smooth ring-enhancing lesion is a pyogenic abscess; aspirate for organism and start broad antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old with the same lesion and cyanotic congenital heart disease: what is the mechanism?
questions.explanation: Right-to-left shunts allow venous bacteria to bypass the pulmonary capillary filter and reach the brain.
questions.imageAlt: A: DWI bright central signal within a left frontal lesion. B: T1 precontrast hypointense center. C: T1 post-contrast smooth ring enhancement. D: FLAIR with surrounding vasogenic edema. Marginal note: 26-year-old with severe headache, abscess vs tumor vs metastasis.
questions.context: A 26-year-old with 5 days of severe headache. DWI, T1 pre, T1 post, and FLAIR are shown. The best next step is:
questions.salient: DWI restriction in the cavity distinguishes abscess from necrotic tumor; Rim thinner on ventricular side; ventricular rupture is fatal
questions.learning: DWI restriction in the cavity distinguishes abscess from necrotic tumor. Rim thinner on the ventricular side; ventricular rupture is fatal. Sources: sinusitis/otitis (contiguous), endocarditis (hematogenous, MCA distribution), right-to-left shunt. Stereotactic aspiration for lesions >2.5 cm plus 6 to 8 weeks IV antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy with tuberous sclerosis complex has an enhancing lesion at the foramen of Monro that has grown from 8 mm to 15 mm on serial surveillance MRI. He is asymptomatic and there is no ventriculomegaly. What is the diagnosis and preferred first-line therapy?
questions.explanation: TSC (TSC1/TSC2 loss) drives constitutive mTORC1 activation. For a growing but asymptomatic SEGA, everolimus is first-line (EXIST-1); acute obstructive hydrocephalus or rapidly symptomatic SEGA warrants surgical resection instead.

questions.stem: A brain MRI in an 80-year-old woman with dementia demonstrates recurrent lobar hemorrhages and numerous superficial cortical microbleeds on gradient-echo sequences, with complete sparing of the basal ganglia and pons. What is the underlying pathology?
questions.explanation: CAA results from beta-amyloid deposition in cortical and leptomeningeal arterial walls, predisposing elderly patients to lobar hemorrhages, cortical superficial siderosis, and subcortical microbleeds (Boston criteria 2.0).

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl with focal epilepsy has the coronal T2 image shown, with nodules along the ventricles that are isointense to gray matter. Which gene should be tested?
questions.explanation: FLNA. Bilateral periventricular nodular heterotopia is FLNA (X-linked, female predominance, aortic disease); TS nodules calcify and enhance. Neurons that failed to migrate from the ventricular zone. Bilateral PVNH is classically X-linked FLNA (filamin A) in females, with male lethality, aortic dilatation and valvular disease; ARFGEF2 in the AR microcephalic form. Distinguish from TS subependymal nodules (calcified, enhance, not gray-matter isointense) and subcortical band heterotopia (DCX).
questions.imageAlt: Coronal T2 of a 6-year-old with developmental delay and focal epilepsy: nodules lining the lateral ventricles that are isointense to gray matter on all sequences and do not enhance. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 110)

questions.stem: What is the primary pharmacologic agent administered to reverse an acute malignant hyperthermia crisis?
questions.explanation: Dantrolene acts directly on the ryanodine receptor to block calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, serving as the definitive antidote for malignant hyperthermia.

questions.stem: Fingolimod requires first-dose cardiac observation for at least 6 hours because of what effect?

options.text: Bradycardia and atrioventricular block from S1P receptor agonism on atrial myocytes

questions.explanation: Fingolimod (nonselective S1P receptor modulator) sequesters lymphocytes in lymph nodes; S1P1/S1P3 activation on cardiomyocytes causes transient bradycardia and rarely AV block after the first dose. Other concerns include macular edema, VZV reactivation (verify immunity), and rebound on discontinuation. Newer S1P agents (siponimod, ozanimod, ponesimod) reduce but do not eliminate first-dose effects.

questions.stem: In the cerebellar cortex, climbing fibers provide powerful excitatory glutamatergic input to Purkinje cell dendrites. What is their sole source of origin?
questions.explanation: Climbing fibers arise exclusively from the contralateral inferior olivary complex in the medulla and project directly onto Purkinje cell dendritic trees.

questions.stem: The coronal brain slice shown demonstrates a CSF space between the leaves of the septum pellucidum. In which population is this finding essentially universal?
questions.explanation: Preterm infants. Cavum septum pellucidum is present in nearly all preterm infants and closes by 3-6 months; persistence in adults is a normal variant. Present in essentially all preterm infants and closes from posterior to anterior by about 3-6 months; persists in a minority of adults as a normal variant. A cavum vergae is the posterior extension. Enlarged cavum has been reported in boxers and schizophrenia but is not diagnostic of either.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal brain slice: CSF-filled space between the two leaves of the septum pellucidum, between the frontal horns. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 120)

questions.stem: A child with a short neck and low hairline has the cervical imaging shown. Which of the following is a recognized association?
questions.explanation: Sprengel deformity. Klippel-Feil associations include Sprengel deformity, renal agenesis, congenital heart disease, deafness, Duane syndrome and mirror movements; GDF6, GDF3 and MEOX1 in familial cases. Failure of segmentation of cervical somites (weeks 3-8). Classic triad (short neck, low posterior hairline, restricted neck motion) is present in under half. Associations: Sprengel deformity, scoliosis, renal agenesis, congenital heart disease, hearing loss, Duane syndrome, mirror movements (synkinesia). GDF6, GDF3 and MEOX1 variants in familial cases. Fused segments concentrate stress on adjacent levels, raising risk of instability and myelopathy after minor trauma.
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal MRI, sagittal CT and coronal CT cervical spine: congenital fusion of multiple cervical vertebral bodies with hypoplastic or absent intervertebral discs. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 54)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is found with left hemiplegia and gaze deviation last known well 14 hours earlier. CTA shows a right M1 occlusion; CT perfusion shows a 20 mL core with 110 mL of hypoperfused tissue. What is indicated?

options.text: Mechanical thrombectomy based on DAWN/DEFUSE-3 mismatch criteria

questions.explanation: DAWN (6–24 h, clinical-core mismatch) and DEFUSE-3 (6–16 h, perfusion mismatch) established thrombectomy for anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion in selected late-window patients. Subsequent trials (SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT) extended benefit to large-core infarcts, and ATTENTION/BAOCHE to basilar occlusion.

questions.stem: A 26-week infant develops a bulging fontanelle and acute anemia on day 3. Cranial ultrasound shows a large left intraventricular hemorrhage distending the ventricle with a fan-shaped echodensity in the adjacent periventricular white matter. What is the grade and what is the parenchymal lesion?

options.text: Grade IV; periventricular hemorrhagic venous infarction
Grade I; germinal matrix hemorrhage only

questions.explanation: Germinal matrix-intraventricular hemorrhage (Papile grades I–IV) affects infants <32 weeks, mostly within 72 hours of birth; grade IV is not arterial extension but venous infarction from compressed terminal veins, and strongly predicts contralateral spastic hemiplegia. Grade III/IV risk post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus. Screening ultrasound is performed at 7–10 days and near term-equivalent age. Antenatal steroids and delayed cord clamping reduce risk.

questions.stem: Vigabatrin therapy for infantile spasms requires which specific monitoring?

options.text: Serial ophthalmologic examination and, when feasible, visual field testing for bilateral concentric field constriction
Serial liver function tests for hepatotoxicity

questions.explanation: Vigabatrin (irreversible GABA-transaminase inhibitor) causes permanent bilateral concentric peripheral visual field constriction in roughly a third of exposed patients, cumulative-dose dependent, prompting REMS enrollment and baseline plus periodic ophthalmologic assessment (ERG in infants). It also produces transient symmetric T2/DWI signal in basal ganglia and thalami in infants.

questions.stem: What muscle is spared in a complete common fibular (peroneal) nerve lesion at the fibular head, but denervated in an L5 radiculopathy?
questions.explanation: The tibialis posterior mediates foot inversion and is innervated by the tibial nerve (L5 root); it is spared in common fibular neuropathy but denervated in an L5 radiculopathy. Gluteus medius is another useful L5 tibial/superior gluteal discriminator.

questions.stem: The images shown demonstrate a sellar mass waisted at the diaphragma sellae. A prolactin of 80 ng/mL is most consistent with:

options.text: Stalk effect from a non-functioning macroadenoma

questions.explanation: Stalk effect from a non-functioning macroadenoma. Snowman sign and sellar expansion favor adenoma; modest prolactin elevation reflects stalk compression, whereas prolactinomas of this size run much higher. Soft adenomas indent at the diaphragma sellae, giving the snowman configuration; sellar expansion also favors adenoma over meningioma (which arises above the sella and has a dural base). Presents with bitemporal hemianopia (superior fields first), hypopituitarism, hyperprolactinemia from stalk effect (usually <100-200 ng/mL, versus higher in prolactinoma). Prolactinomas are treated medically with cabergoline; other macroadenomas transsphenoidally.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal T1 (with schematic overlay) and sagittal T1: sellar mass >10 mm expanding the sella and rising into the suprasellar cistern, waisted at the diaphragma sellae. (RITE Review deck, slide 44)

questions.stem: An infant presents with brittle "kinky" hair, hypopigmentation, severe neurodevelopmental arrest, and recurrent subdural hematomas. Serum copper and ceruloplasmin levels are low. What gene is mutated?
questions.explanation: Menkes disease is an X-linked recessive disorder of copper distribution caused by variants in ATP7A, preventing intestinal copper absorption and delivery to cuproenzymes (lysyl oxidase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, cytochrome c oxidase). Early subcutaneous copper histidinate improves outcomes.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male presents with right homonymous hemianopsia and the inability to read written text. He retains the ability to write fluently to dictation, but is unable to read back his own handwriting. Where is the lesion?

options.text: Wernicke area in the left superior temporal gyrus
Left occipital cortex and splenium of the corpus callosum
Broca area in the inferior frontal gyrus

questions.explanation: Alexia without agraphia is a disconnection syndrome caused by infarction of the left visual cortex (right hemianopsia) and the splenium of the corpus callosum, preventing right occipital visual input from reaching the left language centers.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old with chorea, seizures, and cognitive decline has caudate atrophy on MRI; HTT testing is normal. Which phenocopy is most common in European ancestry?
questions.explanation: Huntington-like syndrome with normal HTT testing. C9orf72 is the most frequent HD phenocopy in Europeans; HDL2 predominates in African ancestry; DRPLA in Japan.
questions.imageAlt: Axial T1 and T2: flattening of the caudate heads with boxcar frontal horns and mild generalized atrophy. Marginal note: 38-year-old with cognitive impairment, chorea, athetosis, seizures, normal Huntington testing.
questions.salient: Seizures favor DRPLA, juvenile HD, chorea-acanthocytosis; Check acanthocytes/CK, ceruloplasmin, TBP repeats
questions.learning: Phenocopies: C9orf72 expansion (most common in Europeans), HDL2 (JPH3, African ancestry), SCA17 (TBP), DRPLA (ATN1, Japanese; seizures and myoclonus), chorea-acanthocytosis (VPS13A; orolingual dystonia, seizures, elevated CK), McLeod syndrome (XK), Wilson disease, benign hereditary chorea (NKX2-1).

questions.stem: The cutaneous findings shown accompany proximal weakness in a 55-year-old woman. Which antibody carries the strongest association with malignancy?
questions.explanation: Anti-TIF1-gamma. TIF1-gamma and NXP2 predict cancer in adult DM; MDA5 amyopathic with ILD; Mi-2 classic and treatment responsive. Skin may precede weakness (amyopathic DM). Antibody-phenotype associations: anti-Mi-2 classic rash and treatment responsive; anti-TIF1-gamma and anti-NXP2 malignancy in adults (NXP2 calcinosis in juvenile DM); anti-MDA5 amyopathic with rapidly progressive ILD; anti-SAE. Screen adults for occult cancer for 2-3 years after diagnosis. Juvenile DM: calcinosis and vasculopathy, not malignancy.
questions.imageAlt: Clinical photographs: heliotrope eyelid discoloration, periungual telangiectasia with ragged cuticles, Gottron papules over the knuckles/PIP joints, and truncal erythema. (RITE Review deck, slide 196)

questions.stem: Bilateral symmetric necrosis of the globus pallidus is characteristic of which neurotoxic exposure?
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide intoxication results in severe cellular hypoxia and selectively produces bilateral necrosis of the globus pallidus; delayed leukoencephalopathy may follow weeks later.

questions.stem: In an unconscious patient, caloric irrigation of the left external auditory canal with cold water produces slow deviation of both eyes toward which direction (assuming an intact brainstem vestibulo-ocular reflex)?

options.text: Toward the left ear (slow conjugate drift toward cold water)

questions.explanation: Cold water reduces vestibular firing on that side, driving the eyes in a slow tonic phase toward the irrigated ear; the fast corrective nystagmus (COWS) is toward the opposite ear and requires an intact cortex, so comatose patients show only the tonic deviation.

questions.stem: EEG from a 70-year-old 2 days after a left MCA stroke. The pattern is:
questions.explanation: Lateralized periodic discharges. Stereotyped ~1 Hz sharp complexes confined to the left temporal chain are LPDs.

questions.stem: Which etiology is most classically associated with LPDs in an acutely confused febrile patient?
questions.explanation: Temporal LPDs in febrile encephalopathy point to HSV encephalitis.
questions.imageAlt: Bipolar temporal chains: repetitive, stereotyped sharp-wave complexes at ~1 Hz over the left temporal chain (F7-T3, T3-T5, T5-O1) with a preserved but attenuated background on the right. Marginal note: status post stroke.
questions.context: EEG from a 70-year-old 2 days after a left MCA stroke. The pattern is:
questions.salient: Ictal-interictal continuum; LPDs-plus carry higher seizure risk; 1 Hz generalized periodic discharges plus dementia suggest CJD; triphasic morphology suggests metabolic encephalopathy
questions.learning: Causes: acute stroke, HSV encephalitis, tumor, less often nonketotic hyperglycemia. Ictal-interictal continuum; LPDs-plus (with superimposed fast activity or rhythmicity) carry higher seizure risk. Generalized periodic discharges at 1 Hz in a demented patient suggest CJD; triphasic morphology suggests metabolic encephalopathy.

questions.stem: Biopsy shows perifascicular atrophy with perimysial inflammation. Diagnosis and mechanism?
questions.explanation: Dermatomyositis. Perifascicular atrophy reflects ischemia from C5b-9-mediated endomysial capillary loss in dermatomyositis.

questions.stem: Which antibody most strongly mandates malignancy screening in an adult with this biopsy?
questions.explanation: Anti-TIF1-gamma (and NXP2) carry the highest cancer association in adult dermatomyositis.
questions.imageAlt: H&E: perifascicular atrophy with perimysial and perivascular inflammation. ATPase: atrophic fibers at fascicle periphery.
questions.context: Biopsy shows perifascicular atrophy with perimysial inflammation. Diagnosis and mechanism?
questions.salient: Perifascicular atrophy is diagnostic even without inflammation; Antibodies: TIF1-gamma and NXP2 (cancer), MDA5 (ILD), Mi-2
questions.learning: Perifascicular atrophy is diagnostic even without inflammation. MxA/interferon signature; myositis-specific antibodies (Mi-2, TIF1-gamma with cancer, NXP2 with calcinosis and cancer, MDA5 with ILD, SAE). Cancer screening in adults.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old in Connecticut presents in August with bilateral facial palsy and headache 6 weeks after an expanding annular rash. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

options.text: Early disseminated Lyme neuroborreliosis; ceftriaxone or oral doxycycline

questions.explanation: Lyme neuroborreliosis (Borrelia burgdorferi) produces the triad of lymphocytic meningitis, cranial neuropathy (bilateral facial palsy is highly suggestive), and painful radiculoneuritis (Bannwarth syndrome). Diagnosis uses two-tier serology plus CSF antibody index. Oral doxycycline is now considered equivalent to IV ceftriaxone for most presentations. Late Lyme encephalomyelitis is rare in North America.

questions.stem: A patient with severe traumatic brain injury has a sustained ICP of 32 mm Hg despite head elevation, sedation, and normothermia. Serum sodium is 138. Which is the appropriate next tier of therapy?

options.text: Prolonged prophylactic hyperventilation to PaCO2 25 mm Hg
Hyperosmolar therapy with hypertonic saline or mannitol, targeting CPP 60–70 mm Hg

questions.explanation: Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines support hyperosmolar therapy (hypertonic saline is favored in hypovolemia or hyponatremia; mannitol requires osmolar gap monitoring), CSF drainage, and surgical decompression (RESCUEicp reduced mortality but increased vegetative survival). Hyperventilation is a brief bridge only (vasoconstriction lowers CBF). Corticosteroids increase mortality in TBI (CRASH). Prophylactic hypothermia (Eurotherm, POLAR) is not beneficial.

questions.stem: Coronal T1, CT, FLAIR, and T1 post show a round T1-bright, CT-dense, non-enhancing midline lesion at the foramen of Monro with ventricular dilation. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Colloid cyst of the third ventricle with obstructive hydrocephalus. T1 hyperintensity, CT hyperdensity, and absence of enhancement at the foramen of Monro are diagnostic of colloid cyst.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal T1: round, homogeneously hyperintense midline mass beneath the septum at the foramen of Monro. CT: hyperdense round lesion at the anterior third ventricle with dilated frontal horns. FLAIR: bright lesion; post-contrast T1: no significant enhancement. An additional calcified right periventricular lesion is present.
questions.salient: Sudden death from acute obstruction; positional headache; SEGA would enhance avidly (compare Exam 255)
questions.learning: Classic cause of positional headache and sudden death from acute hydrocephalus. Treat symptomatic or enlarging cysts (endoscopic resection). Histology: simple ciliated columnar/cuboidal epithelium with mucinous content.
questions.note: The right periventricular calcified lesion is unexplained by the image alone; SEGA/TSC would be a consideration if the midline lesion enhanced, which it does not appear to.

questions.stem: A 6-week-old girl develops daily clusters of tonic seizures evolving into spasms, with severe hypotonia, cortical visual impairment, and absent developmental progress. Sequencing identifies a de novo truncating variant in an X-linked gene. What is the disorder and what agent has FDA approval specifically for its seizures?
questions.explanation: CDKL5 deficiency disorder presents with epilepsy at a median of 6 weeks (hypermotor-tonic-spasm sequences), profound developmental impairment, and cortical visual impairment; it is distinct from Rett syndrome despite historical classification as an atypical variant. Ganaxolone (neurosteroid GABA-A modulator) was approved in 2022. PCDH19 causes clustered febrile seizures in females (cellular interference).

questions.stem: The FDG-PET images shown demonstrate progressive frontal and anterior temporal hypometabolism over two years. Which pattern would instead suggest dementia with Lewy bodies?

options.text: Occipital hypometabolism with a preserved posterior cingulate (cingulate island sign)

questions.explanation: Occipital hypometabolism with a preserved posterior cingulate (cingulate island sign). FTD frontal/anterior temporal; AD temporoparietal and posterior cingulate; DLB occipital; CBD asymmetric; semantic dementia left temporal pole. Regional hypometabolism patterns: FTD frontal and anterior temporal; AD temporoparietal and posterior cingulate/precuneus; DLB occipital (with the cingulate island sign, preserved posterior cingulate); CBD asymmetric frontoparietal; semantic dementia left temporal pole. FDG-PET is useful for separating FTD from AD when structural imaging is ambiguous.
questions.imageAlt: Axial FDG-PET one year (top) and three years (bottom) after symptom onset: progressive hypometabolism of the frontal and anterior temporal lobes with relatively preserved posterior metabolism. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 97)

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has a two-year history of stepwise leg weakness worse after walking and when upright; the imaging shown demonstrates long-segment cord edema with dorsal serpentine flow voids. What is the mechanism of cord injury?

options.text: Arterial steal from the anterior spinal artery
Direct compression by a vascular mass

questions.explanation: Venous hypertension and congestive ischemia. An arterialized radicular vein raises intramedullary venous pressure; deficits are reversible if the fistula is disconnected early, and steroids may worsen the picture. Most common spinal vascular malformation; middle-aged men, thoracolumbar. Arterialized radicular vein causes venous hypertension and congestive myelopathy, so deficits are insidious, stepwise and worsened by exertion or upright posture. Cord edema plus flow voids is the MRI signature; catheter angiography is required to find the feeder. Endovascular or surgical disconnection reverses deficits if done early; steroids can precipitate deterioration.
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal T1, T2, T2-CISS and spinal angiography: long-segment central cord T2 hyperintensity with expansion, serpentine dorsal intradural flow voids on T2/CISS, and the fistula on angiography. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 40)

questions.stem: Axial T2 and coronal images show CSF-filled clefts from ventricle to convexity. Which feature distinguishes this from porencephaly?
questions.explanation: Open-lip schizencephaly. A gray-matter-lined pial-ependymal cleft defines schizencephaly (malformation); porencephaly is a gliotic destructive cavity.
questions.imageAlt: A: axial T2 with a large CSF-intensity cleft extending from the lateral ventricles to the convexity, lined by cortex. B: coronal image showing the full-thickness clefts communicating between the ventricular system and the subarachnoid space with gray matter along the walls.
questions.salient: Associated polymicrogyria, absent septum pellucidum (septo-optic dysplasia); COL4A1, EMX2
questions.learning: Schizencephaly is a malformation of cortical development (post-migrational disruption or abnormal neuronal migration) defined by a gray-matter-lined cleft; the pial-ependymal seam differentiates it from porencephaly. Associated with polymicrogyria lining the cleft, septo-optic dysplasia (absent septum pellucidum), and COL4A1 or EMX2 variants. Bilateral open-lip: severe developmental delay, spastic quadriparesis, epilepsy.
questions.note: Revised after review; original draft misread this as a butterfly glioma.

questions.stem: The images shown demonstrate a non-enhancing, non-calcified sellar cyst lined by a single epithelial layer. What is the appropriate management if asymptomatic?
questions.explanation: Observation. Rathke cleft cyst is treated only when symptomatic, by drainage. Remnant of Rathke pouch, between adenohypophysis and neurohypophysis. Usually incidental; can cause headache or hypopituitarism. Signal varies with protein content (may be T1 bright); a small T2-dark intracystic nodule is characteristic. Unlike craniopharyngioma there is no calcification, no solid enhancing component and no wet keratin. Treated only if symptomatic, by drainage rather than resection.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal T1 pre- and post-gadolinium and histology: smooth, non-enhancing intrasellar/suprasellar cyst without calcification; wall is a single layer of ciliated columnar epithelium. (RITE Review deck, slide 50)

questions.stem: A male infant with microcephaly presents with ambiguous genitalia, cleft palate, and 2–3 syndactyly of the toes. Plasma sterol analysis shows markedly elevated 7-dehydrocholesterol with low cholesterol. What enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of 3-beta-hydroxysterol delta-7-reductase (DHCR7), impairing cholesterol biosynthesis and elevating the precursor 7-dehydrocholesterol.

questions.stem: Lobulated cerebellopontine angle mass following CSF on T1/T2 but bright on DWI and non-enhancing. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Epidermoid cyst. DWI restriction and heterogeneous FLAIR distinguish epidermoid from arachnoid cyst.
questions.imageAlt: T1 post-contrast: nonenhancing lobulated cerebellopontine angle mass. T2: CSF-like signal insinuating around structures. DWI: markedly bright (restricted diffusion).
questions.salient: Keratinizing squamous lining; rupture causes chemical meningitis; Dermoid: midline, fat-bright on T1, adnexal structures
questions.learning: DWI restriction and heterogeneous FLAIR signal distinguish epidermoid from arachnoid cyst, which follows CSF on all sequences.
