Cerebellopontine angle (third most common CPA lesion after schwannoma and meningioma) and parasellar locations. Lined by keratinizing squamous epithelium with lamellated keratin; rupture causes chemical meningitis. Dermoid contains adnexal structures and is fat-bright on T1, midline.

questions.stem: On the labeled MR venogram shown, which structure receives the vein of Galen and the inferior sagittal sinus?
questions.explanation: Straight sinus. The straight sinus carries deep venous drainage to the torcular; the right transverse sinus is usually dominant. Board-relevant anatomy: the straight sinus receives the vein of Galen and inferior sagittal sinus and runs to the torcular; the internal cerebral veins and basal veins of Rosenthal form the deep system. The right transverse sinus is usually dominant; hypoplastic left transverse sinus is a common normal variant and a thrombosis mimic.
questions.imageAlt: Labeled AP and lateral MRV: superior and inferior sagittal sinuses, internal cerebral veins, vein of Galen, straight sinus, confluence (torcular), transverse and sigmoid sinuses, cavernous sinus, superior ophthalmic vein, jugular. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 77)

questions.stem: The lesion shown is bright on T1 and dark on T2, GRE and DWI. What is the approximate age of the hemorrhage?
questions.explanation: 2 days to 1 week. T1 bright with T2 dark is intracellular methemoglobin, the early subacute stage. Fe3+ metHb has 5 unpaired electrons and, unlike deoxy-Hb, lets water approach the iron (inner-sphere relaxation), producing T1 shortening. Still intracellular, so T2 stays dark. Mnemonic: Bleed Die (bright T1 / dark T2).
questions.imageAlt: Axial T1 bright, T2 dark, GRE dark, DWI dark. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 9)

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with cervical spondylosis falls and hyperextends his neck. He has severe weakness of the hands and arms with relatively preserved leg strength and urinary retention. What is the syndrome?
questions.explanation: Central cord syndrome is the most common incomplete spinal cord injury; hyperextension pinches the cord between osteophytes and the buckled ligamentum flavum, injuring the central gray and medial corticospinal fibers (arms are represented medially in the lateral corticospinal tract). Prognosis for leg recovery is good; hand function recovers least.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl experiences multiple brief (5–10 second) staring spells per day. Hyperventilation induces an episode. EEG demonstrates generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges. What is the first-line medication?
questions.explanation: Ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels in thalamic relay neurons and is first-line for childhood absence epilepsy (Glauser 2010: equal efficacy to valproate with fewer attentional side effects). Carbamazepine and phenytoin may worsen absence seizures.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man develops painless subacute central vision loss in one eye, followed by the other eye 8 weeks later; fundoscopy shows peripapillary telangiectasia without leakage on fluorescein angiography. His maternal uncle is blind. What is the most common causative variant?
questions.explanation: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is caused by three primary complex I variants (11778 ~70%, 3460, 14484), with incomplete penetrance strongly biased toward males (~50% of male vs ~10% of female carriers). m.14484 has the best spontaneous recovery. Idebenone has regulatory approval in Europe; smoking and alcohol increase penetrance. OPA1 causes dominant optic atrophy.

questions.stem: Histology shows meningothelial whorls and laminated calcified bodies. What are the calcified structures?
questions.explanation: Meningioma. Psammoma bodies are concentric calcifications typical of psammomatous meningioma.
questions.imageAlt: Meningothelial whorls of spindle to epithelioid cells with indistinct borders; concentric laminated calcified psammoma bodies in a psammomatous meningioma.
questions.salient: EMA, SSTR2, progesterone receptor positive; Grade 2: 4 to 19 mitoses, brain invasion; grade 3: TERT/CDKN2A
questions.learning: EMA and SSTR2 positive, progesterone receptor positive. Grade 2 (atypical): 4 to 19 mitoses/10 HPF, brain invasion, chordoid or clear cell; grade 3: anaplastic, papillary, rhabdoid, or TERT promoter/CDKN2A alterations. NF2 loss most common driver; skull base tumors carry AKT1, SMO, KLF4/TRAF7.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male presents with progressive orthostatic hypotension unresponsive to conservative measures and fludrocortisone. What direct alpha-1 adrenergic prodrug is indicated?
questions.explanation: Midodrine is an oral prodrug metabolized to the selective alpha-1 agonist desglymidodrine, elevating vascular resistance in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension; supine hypertension is the main limitation. Droxidopa (norepinephrine prodrug) is an alternative.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old with dysarthria, dystonia and psychiatric symptoms has the T2 image shown. Which laboratory finding is expected?

options.text: Low serum ceruloplasmin with high 24-hour urine copper

questions.explanation: Low serum ceruloplasmin with high 24-hour urine copper. Wilson disease (ATP7B): putaminal/thalamic signal, face of the giant panda, Kayser-Fleischer rings. ATP7B, AR, hepatolenticular degeneration; onset adolescence to early adulthood with dysarthria, dystonia, wing-beating tremor, parkinsonism, psychiatric change, Kayser-Fleischer rings (near-universal with neurologic disease). Low ceruloplasmin, high 24-h urine copper, high hepatic copper. MRI: putamen, thalamus, midbrain (face of the giant panda), pons, dentate. Deck\'s differential: CO poisoning affects globus pallidus only; Huntington shows caudate atrophy; PD is imaging-normal.
questions.imageAlt: Axial T2: symmetric hyperintensity of the bilateral putamina and thalami. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 123)

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman has pes cavus, distal leg atrophy, and areflexia since adolescence; her father is similarly affected. Nerve conduction studies show uniformly slowed motor velocities of 20 m/s in all nerves without conduction block. What is the most likely genetic finding?
questions.explanation: CMT1A (~50% of all CMT) results from PMP22 duplication by unequal crossing over; uniform slowing distinguishes hereditary from acquired demyelinating neuropathy. The reciprocal deletion causes HNPP (recurrent pressure palsies). GJB1 (CMTX1) shows intermediate velocities and male predominance; MFN2 causes axonal CMT2A. Pathogenic variants in >100 genes are known.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with gait regression and areflexia has the MRI shown, with confluent periventricular signal sparing the U-fibers and a tigroid pattern. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: Arylsulfatase A. Metachromatic leukodystrophy; peripheral neuropathy and high CSF protein accompany. Check urine sulfatides because ARSA pseudodeficiency is common. Arylsulfatase A deficiency (ARSA; rarely PSAP saposin B), AR, sulfatide accumulation. Late-infantile form (most common, 1-2 y) presents with gait regression and peripheral neuropathy (slow conduction velocities, high CSF protein) before cognitive decline. Diagnosis by enzyme assay plus urine sulfatides (pseudodeficiency alleles are common). HSCT for presymptomatic/early juvenile disease; gene therapy (arsa-cel) approved for early forms.
questions.imageAlt: Axial T2/FLAIR: confluent, symmetric periventricular and deep white matter hyperintensity sparing the subcortical U-fibers; radiating perivascular stripes (tigroid/leopard pattern) within the abnormal white matter. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 107)

questions.stem: Coronal gross section through the diencephalon with petechial hemorrhage in the walls of the third ventricle. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Periventricular hemorrhagic necrosis of Wernicke encephalopathy, gross. Periventricular petechial hemorrhagic necrosis of hypothalamus/thalamus/mammillary bodies is acute Wernicke encephalopathy.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal section through the diencephalon with brownish petechial discoloration in the walls of the third ventricle and adjacent hypothalamus/thalamus.
questions.salient: Chronic: mammillary body atrophy and browning; Korsakoff amnesia from mediodorsal thalamus and mammillary bodies
questions.learning: Thiamine deficiency; mammillary bodies, medial thalamus, periaqueductal gray, floor of the fourth ventricle. Chronic: mammillary body atrophy and brownish discoloration. Korsakoff amnesia from mediodorsal thalamus and mammillary body injury.
questions.note: Inferred from lesion distribution; marginal note partially illegible.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with visual loss, diabetes insipidus, and a calcified suprasellar mass. Histology shown. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma, H&E. Palisading epithelium, stellate reticulum, wet keratin, and calcification are adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma.
questions.imageAlt: Epithelial nests with peripheral palisading columnar cells, loose stellate reticulum, nodules of anucleate ghost cells (wet keratin), calcification, and cholesterol clefts with adjacent gliotic brain. Marginal note: 10-year-old with visual disturbance, diabetes insipidus, suprasellar mass.
questions.salient: CTNNB1 mutation (children, calcified) versus BRAF V600E papillary (adults); Machine-oil fluid; hypothalamic obesity after resection
questions.learning: Derived from Rathke pouch remnants; CTNNB1 (beta-catenin) mutations with nuclear beta-catenin staining. Bimodal: children (adamantinomatous) and adults 50 to 70 (papillary, BRAF V600E, non-calcified, solid). Machine-oil cyst fluid. Recurrence common; hypothalamic obesity after resection.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man on haloperidol and sertraline presents with hyperthermia, altered mental status, and tachycardia. Which feature favors serotonin syndrome over neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

options.text: Inducible clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, and onset within 24 hours of a serotonergic change
Lead-pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia developing over days

questions.explanation: Serotonin syndrome (Hunter criteria) is rapid in onset with neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor), GI symptoms, and mydriasis; treat with cessation, benzodiazepines, and cyproheptadine. NMS evolves over days with bradykinetic "lead-pipe" rigidity, hyporeflexia, and very high CK; treat with cessation, dantrolene, bromocriptine, and supportive care. Both require aggressive cooling.

questions.stem: A patient presents with finger agnosia, right-left disorientation, agraphia, and acalculia. Where is the lesion?
questions.explanation: The tetrad of Gerstmann syndrome (acalculia, agraphia, right-left disorientation, and finger agnosia) localizes to the dominant (usually left) angular gyrus (Brodmann area 39).

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with encephalopathy and hearing loss has the MRI shown, with central callosal snowball lesions. Which examination confirms the diagnosis?

options.text: Fluorescein angiography for branch retinal artery occlusions

questions.explanation: Fluorescein angiography for branch retinal artery occlusions. Susac syndrome: brain, retina, cochlea endotheliopathy; callosal lesions are central, not on the undersurface as in MS. Autoimmune endotheliopathy of brain, retina and cochlea: encephalopathy, branch retinal artery occlusions (fluorescein angiography shows arterial wall hyperfluorescence), and low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Women 20-40. Central callosal lesions with sparing of the periphery and later central callosal holes distinguish it from MS (undersurface, Dawson fingers). Also leptomeningeal enhancement, deep gray lesions. Treat aggressively with steroids, IVIG, cyclophosphamide/mycophenolate.
questions.imageAlt: Axial T2 and sagittal FLAIR: multiple small hyperintense lesions in the central fibers of the corpus callosum (snowball lesions) with scattered subcortical white matter foci. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 138)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman develops paraparesis over 3 days; the MRI shown demonstrates a fusiform cord lesion spanning four vertebral segments. Which test is most important to send next?
questions.explanation: Serum AQP4-IgG. A longitudinally extensive lesion (3+ segments) argues against MS and for NMOSD or MOGAD; AQP4 and MOG antibodies change treatment. Longitudinally extensive lesions (3+ segments, central gray involvement) point to NMOSD (AQP4-IgG), MOGAD, SLE/Sjogren or infectious/parainfectious myelitis; ADEM in children; MS plaques are short (<2 segments), peripheral and asymmetric. Work-up: AQP4 and MOG antibodies, CSF, brain MRI, and exclusion of a compressive or vascular mimic (SDAVF is the classic false positive).
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal T2 cervical spine (two cases): fusiform cord expansion with intramedullary T2 hyperintensity extending over several vertebral segments, with variable enhancement. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 45)

questions.stem: An incidental extra-axial lesion following CSF signal on all sequences is shown. Which sequence best distinguishes it from an epidermoid cyst?
questions.explanation: Diffusion-weighted imaging. Epidermoids are bright on DWI and dirty on FLAIR; arachnoid cysts follow CSF on everything. Common incidental finding (middle cranial fossa and CPA most often), usually asymptomatic and requires no follow-up. The differential is epidermoid cyst, which also looks like CSF on T1/T2 but is bright on DWI and dirty on FLAIR. Large temporal cysts are associated with subdural hematoma after minor trauma.
questions.imageAlt: Axial FLAIR and T1: extra-axial, sharply marginated lesion that follows CSF signal on every sequence, remodeling adjacent bone and displacing brain without edema. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 101)

questions.stem: An asymptomatic 35-year-old has the lumbar MRI shown, with a mass at L4-L5 that is hyperintense on both T1 and T2. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassurance; no further work-up unless symptomatic

questions.explanation: Reassurance; no further work-up unless symptomatic. A lesion bright on both T1 and T2 is fat; intradural lipoma needs nothing unless it causes mass effect. The only common intradural lesion that is bright on T1 and T2 is fat (confirm with fat suppression; dermoid and hemorrhage are the mimics). The slide\'s teaching point: recognize it and stop, no LP, cultures, neurosurgical or oncologic referral unless symptomatic from mass effect. Filar lipomas are often associated with tethering.
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal T1 (A) and T2 (B) lumbar spine: well-defined intradural mass at L4-L5 that is hyperintense on both sequences. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 50)

questions.stem: Which antiseizure medication inhibits carbonic anhydrase, predisposing patients to nephrolithiasis, metabolic acidosis, hypohidrosis, and cognitive word-finding difficulties?
questions.explanation: Topiramate (and zonisamide) inhibits carbonic anhydrase, resulting in alkaline urine, calcium phosphate stones, systemic acidosis, hypohidrosis, and dysnomia; acute angle-closure glaucoma is another recognized effect.

questions.stem: A muscle biopsy demonstrating prominent perifascicular atrophy of muscle fibers alongside perivascular and perimysial CD4+ inflammatory infiltrates is diagnostic of:
questions.explanation: Dermatomyositis is an antibody- and complement-mediated microangiopathy targeting endomysial capillaries, resulting in ischemic perifascicular atrophy, perivascular CD4+ infiltrates, and MxA/interferon signature.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with laughing spells and precocious puberty. Sagittal T1 and axial T2 shown. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypothalamic hamartoma. A non-enhancing gray-matter-isointense mass of the tuber cinereum with gelastic seizures is a hypothalamic hamartoma.
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal T1 and axial T2: non-enhancing, gray-matter-isointense sessile mass in the tuber cinereum/floor of the third ventricle between the infundibulum and mammillary bodies.
questions.salient: Pallister-Hall (GLI3): polydactyly, bifid epiglottis; Laser ablation or disconnection; medications ineffective for the seizures
questions.learning: Gelastic seizures (laughing) with later refractory epilepsy and encephalopathy; central precocious puberty (GnRH-secreting). Pallister-Hall syndrome (GLI3): polydactyly, bifid epiglottis. Treatment: laser interstitial thermal therapy, radiosurgery, or endoscopic disconnection; medications are ineffective for the seizures.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old with visual disturbance and an endocrinologically silent sellar mass. Histology shown. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Null-cell pituitary adenoma, H&E. Sheets of monotonous round cells with salt-and-pepper chromatin around delicate capillaries indicate adenoma; reticulin stain would show disrupted acini.
questions.imageAlt: Sheets of uniform round cells with stippled (salt-and-pepper) chromatin and scant cytoplasm arranged around delicate capillaries, with loss of the normal acinar reticulin pattern. Marginal note: 55-year-old with visual disturbance, endocrinologically inactive sellar mass.
questions.salient: Transcription factors classify lineage: PIT1, TPIT, SF1; Nonfunctioning adenomas present with mass effect and hypopituitarism
questions.learning: Reticulin stain distinguishes adenoma (disrupted acini) from normal gland. Immunostains and transcription factors (PIT1, TPIT, SF1) classify lineage. Functioning: prolactinoma (most common), GH (acromegaly), ACTH (Cushing). Nonfunctioning tumors present with mass effect and hypopituitarism.

questions.stem: The H&E shown demonstrates round basophilic cytoplasmic inclusions. Which silver stain labels them, and which does not?
questions.explanation: Bielschowsky positive, Gallyas negative. Pick bodies are 3R tau, Bielschowsky positive, Gallyas negative, ubiquitin positive. Pick bodies are 3R tau, argyrophilic with Bielschowsky but not Gallyas, ubiquitin positive; found in dentate gyrus, frontal and temporal cortex. Swollen achromatic Pick cells are the other cytologic feature. Pick disease accounts for a minority of FTLD-tau; MAPT mutations, PSP and CBD (4R) are the others.
questions.imageAlt: H&E of cortex: round, well-demarcated, slightly basophilic cytoplasmic inclusions displacing the nucleus in swollen neurons. (RITE Review deck, slide 113)

questions.stem: The lateral carotid angiogram shown demonstrates filling of the anterior cerebral artery without visualization of sylvian branches. Which clinical syndrome is expected?

options.text: Contralateral face and arm weakness with aphasia or neglect

questions.explanation: Contralateral face and arm weakness with aphasia or neglect. Absent MCA on angiography means M1 occlusion; leg-predominant weakness is ACA, hemianopia PCA, monocular blindness ophthalmic artery. Recognize the normal lateral view (ACA arcing over the corpus callosum, MCA candelabra in the sylvian fissure); absence of the sylvian branches means M1 occlusion. Clinically a proximal MCA syndrome (contralateral face/arm > leg weakness, aphasia or neglect, gaze deviation).
questions.imageAlt: Lateral carotid angiogram: the ICA opacifies and the anterior cerebral artery fills, but no MCA branches are seen. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 64)

questions.stem: A 4-month-old is brought in lethargic with vomiting and a full fontanelle after reportedly rolling off a couch. CT shows bilateral subdural collections of different densities, and fundoscopy shows multilayered retinal hemorrhages extending to the periphery. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Benign enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces

questions.explanation: Abusive head trauma. Mixed-density subdural hematomas with extensive multilayered retinal hemorrhages in an infant with an implausible history are the classic triad of abusive head trauma; skeletal survey (metaphyseal corner fractures, posterior rib fractures) and coagulation studies complete the evaluation. Glutaric aciduria type 1 and Menkes can mimic subdurals but do not produce this retinal pattern; benign external hydrocephalus produces bilateral frontal subarachnoid enlargement without hemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy has episodic burning hand and foot pain triggered by heat and exercise, hypohidrosis, and clustered purple papules over the umbilicus and groin; slit-lamp shows whorl-like corneal opacities. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Fabry disease (X-linked GLA, alpha-galactosidase A deficiency)

questions.explanation: Fabry disease causes globotriaosylceramide accumulation; small-fiber neuropathy, angiokeratomas, cornea verticillata, and later renal failure, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and cryptogenic stroke in young adults (dolichoectasia, pulvinar sign). Heterozygous females can be symptomatic. Diagnosis in males is by enzyme assay; in females, gene sequencing and lyso-Gb3. Enzyme replacement (agalsidase) and the chaperone migalastat (amenable variants) are approved; carbamazepine or gabapentin for pain.

questions.stem: Ulnar motor study in a 13-year-old with foot drop: distal latency 8.8 ms, CV 17 m/s forearm and 11.5 m/s across elbow, amplitudes preserved without block. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Uniform demyelinating slowing in hereditary neuropathy. Uniform severe slowing with preserved amplitudes and no block is hereditary demyelination (PMP22 duplication).

questions.stem: The reciprocal genetic lesion at this locus causes which disorder?

options.text: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies

questions.explanation: PMP22 deletion (reciprocal to the CMT1A duplication) causes HNPP.
questions.imageAlt: Ulnar motor study recording abductor digiti minimi: wrist latency 8.8 ms, amplitude 8.4 mV; below-elbow 19.9 ms, 7.15 mV; above-elbow 29.4 ms, 6.15 mV. Conduction velocities 17.1 m/s (forearm) and 11.5 m/s (across elbow) with no conduction block or temporal dispersion. Marginal note: 13-year-old with foot drop.
questions.context: Ulnar motor study in a 13-year-old with foot drop: distal latency 8.8 ms, CV 17 m/s forearm and 11.5 m/s across elbow, amplitudes preserved without block. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.salient: Uniform slowing = hereditary; block and dispersion = acquired; Upper-limb CV <38 m/s defines CMT1; intermediate 25 to 45 suggests CMTX
questions.learning: Hereditary demyelination is uniform and symmetric without block; acquired (CIDP, GBS, MMN) is patchy with conduction block, temporal dispersion, and prolonged F-waves. Velocities <38 m/s in the upper limb define CMT1; intermediate 25 to 45 m/s suggests CMTX (GJB1).

questions.stem: Adult with an enhancing pineal mass; histology shows large anuclear fibrillary rosettes. Diagnosis?

options.text: Papillary tumor of the pineal region

questions.explanation: Pineocytoma. Pineocytomatous rosettes (large anuclear areas) define pineocytoma.
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal T1 post-contrast: well-circumscribed enhancing pineal mass. H&E: small uniform cells with large anuclear fibrillary areas (pineocytomatous rosettes).
questions.salient: Pineoblastoma: children, small blue cells, RB1 trilateral retinoblastoma; Synaptophysin and neurofilament positive
questions.learning: Adults; synaptophysin and neurofilament positive; large pineocytomatous rosettes distinguish it from the Homer Wright rosettes of pineoblastoma (children, small blue cells, associated with RB1 in trilateral retinoblastoma). Pineal parenchymal tumor of intermediate differentiation lies between.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old male presents with fluctuating attention, detailed recurrent visual hallucinations, and spontaneous asymmetric parkinsonism. Autopsy reveals alpha-synuclein-positive intracytoplasmic inclusions throughout the cerebral cortex and brainstem. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: DLB is characterized by cognitive fluctuations, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and RBD (core features), with diffuse cortical Lewy bodies. Dementia precedes or accompanies parkinsonism within one year (the "one-year rule" distinguishing DLB from PDD). Avoid typical neuroleptics.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old with seizures has the imaging shown, including a calcified frontal cortical mass. Which molecular profile defines this tumor?
questions.explanation: IDH-mutant with 1p/19q codeletion. Oligodendroglioma: calcified in 70-90%, chemosensitive (PCV/temozolomide), TERT promoter mutation near-universal. Frontal lobe, cortical/subcortical, calcified in 70-90% (the most calcified primary glioma), frequently presents with seizures. WHO 2021 definition requires IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion; TERT promoter mutation is near-universal, CIC and FUBP1 common. Grade 2 or 3; chemosensitive (PCV or temozolomide) with long survival. Calcified cortical tumor in a young adult with seizures: think oligodendroglioma, ganglioglioma, DNET.
questions.imageAlt: Post-contrast T1 (two cases), non-contrast CT and T1: cortically based frontal masses with patchy enhancement; CT shows coarse calcification. (RITE Review deck, slide 26)

questions.stem: What mutation underlies Central Core Myopathy, predisposing affected individuals to fatal malignant hyperthermia upon exposure to volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine?
questions.explanation: Central core myopathy is linked to variants in the ryanodine receptor gene (RYR1), which regulates calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum; volatile halogenated anesthetics and succinylcholine trigger malignant hyperthermia.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old female presents with postural headache relieved by lying flat and worsened by upright posture. Brain MRI displays smooth, diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement and brainstem sagging. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Intracranial hypotension from a spinal CSF leak leads to compensatory dilation of dural venous structures, producing diffuse dural enhancement and downward brain sagging; epidural blood patch is first-line.

questions.stem: The FLAIR images shown demonstrate an infiltrative non-enhancing mass in an older adult. Which statement is correct?

options.text: About 15-20% of glioblastomas do not enhance at diagnosis
Gliomatosis cerebri is a distinct WHO entity
Non-enhancing tumors do not need biopsy

questions.explanation: About 15-20% of glioblastomas do not enhance at diagnosis. Non-enhancing glioblastoma occurs; perfusion and MRS help; gliomatosis was removed as an entity in 2016. About 15-20% of glioblastomas do not enhance at diagnosis; absence of enhancement does not exclude grade 4, and a non-enhancing infiltrative mass in an older adult should be biopsied. Perfusion (elevated rCBV) and MRS (high choline/NAA, lactate) help. Gliomatosis cerebri (3+ lobes) was removed as an entity in WHO 2016 and is now a growth pattern.
questions.imageAlt: Axial FLAIR at three levels: expansile, infiltrative T2/FLAIR hyperintensity involving the left frontal lobe and insula with mass effect, without a discrete enhancing component. (RITE Review deck, slide 20)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops subacute, rapidly progressive pancerebellar ataxia and dysarthria over 6 weeks; MRI is normal. Which paraneoplastic antibody and associated malignancy are most likely?
questions.explanation: Anti-Yo targets cerebellar degeneration-related protein 2 in Purkinje cells and is nearly exclusive to women with gynecologic or breast malignancy; response to immunotherapy is poor. Anti-Hu causes sensory neuronopathy, limbic encephalitis, and autonomic dysfunction with SCLC; anti-Ma2 causes limbic/diencephalic encephalitis in young men with testicular tumors. Antibodies to intracellular antigens are T-cell mediated and prognostically worse than surface antigens.

questions.stem: A woman with 40% heteroplasmy for m.8993T>G (MT-ATP6) has one child with NARP and another with Leigh syndrome. What principle explains the discordant phenotypes among her children?

options.text: The mitochondrial genetic bottleneck during oogenesis produces widely varying heteroplasmy levels in offspring

questions.explanation: mtDNA is strictly maternally inherited; a small number of mtDNA molecules populate each primordial oocyte, so offspring heteroplasmy can differ dramatically from the mother's. For m.8993, <~70% mutant load is often asymptomatic or NARP, whereas >90% produces maternally inherited Leigh syndrome. Threshold effects also explain tissue-specific expression.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old with episodic speech arrest. T1 and T2 are shown. What is the lesion?
questions.explanation: Temporal lobe arteriovenous malformation. A tightly packed cluster of serpiginous flow voids without edema is an AVM.

questions.stem: Which feature most increases the annual hemorrhage risk of this lesion?
questions.explanation: Prior hemorrhage is the strongest predictor; deep venous drainage, deep location, and associated aneurysms also raise risk.
questions.imageAlt: A: T1 and B: T2 axial images with a tightly packed cluster of serpiginous flow voids in the left temporal lobe without surrounding edema. Marginal note: 36-year-old with episodic speech arrest.
questions.context: A 36-year-old with episodic speech arrest. T1 and T2 are shown. What is the lesion?
questions.salient: Annual hemorrhage risk 2 to 4%, higher with prior bleed, deep drainage, deep location; Spetzler-Martin grades size, eloquence, venous drainage; ARUBA favored medical management for unruptured AVMs
questions.learning: Annual hemorrhage risk ~2 to 4%, higher with prior hemorrhage, deep venous drainage, deep location, associated aneurysm. Spetzler-Martin grade (size, eloquence, venous drainage) guides surgery. ARUBA favored medical management for unruptured AVMs. Consider HHT if multiple.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has 8 months of progressive leg weakness worse with exertion and standing. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Spinal dural arteriovenous fistula. Dorsal serpiginous flow voids with central cord T2 signal and swelling indicate venous congestive myelopathy from a dural AV fistula.

questions.stem: What is the mechanism of cord injury in this condition?
questions.explanation: The fistula arterializes the coronal venous plexus, raising intramedullary venous pressure (Foix-Alajouanine).
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal T2: serpiginous flow voids along the dorsal cord surface from T9 caudally with central cord T2 hyperintensity and swelling; coronal CISS shows the engorged perimedullary veins.
questions.context: A 66-year-old man has 8 months of progressive leg weakness worse with exertion and standing. What is the diagnosis?
questions.salient: Dorsal flow voids plus long-segment cord edema in an older man = dural AV fistula; Steroids can precipitate acute worsening; treat by embolization or surgical disconnection
questions.learning: Older men, slowly progressive myelopathy worsened by exertion or standing; venous hypertension, not ischemia from steal. Steroids can precipitate acute worsening. Spinal angiography for diagnosis; endovascular embolization or surgical disconnection.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old female presents with subacute psychosis, severe insomnia, behavioral changes, catatonia, autonomic instability, and prominent oral-facial dyskinesias. Serum and CSF are positive for antibodies against GluN1 subunits. What underlying neoplasm is most commonly identified?
questions.explanation: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis occurs predominantly in young women and is associated with an ovarian teratoma containing neural elements in roughly a third to half; CSF testing is more sensitive than serum. Extreme delta brush on EEG is characteristic.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old with progressive sensorineural hearing loss and ataxia has the MRI shown. What is the most important next step?

options.text: Whole-neuraxis imaging to find a source of chronic subarachnoid bleeding

questions.explanation: Whole-neuraxis imaging to find a source of chronic subarachnoid bleeding. Superficial siderosis arises from occult recurrent SAH: dural tears, ependymoma, vascular malformation. Hemosiderin deposition in the subpial layer from chronic or recurrent subarachnoid bleeding; presents with slowly progressive sensorineural hearing loss, cerebellar ataxia and myelopathy. Search the entire neuraxis for the source: dural tear/pseudomeningocele after spinal surgery or trauma, myxopapillary ependymoma, vascular malformation, prior hemispherectomy. GRE/SWI is the most sensitive sequence. Deferiprone has been tried; treat the source.
questions.imageAlt: Axial T2 (three levels) and sagittal T1: a thin rim of low signal coating the cerebellar folia, brainstem and cranial nerves VIII, with cerebellar atrophy. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 140)

questions.stem: Cervical coronal post-contrast and axial T1 in a 33-year-old show an enhancing intraspinal mass extending through the foramen. Most likely?
questions.explanation: Dumbbell intradural extramedullary tumor. An intradural extramedullary dumbbell mass is a nerve sheath tumor.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal post-contrast T1 of the cervical spine and axial T1: round enhancing intraspinal mass displacing and flattening the cord, extending laterally through the neural foramen. Marginal note: 33-year-old man.
questions.salient: Intradural extramedullary: schwannoma, meningioma, drop mets; Multiple schwannomas: NF2 or schwannomatosis
questions.learning: Intradural extramedullary: schwannoma, meningioma, drop metastasis. Intramedullary: ependymoma (adults, central, hemosiderin cap), astrocytoma (children, eccentric), hemangioblastoma. Multiple schwannomas suggest NF2 or schwannomatosis; plexiform neurofibromas suggest NF1.

questions.stem: What are the only projection neurons that convey the total neurochemical output of the cerebellar cortex to the deep cerebellar nuclei?
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells provide the sole efferent output of the cerebellar cortex, utilizing GABA to exert inhibitory tone on the deep cerebellar and vestibular nuclei.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy reports morning jerks that make him drop his toothbrush, and had his first generalized tonic-clonic seizure after an all-night study session. EEG shows generalized 4–6 Hz polyspike-and-wave with a photoparoxysmal response. Which agent should be avoided because it may aggravate his myoclonus?
questions.explanation: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is a lifelong genetic generalized epilepsy. Valproate is most effective (SANAD II) but avoided in females of childbearing potential, where levetiracetam is preferred; lamotrigine helps GTCs but may worsen myoclonus. Carbamazepine and phenytoin also aggravate.

questions.stem: Sagittal cervical T2 in a 68-year-old with spastic gait and hand clumsiness. Which feature most supports surgical decompression?

options.text: Intramedullary T2 hyperintensity at the stenosis

questions.explanation: High-grade cervical spondylotic stenosis with myelopathy. Cord signal change with high-grade stenosis indicates myelopathy and favors decompression.
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal cervical T2: multilevel disc-osteophyte complexes with severe canal narrowing at C3-4 and C4-5, effacement of the CSF space, cord flattening, and intramedullary T2 hyperintensity at the level of maximal compression.
questions.salient: Inverted radial reflex, Hoffmann, Lhermitte; T1 hypointensity predicts poorer recovery
questions.learning: Intramedullary T2 signal at the stenosis predicts worse outcome and supports decompression; T1 hypointensity is a poorer prognostic sign. Clinical: gait spasticity, hand clumsiness, Lhermitte, inverted radial reflex (C5-6 compression), Hoffmann. OPLL is a common cause in East Asian patients. Progressive myelopathy is a surgical indication; MRI-negative myelopathy should prompt dynamic (flexion-extension) imaging.
questions.note: Revised after review; original draft called this an intramedullary inflammatory lesion.

questions.stem: The photographs shown demonstrate ptosis with ophthalmoparesis. Which additional finding would point to Kearns-Sayre syndrome?

options.text: Pigmentary retinopathy with cardiac conduction block

questions.explanation: Pigmentary retinopathy with cardiac conduction block. KSS: single mtDNA deletion, onset before 20, retinopathy, heart block, CSF protein >100; OPMD gives dysphagia (PABPN1); MG gives fatigability. Eyeball pattern (MP5). Ptosis without ophthalmoplegia: myotonic dystrophy, congenital myopathies. Ptosis with ophthalmoplegia: oculopharyngeal dystrophy (PABPN1 GCN expansion, French-Canadian, dysphagia), mitochondrial CPEO/Kearns-Sayre (single mtDNA deletion, pigmentary retinopathy, heart block, CSF protein >100), centronuclear myopathy. NMJ disease adds fatigability and diplopia: MG, LEMS, botulism, congenital myasthenic syndromes. FSHD spares extraocular muscles.
questions.imageAlt: Clinical photographs: bilateral symmetric ptosis with facial weakness in one patient; ptosis with ophthalmoparesis in another. (RITE Review deck, slide 211)

questions.stem: LFB-stained white matter 2 weeks after a viral illness shows a cuffed venule with a sleeve of demyelination. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Perivenous demyelination with perivascular inflammation. Perivenous sleeves of demyelination with macrophages and lymphocytes are ADEM; MS shows confluent plaques.
questions.imageAlt: Luxol fast blue-stained white matter with a central venule cuffed by lymphocytes and macrophages and a surrounding sleeve of myelin pallor; scattered perivascular inflammatory foci. Marginal note: 54-year-old, encephalopathy 2 weeks after a viral illness, cerebral swelling, some contrast enhancement.
questions.salient: Weston Hurst: hemorrhagic, fibrinoid necrosis; HIV: multinucleated giant cells; PML: oligodendroglial inclusions, bizarre astrocytes
questions.learning: ADEM pathology: sleeves of perivenous demyelination with macrophages and lymphocytes, in contrast to the confluent plaques of MS. Acute hemorrhagic leukoencephalitis (Weston Hurst) is the fulminant variant with fibrinoid necrosis and hemorrhage. HIV encephalitis is defined by multinucleated giant cells; PML by oligodendroglial inclusions and bizarre astrocytes.
questions.note: Revised after review from an HIV-encephalitis reading; still inferred.

questions.stem: Muscle biopsy panels show endomysial inflammation with lymphocytes invading non-necrotic fibers. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Polymyositis. Endomysial CD8+ cells invading MHC-I-expressing non-necrotic fibers define polymyositis.
questions.imageAlt: H&E: endomysial mononuclear infiltrates between and around individual myofibers; lymphocytes invading a non-necrotic fiber. ATPase panel: normal checkerboard (type 1 dark, 2A light, 2B intermediate) contrasted with fiber type grouping.
questions.salient: Pure polymyositis is rare; reconsider IBM, IMNM, antisynthetase, overlap; Fiber type grouping and type 2 atrophy panels are nonspecific
questions.learning: Polymyositis as a pure entity is now uncommon; many historical cases are IBM, IMNM, antisynthetase syndrome, or overlap myositis. Fiber type grouping and type 2 atrophy shown here are nonspecific (reinnervation, disuse/steroids).

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with late-onset cerebellar ataxia, sensory neuronopathy, and chronic cough has a normal whole-exome sequencing result. What class of variant is most likely to have been missed?

options.text: A biallelic intronic pentanucleotide (AAGGG) repeat expansion in RFC1
A missense variant in a coding exon

questions.explanation: Short-read exome sequencing does not detect repeat expansions (RFC1 CANVAS, FXN, DMPK, C9orf72, HTT, ATXN genes, FMR1), deep intronic variants, low-level mosaicism, or some copy-number changes; targeted repeat-primed PCR or long-read sequencing is needed. CANVAS (cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy, vestibular areflexia syndrome) is a common cause of late-onset ataxia and was only genetically resolved in 2019. Negative exome in a strong phenotype warrants targeted testing, genome sequencing, and periodic reanalysis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman at 36 weeks gestation presents with headache, cortical blindness, and a seizure; blood pressure is 180/115. MRI shows symmetric bilateral parieto-occipital vasogenic edema without diffusion restriction. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) due to eclampsia

questions.explanation: PRES reflects failure of cerebral autoregulation and endothelial dysfunction, favoring the posterior circulation (less sympathetic innervation). Triggers include hypertensive emergency, eclampsia, calcineurin inhibitors, chemotherapy, and renal failure. Treatment is blood pressure control (magnesium and delivery in eclampsia); lesions typically resolve.

questions.stem: A newborn presents with profound hypotonia, respiratory failure, club feet, and a tented upper lip. Her mother has mild facial weakness, ptosis, and cataracts and cannot release her grip on the examiner's hand. What is the genetic mechanism?

options.text: Large maternally transmitted CTG expansion (>1000 repeats) in the 3' UTR of DMPK
CNBP CCTG expansion inherited from the father

questions.explanation: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 shows anticipation; congenital DM1 nearly always results from maternal transmission of large expansions. Toxic CUG RNA sequesters MBNL splicing regulators. Adult DM1 features distal weakness, grip/percussion myotonia, cataracts, cardiac conduction block (major cause of death; annual ECG), insulin resistance, and hypersomnia. DM2 (CNBP) is proximal, milder, and without a congenital form.

questions.stem: The hematoma shown is isointense on T1 and markedly hypointense on T2, GRE and DWI. What property of the responsible hemoglobin species explains the T2 signal loss without T1 shortening?

options.text: Paramagnetic iron that remains compartmentalized within intact red cells
Loss of all unpaired electrons after conversion to hemichromes
Inner-sphere water access to ferric iron

questions.explanation: Paramagnetic iron that remains compartmentalized within intact red cells. Inner-sphere water access describes methemoglobin and T1 shortening; superparamagnetism is ferritin/hemosiderin; hemichromes are the chronic cavity. Deoxy-Hb has 4 unpaired electrons (paramagnetic) but is compartmentalized in intact RBCs, so it produces susceptibility T2* loss without T1 shortening. Mnemonic: I Die (iso T1 / dark T2).
questions.imageAlt: Axial T1, T2, GRE and DWI: hematoma isointense on T1, dark on T2, markedly dark on GRE and DWI, with surrounding edema. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 8)

questions.stem: A 17-year-old has excessive daytime sleepiness, sleep paralysis, and episodes of knee buckling when laughing. MSLT shows mean sleep latency 3 minutes with 3 sleep-onset REM periods. Which statement is correct?

options.text: CSF hypocretin-1 is expected to be <110 pg/mL; HLA-DQB1*06:02 is present in ~98%; sodium oxybate treats both cataplexy and sleepiness
The condition is caused by autoimmune destruction of pineal melatonin neurons
CSF hypocretin-1 is expected to be elevated

questions.explanation: Narcolepsy type 1 results from loss of lateral hypothalamic hypocretin (orexin) neurons, likely T-cell mediated (association with H1N1 infection/Pandemrix). Cataplexy is REM atonia intruding into wakefulness. Diagnosis requires MSLT with mean latency ≤8 min and ≥2 SOREMPs (one may be from preceding PSG) or low CSF hypocretin. Treatments: modafinil/armodafinil, solriamfetol, pitolisant (H3 inverse agonist, treats cataplexy), sodium or lower-sodium oxybate, and venlafaxine/tricyclics for cataplexy.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy has progressive rigidity, bradykinesia, dystonia, seizures, and cognitive decline; his father developed chorea at age 40. What CAG repeat size is expected in the child?
questions.explanation: Juvenile (Westphal variant) Huntington disease, onset <20 years, presents with parkinsonism rather than chorea, seizures, myoclonus, and rapid decline; it nearly always follows paternal transmission with repeats >60 (often >80). Age of onset correlates inversely with CAG length, which accounts for ~60% of variance. Tetrabenazine/deutetrabenazine treat chorea; huntingtin-lowering trials (tominersen) have so far not shown benefit.

questions.stem: A 5-month-old infant presents with seizures beginning at 3 months, paroxysmal eye-head movements, and deceleration of head growth. CSF analysis shows marked hypoglycorrhachia (CSF:serum glucose ratio 0.3) with low CSF lactate and normal serum glucose. What condition is this, and what is the definitive therapy?
questions.explanation: GLUT1 deficiency (SLC2A1, usually de novo heterozygous) impairs glucose transport across the blood-brain barrier. Onset is typically 1–4 months with acquired microcephaly and paroxysmal eye-head movements. Ketone bodies enter the brain via monocarboxylate transporters, bypassing the defect.

questions.stem: A 3-day-old term neonate has brief tonic seizures with apnea and cyanosis several times daily; interictal EEG is normal, and the father and paternal grandmother had neonatal seizures that resolved by 6 months. What gene is likely, and what is a rational therapeutic choice?

options.text: KCNQ2; sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine are particularly effective

questions.explanation: Self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy is autosomal dominant with KCNQ2 (or KCNQ3) loss-of-function reducing the M-current; de novo dominant-negative KCNQ2 variants cause a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with burst-suppression. Both respond preferentially to sodium channel blockers. Ezogabine (retigabine), a KCNQ opener, has been reformulated (XEN496) for KCNQ2-DEE trials. The other classic neonatal-onset DEE genes include KCNT1, SCN2A (gain-of-function, also responds to Na-blockers), and STXBP1.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has 4 months of progressive symmetric proximal and distal weakness with large-fiber sensory loss and areflexia; NCS shows prolonged distal latencies, conduction block, and absent F-waves. He improves substantially with IVIG. What distinguishes his disorder from Guillain-Barré syndrome in treatment responsiveness?

options.text: Corticosteroids are effective in CIDP but not in GBS
Rituximab is first-line for typical CIDP

questions.explanation: CIDP progresses beyond 8 weeks and responds to IVIG, corticosteroids, and plasma exchange (each roughly 60–70%), unlike GBS where steroids fail. Subcutaneous IG and efgartigimod are newer options. Nodal/paranodal antibodies (NF155, CNTN1, CASPR1) define autoimmune nodopathies with tremor, ataxia, poor IVIG response, and rituximab responsiveness. Exclude POEMS and MGUS.

questions.stem: Gross brain from a patient who died 36 hours after presenting with fever and neck stiffness. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Purulent leptomeningitis, gross. Opaque yellow-green exudate filling the sulci over the convexity is acute pyogenic meningitis.

questions.stem: Adjunctive dexamethasone has proven mortality benefit for which organism?
questions.explanation: de Gans 2002: dexamethasone before or with the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality in pneumococcal meningitis.
questions.imageAlt: Lateral view of the brain with opaque yellow-green exudate filling the sulci and cisterns over the convexity, most prominent along vessels.
questions.context: Gross brain from a patient who died 36 hours after presenting with fever and neck stiffness. Diagnosis?
questions.salient: Convexity exudate: pneumococcus; basal exudate: TB, fungal, Listeria; Complications: vasculitic infarct, hydrocephalus, venous thrombosis
questions.learning: Exudate distribution hints at organism: convexity (pneumococcus), basal (TB, fungal, Listeria). Complications: vasculitic infarcts, cerebral edema, hydrocephalus, venous thrombosis, abscess, hearing loss. Organisms by age: GBS/E. coli/Listeria (neonate), S. pneumoniae/N. meningitidis (child-adult), plus Listeria >50.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old male presents with early unprovoked backward falls, axial rigidity, pseudobulbar affect, and restricted voluntary vertical downward saccades. What neuropathological diagnosis is made?
questions.explanation: PSP is a 4-repeat (4R) tauopathy (tufted astrocytes, globose tangles) characterized by symmetric axial rigidity, early falls, and vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (downward gaze affected earliest); midbrain atrophy gives the "hummingbird sign."

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has a serum sodium of 108 mEq/L corrected to 128 mEq/L within 24 hours. Five days later he develops dysarthria, quadriparesis, and pseudobulbar affect. What is the diagnosis and preventive principle?

options.text: Osmotic demyelination syndrome; limit sodium correction to ≤8 mEq/L per 24 hours in high-risk patients

questions.explanation: Osmotic demyelination (central pontine and extrapontine myelinolysis) follows overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia, especially with alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia, or liver disease. MRI changes may lag by 1–2 weeks. Overcorrection is treated with desmopressin and D5W relowering.

questions.stem: Needle EMG of the tibialis anterior in a patient with a 4-week-old L5 radiculopathy is most likely to show which findings?

options.text: Fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves at rest with reduced recruitment of normal-morphology motor units
Small, short-duration, polyphasic motor units with early recruitment

questions.explanation: After axon loss, spontaneous fibrillations/PSWs appear at 2–3 weeks (paraspinals first, distal muscles last), while reduced recruitment appears immediately. Reinnervation over months produces large-amplitude, long-duration polyphasic MUAPs. Myopathic units are small, short, polyphasic with early/full recruitment. Radiculopathy is distinguished from plexopathy by paraspinal involvement and preserved SNAPs (dorsal root ganglion is distal to the lesion).

questions.stem: A child with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy has a heterozygous KCNQ2 variant reported as a variant of uncertain significance. What is the appropriate next step?

options.text: Treat the child as having KCNQ2 encephalopathy and counsel a 50% recurrence risk
Pursue parental segregation testing, phenotype correlation, and periodic reclassification; do not base irreversible clinical or reproductive decisions on a VUS
Order repeat sequencing in a different lab

questions.explanation: ACMG/AMP classification integrates population frequency (gnomAD), computational prediction, functional data, segregation, and de novo status; a de novo occurrence in a well-matched phenotype (PS2) can upgrade a VUS. Laboratories reclassify variants over time, and clinicians should request reanalysis every 1–2 years. Gene-specific resources (ClinGen expert panels, RettBASE, CDKL5 databases) and functional assays for channels (patch clamp) increasingly resolve uncertainty.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and a prior stroke has loud snoring, witnessed apneas, and an apnea-hypopnea index of 32 events/hour. What is the first-line treatment, and what neurologic outcome is most clearly linked to this disorder?

options.text: Continuous positive airway pressure; increased risk of stroke and AF recurrence, with reduced daytime sleepiness and BP on treatment

questions.explanation: OSA is severe at AHI ≥30 and moderate at 15–30. CPAP improves sleepiness, blood pressure, and AF recurrence; SAVE did not show reduced cardiovascular events overall, likely due to poor adherence. Hypoglossal nerve stimulation is an option for CPAP-intolerant patients with BMI <32–35 without concentric collapse. Tirzepatide was approved for OSA with obesity in 2024. Untreated OSA worsens epilepsy control and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with low back pain and sciatica has the post-contrast lumbar MRI shown. Which tumor is most likely?
questions.explanation: Myxopapillary ependymoma. An enhancing intradural mass at the conus/filum in an adult is myxopapillary ependymoma until proven otherwise; it is also the tumor classically linked to superficial siderosis. The most common tumor of the conus/filum in adults; arises from ependymal rests of the filum. Prone to hemorrhage and subarachnoid seeding, and is the classic tumor cause of superficial siderosis. WHO grade 2 since 2021. En bloc resection is curative; capsule violation predicts recurrence. Differential on the slide: metastasis, schwannoma/neurofibroma, herniated disc, schistosomiasis.
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal post-contrast T1 lumbar spine: rounded, avidly and homogeneously enhancing intradural mass at the conus/filum terminale. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 26)

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with headache, neck pain and transient paresthesias has the angiogram shown. Which of the following is a recognized complication of this condition?
questions.explanation: Intracranial aneurysm. Fibromuscular dysplasia (string of beads) is associated with aneurysm and dissection; screen the renal arteries. Idiopathic, non-inflammatory, non-atherosclerotic arteriopathy of medium arteries; medial fibroplasia is the usual type. Young to middle-aged women; renal arteries first, cervicocephalic second. Complications: dissection, intracranial aneurysm (roughly 20% in registry data, up to a third in some series), TIA/stroke, headache and pulsatile tinnitus. Antiplatelet therapy; screen for renal disease and aneurysm.
questions.imageAlt: AP (A) and lateral (B) carotid angiograms: string-of-beads appearance of the mid-to-distal cervical ICA. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 61)

questions.stem: Myelin-stained medulla with an arrow on a convoluted nucleus. This structure is the sole source of:

options.text: Climbing fibers to the contralateral cerebellum

questions.explanation: Medulla at the level of the inferior olives, myelin stain: anatomy. The inferior olivary nucleus projects climbing fibers via the inferior cerebellar peduncle to contralateral Purkinje cells.
questions.imageAlt: Transverse myelin-stained section of the rostral medulla: pyramids ventrally, symmetric convoluted inferior olivary nuclei, medial lemniscus and MLF paramedian, fourth ventricle floor dorsally with hypoglossal and vagal nuclei; the arrow marks the inferior olivary nucleus.
questions.salient: Guillain-Mollaret triangle and hypertrophic olivary degeneration with palatal tremor; Medial medullary syndrome: pyramid, medial lemniscus, CN XII
questions.learning: Inferior olive: sole source of climbing fibers to the contralateral cerebellar cortex via the inferior cerebellar peduncle. Guillain-Mollaret triangle (red nucleus, ipsilateral inferior olive via central tegmental tract, contralateral dentate) underlies hypertrophic olivary degeneration and oculopalatal tremor. Medial medullary syndrome (Dejerine): pyramid, medial lemniscus, hypoglossal nerve.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with bitemporal visual field loss and decreased libido. Post-contrast images are shown. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sellar/suprasellar macroadenoma. A homogeneously enhancing sellar mass extending through the diaphragma with a waist (snowman) is a macroadenoma.

questions.stem: Prolactin returns at 95 ng/mL. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Stalk effect from loss of dopaminergic inhibition

questions.explanation: Mild elevation (<150 to 200) with a macroadenoma reflects stalk compression; prolactinomas of this size produce very high levels. The hook effect causes falsely low values.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal post-contrast T1: homogeneously enhancing mass arising from the sella and extending superiorly through the diaphragma sellae with a waist (snowman/figure-of-eight). Axial post-contrast: round suprasellar mass.
questions.context: A 45-year-old man with bitemporal visual field loss and decreased libido. Post-contrast images are shown. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.salient: Superior temporal fields lost first from chiasmal compression; Prolactinoma: dopamine agonist first; others: transsphenoidal surgery
questions.learning: Bitemporal hemianopia from chiasmal compression (superior fields first), hypopituitarism, cavernous sinus invasion. Prolactinoma: dopamine agonist first; others: transsphenoidal surgery. Pituitary apoplexy: sudden headache, ophthalmoplegia, adrenal crisis. Differential: craniopharyngioma (calcified, cystic), meningioma, Rathke cleft cyst, germinoma, hypophysitis.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old presents with regression, hypotonia, feeding difficulty, and lactic acidosis after a viral illness. MRI shows bilateral symmetric T2 hyperintensity of the putamina, periaqueductal gray, and brainstem. What is the syndromic diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Leigh syndrome is a clinical-radiologic entity with >75 causative genes across nuclear and mitochondrial genomes (SURF1, MT-ATP6, complex I subunits, PDHA1). Metabolic decompensation with infection is typical. Biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease (SLC19A3) is a treatable mimic and justifies empiric high-dose biotin and thiamine in any child with this picture.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old regresses after a viral illness and has the FLAIR/DWI images shown, with symmetric striatal signal. Which statement about the genetics is correct?

options.text: Nuclear gene variants account for about three quarters of cases
MT-ATP6 is the most common cause overall
It is X-linked in most families

questions.explanation: Nuclear gene variants account for about three quarters of cases. Leigh syndrome: nuclear genes (SURF1, complex I, PDHA1) \~75%; mtDNA (MT-ATP6, MT-ND) \~25%. Subacute necrotizing encephalomyelopathy: symmetric, often cavitating T2 lesions of putamen, caudate, periaqueductal gray, brainstem tegmentum, dentate, with lactate on MRS. Most common pediatric mitochondrial disease; nuclear genes in \~75% (SURF1, complex I subunits, PDHA1) and mtDNA in \~25% (MT-ATP6 m.8993T>G, MT-ND genes). Onset usually before age 2 with regression after intercurrent illness, hypotonia, dystonia, ophthalmoplegia, respiratory dysrhythmia. Distinguish from Wilson (thalami/putamen, older), CO poisoning (globus pallidus) and Fahr (calcification).
questions.imageAlt: Axial FLAIR and DWI: symmetric hyperintensity and restricted diffusion of the putamina and caudate heads. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 114)

questions.stem: What vascular malformation of the posterior cerebral circulation in neonates presents clinically with severe high-output congestive heart failure and an audible cranial bruit over the fontanelle?
questions.explanation: Vein of Galen malformations are arteriovenous fistulas draining into the persistent median prosencephalic vein of Markowski, causing massive low-resistance shunting and high-output cardiac failure in neonates.

questions.stem: Lateral catheter angiograms show irregular narrowing of the left ICA and a tapered flame-shaped occlusion on the right in a 38-year-old with neck pain. Highest on the differential?
questions.explanation: Carotid angiography: tapered occlusion/string sign. Tapered occlusion or string sign a few centimeters above the bulb in a young patient with neck pain indicates dissection; fibromuscular dysplasia (string of beads) is the alternative.
questions.imageAlt: Lateral catheter angiograms: left cervical ICA with irregular narrowing; right ICA with tapered flame-shaped occlusion a few centimeters above the bifurcation.
questions.salient: Painful Horner syndrome; fat-sat T1 crescent; CADISS: antiplatelet equals anticoagulation
questions.learning: Dissection: young patients, neck pain, painful Horner syndrome, then embolic stroke; T1 fat-saturated MRI shows crescentic intramural hematoma. Antiplatelet and anticoagulation equivalent (CADISS). FMD is bilateral in ~60% and associated with aneurysms.
questions.note: Angiographic diagnosis inferred; marginal note reads only "dx for R".

questions.stem: Coronal and sagittal post-contrast T1 in a 55-year-old woman with new seizures. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Dural-based convexity meningioma. Homogeneous enhancement, broad dural base, sharp margins, and buckled cortex indicate an extra-axial meningioma.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal and sagittal post-contrast T1: homogeneously enhancing, sharply marginated extra-axial mass on the left frontal convexity with a broad dural base and buckled underlying cortex.
questions.salient: Extra-axial signs: CSF cleft, cortical buckling, dural tail, hyperostosis; NF2 loss is the most common driver; progesterone receptor positive
questions.learning: Extra-axial signs: CSF cleft, cortical buckling, dural tail, broad dural base, adjacent hyperostosis. Most common primary intracranial tumor; associated with NF2 (merlin loss), prior radiation, and progestin exposure.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old with NF1 has the FLAIR image shown. Which feature would raise concern that a lesion is a glioma rather than a focal area of signal intensity?

options.text: New enlargement after age 10 with mass effect
Presence in the cerebellar white matter

questions.explanation: New enlargement after age 10 with mass effect. FASI peak around age 10 and regress; growth beyond that, enhancement, T1 signal or mass effect suggest tumor. FASI are not a diagnostic criterion. Most common MRI finding in NF1 (up to \~85% of children), typically basal ganglia, thalamus, brainstem, cerebellar white matter and dentate; histologically vacuolar myelinopathy, not tumor. They increase in number until about age 10 and then regress; new or enlarging lesions after 10, enhancement, T1 signal or mass effect should raise concern for glioma. FASI are not among the NIH/2021 revised diagnostic criteria.
questions.imageAlt: Axial FLAIR: bilateral symmetric hyperintense foci in the globus pallidus/basal ganglia without mass effect, edema or enhancement. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 87)

questions.stem: The tau immunostain shown demonstrates a flame-shaped neuronal inclusion. Which tau isoform composition is found in this disease?
questions.explanation: Mixed 3R and 4R. AD tangles are mixed 3R/4R paired helical filaments; Pick 3R; PSP/CBD 4R. Tangle burden correlates with cognition. Tangles are paired helical filaments of hyperphosphorylated tau (3R plus 4R in AD). Tau IHC detects pretangles and mature tangles but not extracellular ghost tangles. Tangle burden, not plaque burden, correlates with cognitive decline. Tau IHC also defines the other tauopathies: 3R Pick disease, 4R PSP/CBD/argyrophilic grain disease, and CTE.
questions.imageAlt: Anti-phosphorylated tau immunostain: a pyramidal neuron with a dense brown flame-shaped cytoplasmic tangle and dystrophic neurites, plus dispersed pretangle granules in neighboring cells. (RITE Review deck, slide 86)

questions.stem: Biopsy shows small fibers each with a single central nucleus and perinuclear halo. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Centronuclear (myotubular) myopathy. A single central nucleus per fiber with a myofibril-free halo defines centronuclear myopathy.
questions.imageAlt: H&E and trichrome: small rounded fibers each with a single centrally placed nucleus surrounded by a perinuclear clear halo devoid of myofibrils.
questions.salient: MTM1 X-linked (severe neonatal), DNM2 dominant (ptosis, ophthalmoplegia); Contrast with chains of internal nuclei in DM1
questions.learning: X-linked myotubular myopathy (MTM1): severe neonatal hypotonia and respiratory failure, males; autosomal dominant DNM2 (later onset, ptosis, ophthalmoplegia); recessive BIN1, RYR1, TTN. Single central nucleus per fiber versus chains of internal nuclei in DM1.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old with growth failure and visual loss has the imaging shown, with cystic and solid suprasellar components. Which mutation is characteristic of the childhood subtype?
questions.explanation: CTNNB1. Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma (CTNNB1, calcified, machine-oil fluid) in children; papillary (BRAF V600E) in adults. Bimodal: adamantinomatous type in children 5-15 years (CTNNB1/beta-catenin, calcified, machine-oil cyst fluid, wet keratin) and papillary type in adults (BRAF V600E, solid, rarely calcified). Rule of 90s for the childhood type: 90% cystic, 90% calcified, 90% enhance. Presents with growth failure, diabetes insipidus, visual loss, hydrocephalus. Hypothalamic obesity and panhypopituitarism are the main surgical morbidities; subtotal resection plus radiation is often preferred.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal and sagittal post-contrast T1: suprasellar mass with both cystic (yellow arrows) and enhancing solid (red arrows) components; blue arrows mark the superior extent of the lesion against the third ventricle. (RITE Review deck, slide 48)

questions.stem: In the classic Papez circuit mediating memory and emotion, what tract connects the mammillary bodies to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus?
questions.explanation: The Papez circuit follows: Hippocampus → Fornix → Mammillary bodies → Mammillothalamic tract → Anterior thalamic nucleus → Cingulate cortex → Entorhinal cortex → Hippocampus.

questions.stem: A patient presents with upward gaze paralysis, defective convergence, convergence-retraction nystagmus, and light-near pupillary dissociation. Where is the lesion?
questions.explanation: Dorsal midbrain (pretectal, Parinaud) syndrome is caused by compression or damage to the posterior commissure and pretectal area, classically by pineal region tumors or hydrocephalus.

questions.stem: T2 shows a cluster of small CSF-intensity foci in the subcortical white matter of an 82-year-old with no SWI blooming, no TOF correlate, and no enhancement. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Clustered T2-bright foci without susceptibility in an 82-year-old. Foci that follow CSF on all sequences without susceptibility, flow, or enhancement are enlarged Virchow-Robin spaces.
questions.imageAlt: T2: a cluster of small round hyperintense foci in the right frontal subcortical white matter (arrow). SWI: no corresponding blooming; TOF MRA: no vascular correlate; T1 and FLAIR: foci follow CSF (dark) without surrounding edema.
questions.salient: Type 1 basal ganglia, type 2 centrum semiovale, type 3 midbrain; Giant tumefactive PVS can mimic cystic tumor
questions.learning: Perivascular spaces follow CSF on all sequences, cluster in the basal ganglia (type 1), centrum semiovale (type 2), and midbrain (type 3), and lack enhancement. Giant tumefactive perivascular spaces can mimic cystic tumor. Enlarged PVS burden is a small-vessel disease and CAA marker. Differential: cystic neoplasm (DNET), cryptococcal gelatinous pseudocysts (immunocompromised), mucopolysaccharidosis in children.
questions.note: Revised after review; original draft called this CAA microbleeds. SWI dots in the original reproduction are cortical veins.

questions.stem: A patient presents with numbness of the fourth and fifth digits and weakness of the first dorsal interosseous and abductor digiti minimi. Forearm flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) to digits 4 and 5 is also weak. Where is the nerve entrapment?

options.text: Radial nerve in the spiral groove
Ulnar nerve at Guyon's canal in the wrist
Ulnar nerve at the retrocondylar groove / cubital tunnel of the elbow
Median nerve at the pronator teres

questions.explanation: The motor branches to FDP IV/V and flexor carpi ulnaris arise in the proximal forearm; their weakness localizes the ulnar lesion to the elbow rather than the wrist (Guyon's canal), as does involvement of the dorsal ulnar cutaneous territory.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with progressive cerebellar ataxia, choreoathetosis, and multiple recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections. Physical examination reveals prominent conjunctival and cutaneous telangiectasias. What serum biomarker elevation is characteristic of this condition?
questions.explanation: Ataxia-telangiectasia (ATM mutation causing defective DNA double-strand break repair) features progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasias, immunodeficiency, and elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein.

questions.stem: The line cancellation and clock drawing shown are from a stroke patient. Where is the lesion most likely?
questions.explanation: Right inferior parietal lobe. Left hemispatial neglect localizes to the right parietal/temporoparietal region; attention to the right is represented bilaterally. Right inferior parietal (and temporoparietal junction, frontal) lesions cause contralesional neglect; left-sided lesions rarely cause lasting neglect because attention to the right is represented bilaterally. Other bedside tests: line bisection (deviation toward the lesion), double simultaneous stimulation (extinction), figure copying, reading. Anosognosia and dressing apraxia are frequent companions; neglect predicts poor rehabilitation outcome.
questions.imageAlt: Line cancellation task with omitted lines on the left, and a clock drawing with all numerals crowded onto the right half. (RITE Review deck, slide 175)

questions.stem: The MRA shown fails to demonstrate the basilar artery. Which presentation is most characteristic of occlusion of this vessel?

options.text: Coma or locked-in state with quadriparesis and crossed cranial nerve signs

questions.explanation: Coma or locked-in state with quadriparesis and crossed cranial nerve signs. Basilar occlusion produces bilateral brainstem signs; thrombectomy windows are extended relative to anterior circulation. Absent flow-related enhancement in the basilar with preserved anterior circulation. Basilar occlusion produces coma, quadriparesis, crossed cranial nerve signs, locked-in state or top-of-the-basilar syndrome; mortality is high without recanalization and thrombectomy windows are extended relative to anterior circulation stroke.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal TOF MRA (A, B): the vertebrobasilar system is not visualized; the carotid circulation and its distal branches fill normally. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 65)

questions.stem: The coronal brain slice shown is from a 26-week infant who died on day 4. Which grade best describes hemorrhage that has extended into the ventricles with ventricular dilatation?
questions.explanation: Grade III. Papile: I matrix only; II intraventricular without dilatation; III with dilatation; IV parenchymal (periventricular hemorrhagic infarction). The germinal matrix is a fragile, highly vascular proliferative zone that involutes by 34-36 weeks; hemorrhage occurs in the first 72 h of life with fluctuating cerebral blood flow. Papile grades: I confined to matrix; II intraventricular without dilatation; III with ventricular dilatation; IV parenchymal (now understood as periventricular hemorrhagic venous infarction, not extension). Cranial ultrasound screening in infants <30 weeks; grades III/IV predict posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus and cerebral palsy.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal brain slice of a preterm infant: hemorrhage in the subependymal germinal matrix at the caudothalamic groove with extension into dilated lateral ventricles and into periventricular white matter. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 142)

questions.stem: A previously healthy 9-month-old infant with macrocephaly experiences acute encephalopathy, dystonia, and striatal injury following a febrile gastroenteritis. Brain MRI reveals wide-open Sylvian fissures ("bat-wing" frontotemporal opercular hypoplasia) and subdural fluid collections. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Glutaric aciduria type 1 (glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency) characteristically presents with baseline macrocephaly, open Sylvian fissures, chronic subdural hematomas, and acute striatal necrosis triggered by catabolic stress.

questions.stem: Lateral ventricle tumor in a 2-year-old with hydrocephalus; papillary fronds lined by a single epithelial layer. Diagnosis and mechanism of hydrocephalus?
questions.explanation: Choroid plexus papilloma. Choroid plexus papilloma resembles normal plexus and can overproduce CSF.
questions.imageAlt: Papillary fronds with a single layer of bland cuboidal epithelium over fibrovascular cores, resembling normal choroid plexus.
questions.salient: Atrium in children, fourth ventricle in adults; transthyretin positive; Carcinoma associated with Li-Fraumeni (TP53)
questions.learning: Lateral ventricle atrium in children, fourth ventricle in adults; hydrocephalus from CSF overproduction. Carcinoma (grade 3) in young children, associated with Li-Fraumeni (TP53). Transthyretin and cytokeratin positive.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male with small cell lung carcinoma presents with proximal leg weakness and dry mouth. Rapid repetitive nerve stimulation at 30 Hz produces a marked increase (>100%) in CMAP amplitude. What is the underlying antigenic target?
questions.explanation: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is caused by autoantibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type calcium channels, reducing baseline ACh release that increments (>100%) after high-frequency stimulation or brief exercise. Amifampridine is first-line symptomatic therapy.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old male presents with dream-enactment behaviors during sleep, thrashing and yelling while dreaming of defending himself. Polysomnography reveals REM sleep without muscle atonia on chin electromyography. What is the preferred initial pharmacotherapy?
questions.explanation: REM sleep behavior disorder involves loss of physiological motor atonia during REM sleep. Low-dose clonazepam or high-dose melatonin are first-line. Isolated RBD converts to a synucleinopathy in the large majority within 10–15 years.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with intractable focal seizures, developmental regression, and occipital-predominant epileptiform discharges is being considered for valproate. Before starting, what condition must be excluded because valproate may precipitate fulminant hepatic failure?
questions.explanation: Biallelic POLG variants (Alpers syndrome: refractory occipital epilepsy, epilepsia partialis continua, regression, liver disease) confer a high risk of valproate-induced hepatic failure; the FDA label contraindicates valproate in known POLG disease and advises testing in young children with suggestive features. mtDNA depletion drives the liver injury.

questions.stem: Recreational inhalation of nitrous oxide ("whippets") produces subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord through what biochemical mechanism?

options.text: Irreversible oxidation and inactivation of the cobalt core of cobalamin (Vitamin B12)

questions.explanation: Nitrous oxide irreversibly oxidizes the monovalent cobalt of methylcobalamin, inactivating methionine synthase and producing a myeloneuropathy identical to B12 deficiency, often with normal B12 levels but elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine.

questions.stem: A patient bitten by a bat develops hydrophobia, aerophobia, and agitation 5 weeks later and dies. What histopathologic finding is characteristic, and what should have been done after the bite?

options.text: Negri bodies in Purkinje cells and hippocampal pyramidal neurons; wound cleansing, rabies immune globulin infiltrated at the wound, and vaccine on days 0, 3, 7, 14

questions.explanation: Rabies is nearly uniformly fatal after symptom onset; post-exposure prophylaxis is essentially 100% effective if begun promptly. Bat exposures warrant prophylaxis even without a recognized bite. A paralytic (GBS-like) form occurs in ~20%. The Milwaukee protocol has not been reproducibly successful.

questions.stem: The post-contrast images shown demonstrate a dural-based enhancing mass with a dural tail. Which finding would upgrade this tumor to grade 3 under WHO 2021?

options.text: CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion or TERT promoter mutation

questions.explanation: CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion or TERT promoter mutation. Brain invasion or 4+ mitoses defines atypical (grade 2); CDKN2A/B loss or TERT mutation defines anaplastic; NF2 for multiple. Extra-axial clues: CSF cleft, buckled gray-white interface, dural tail (reactive, not tumor), hyperostosis on CT. Arachnoid cap cell origin; more common in women (progesterone receptors), after radiation, and multiple in NF2 (22q, merlin). Non-NF2 drivers: TRAF7, KLF4, AKT1, SMO, PIK3CA. Grade 1 in \~80%; atypical (grade 2) by mitoses 4+/10 HPF or brain invasion; CDKN2A/B loss or TERT promoter mutation defines grade 3 in WHO 2021. Psammoma bodies and whorls on histology.
questions.imageAlt: Axial (A) and coronal (B) post-contrast T1: homogeneously, avidly enhancing extra-axial mass with a broad dural base and dural tail (arrows), compressing but not invading the adjacent brain. (RITE Review deck, slide 43)

questions.stem: A coronal brain autopsy of a chronic alcoholic patient reveals hemorrhagic necrosis and petechiae restricted to the mammillary bodies and periaqueductal gray. What deficiency is responsible?
questions.explanation: Wernicke encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency) produces vascular congestion, petechial hemorrhages, and gliosis selectively in the mammillary bodies, periaqueductal gray, and medial thalami. Give thiamine before glucose.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old develops chaotic multidirectional conjugate eye movements, myoclonic jerks, ataxia, and irritability over 2 weeks. Which investigation is most likely to identify the underlying cause?

options.text: Urine homovanillic and vanillylmandelic acid with MIBG scan

questions.explanation: Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome. About half of pediatric cases are paraneoplastic from neuroblastoma, often small and occult; urine catecholamine metabolites, MIBG scintigraphy, and body imaging are required. Treatment: tumor resection plus immunotherapy (ACTH or steroids, IVIG, rituximab); neurologic outcome is independent of oncologic outcome and many children have residual cognitive and behavioral deficits.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with developmental delay and epilepsy has the T2 image shown, with posterior-predominant thick cortex and few gyri. Which gene is most likely?
questions.explanation: PAFAH1B1 (LIS1). LIS1 lissencephaly is posterior-predominant; DCX is anterior-predominant (band heterotopia in carrier females); POMT1 causes cobblestone lissencephaly; FLNA periventricular heterotopia. A disorder of neuronal migration (roughly weeks 8-20 of gestation). Classic (type 1) lissencephaly gradients localize the gene: posterior-predominant with PAFAH1B1/LIS1 (Miller-Dieker if deletion includes YWHAE), anterior-predominant with DCX (X-linked; carrier females have subcortical band heterotopia), TUBA1A with brainstem/cerebellar hypoplasia. Cobblestone (type 2) lissencephaly is an overmigration defect in dystroglycanopathies (Walker-Warburg, muscle-eye-brain).
questions.imageAlt: Axial T2 of a 4-year-old with developmental delay and epilepsy: thickened cortex with few, broad, shallow gyri and a smooth cortical surface; shallow sylvian fissures give a figure-of-eight configuration. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 104)

questions.stem: A patient with Hunt-Hess grade 3 aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage undergoes coiling on day 1. What intervention has proven benefit in reducing poor neurologic outcome from delayed cerebral ischemia?

options.text: Oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days

questions.explanation: Nimodipine improves outcome after SAH (Pickard 1989) without consistently reducing angiographic vasospasm, suggesting neuroprotective mechanisms. Delayed cerebral ischemia peaks days 4–14. Euvolemia is maintained; prophylactic hypervolemia, magnesium (MASH-2), and statins (STASH) failed in trials. Induced hypertension is used for symptomatic DCI.
