questions.stem: Frontal lobe tumor in a 45-year-old with seizures. H&E shows fried-egg cells and chicken-wire vessels. Which is required for the 2021 WHO diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Oligodendroglioma. Oligodendroglioma is defined molecularly by both IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion.
questions.imageAlt: H&E: monomorphic round nuclei with perinuclear clear halos (fried egg) and a delicate branching capillary network (chicken wire); companion GFAP stain highlights entrapped reactive astrocytes.
questions.salient: Fried-egg halo is a fixation artifact absent on frozen section; Chemosensitive (PCV/temozolomide); CDKN2A deletion worsens grade 3
questions.learning: 2021 WHO requires both IDH mutation and whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion. Frontal lobe, calcification on CT, adults 40 to 50, seizures. Chemosensitive (PCV or temozolomide plus radiation); grade 3 with CDKN2A deletion is worse. The fried-egg artifact is a formalin fixation effect absent on frozen sections.

questions.stem: What EEG pattern is characterized by high-voltage, frontally predominant, bilaterally synchronous negative-positive-negative complexes occurring in runs in patients with metabolic or hepatic encephalopathy?
questions.explanation: Triphasic waves (generalized periodic discharges with triphasic morphology) show frontal predominance and anterior-posterior lag, reflecting severe metabolic encephalopathy such as hepatic failure or uremia.

questions.stem: A man with untreated HIV (CD4 40 cells/µL) presents with a right hemiparesis. MRI shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia and gray-white junction. Serum Toxoplasma IgG is positive. What is the appropriate first step?

options.text: Empiric pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine (or TMP-SMX) with reassessment imaging in 10–14 days

questions.explanation: Multiple lesions with positive toxoplasma serology warrant empiric therapy; clinical-radiologic response within 2 weeks confirms the diagnosis. Primary CNS lymphoma favors solitary periventricular lesions with CSF EBV PCR positivity and increased thallium/FDG uptake, and is biopsied if no response. PML (JC virus) causes non-enhancing white matter lesions without mass effect; CMV causes ventriculitis and polyradiculitis.

questions.stem: The gross and MRI images shown demonstrate a tumor crossing the corpus callosum. Which feature favors lymphoma over glioblastoma?
questions.explanation: Homogeneous enhancement with T2 hypointensity. Both cross the callosum; lymphoma is homogeneous, hypercellular (T2 dark, restricted diffusion) and steroid responsive. Bihemispheric spread through the callosum is characteristic of glioblastoma and primary CNS lymphoma; lymphoma is homogeneous and T2 dark, glioblastoma necrotic and heterogeneous. Callosal involvement tends to present with abulia, apathy and executive dysfunction rather than lateralized deficits.
questions.imageAlt: Gross coronal slice and coronal post-contrast T1: hemorrhagic, necrotic tumor crossing the corpus callosum into both frontal lobes. (RITE Review deck, slide 24)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man develops ascending weakness and areflexia over 5 days after Campylobacter enteritis. Which statement about treatment of Guillain-Barré syndrome is correct?

options.text: Treatment should be deferred until nerve conduction studies confirm demyelination
IVIG (2 g/kg over 2–5 days) and plasma exchange are equally effective; combining them adds no benefit; corticosteroids are ineffective
Plasma exchange is superior to IVIG

questions.explanation: Trials showed equivalence of IVIG and PLEX, no added benefit from sequential therapy, and no benefit of steroids alone or added to IVIG. Treat within 2–4 weeks of onset in non-ambulatory patients. Monitor FVC and NIF (intubate for FVC <20 mL/kg, "20/30/40 rule"), dysautonomia, and cardiac arrhythmia. AMAN (anti-GM1/GD1a) follows Campylobacter and lacks sensory involvement.

questions.stem: The surface-projection FDG-PET shown demonstrates biparietal, temporal and retrosplenial hypometabolism. Which region shows the earliest metabolic change in this disease?
questions.explanation: Posterior cingulate/precuneus. Posterior cingulate hypometabolism precedes atrophy in Alzheimer disease. Posterior cingulate/precuneus hypometabolism is the earliest and most characteristic PET change in AD, preceding atrophy. The deck\'s contrast set: DLB adds occipital hypometabolism; CBD is asymmetric; semantic dementia is left temporal tip. Amyloid PET in the companion deck separates amyloid deposition from neurodegeneration.
questions.imageAlt: 3D stereotactic surface projections: bilateral hypometabolism of the parietal and temporal association cortices and the retrosplenial/posterior cingulate region, sparing primary sensorimotor and occipital cortex. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 99)

questions.stem: An infant with Joubert-like cerebellar vermian hypoplasia, congenital ataxia, and intellectual disability is found to have chorioretinal colobomas and congenital hepatic fibrosis. What variant syndrome is this?
questions.explanation: COACH syndrome is a Joubert-related ciliopathy variant characterized by *Cerebellar vermian hypoplasia, Oligophrenia (intellectual disability), Ataxia, Coloboma, and H*epatic fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl develops toe-walking and leg dystonia that is minimal in the morning and severe by evening; a reflex exam shows brisk knee jerks. She has been misdiagnosed with cerebral palsy. Trial of 100 mg levodopa produces complete, sustained resolution. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Dopa-responsive dystonia (Segawa disease) due to autosomal dominant GCH1 deficiency

questions.explanation: GTP cyclohydrolase 1 deficiency impairs tetrahydrobiopterin and thus tyrosine hydroxylase; the phenotype includes diurnal fluctuation, parkinsonism, and spasticity-like signs, and responds permanently to low-dose levodopa without dyskinesia. Any childhood-onset dystonia deserves a levodopa trial. Recessive forms (tyrosine hydroxylase, sepiapterin reductase deficiency) are more severe with CSF neurotransmitter abnormalities.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old female presents with an unreactive, dilated right pupil that responds poorly to light but constricts slowly on near accommodation. Instillation of dilute (0.1%) pilocarpine constricts the right pupil but has no effect on the normal left pupil. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Adie tonic pupil results from postganglionic parasympathetic denervation of the ciliary ganglion, producing cholinergic supersensitivity demonstrated by constriction to dilute pilocarpine. A pharmacologically dilated pupil fails to constrict even to 1% pilocarpine.

questions.stem: Healthy parents have a child with a de novo pathogenic SCN2A variant; neither parent carries the variant in blood-derived DNA. What recurrence risk should be quoted for future pregnancies?

options.text: Approximately 1–2%, because of possible parental germline (gonadal) mosaicism

questions.explanation: Apparent de novo variants may arise from a mosaic parental germline undetectable in blood; empirical recurrence is ~1–2% (higher, ~4–5%, for some genes). Prenatal or preimplantation testing can be offered. Deep sequencing of parental blood or sperm can sometimes detect low-level mosaicism and refine risk. Paternal age drives most de novo SNVs.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male presents with asymmetric weakness of finger flexion (flexor digitorum profundus) and knee extension (quadriceps). Muscle biopsy reveals endomysial CD8+ T-cell infiltrates invading non-necrotic fibers and rimmed vacuoles. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Inclusion body myositis characteristically affects older adults with asymmetric deep finger flexor and quadriceps weakness; pathology shows rimmed vacuoles on Gomori trichrome, Congo red–positive amyloid deposits, and p62/TDP-43 inclusions. Anti-cN1A antibodies are present in roughly a third. It is refractory to immunosuppression.

questions.stem: A macrocephalic 9-month-old with hypotonia has the T2 image shown, with white matter signal involving the subcortical U-fibers. Which MR spectroscopy finding is diagnostic?
questions.explanation: Elevated N-acetylaspartate. Canavan disease (ASPA) is the only leukodystrophy with elevated NAA; U-fiber involvement plus macrocephaly separates it from MLD and X-ALD. Aspartoacylase (ASPA) deficiency, autosomal recessive, Ashkenazi founder variants; spongiform leukodystrophy. Macrocephaly, hypotonia progressing to spasticity, optic atrophy, seizures, death in early childhood. Elevated N-acetylaspartate on MRS and in urine is diagnostic. U-fiber involvement distinguishes it from MLD and X-ALD; the macrocephalic leukodystrophy differential is Alexander (frontal predominant, GFAP, Rosenthal fibers), MLC and glutaric aciduria I.
questions.imageAlt: Axial T2: diffuse, symmetric hyperintensity of cerebral white matter extending into the subcortical U-fibers, with macrocephaly. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 102)

questions.stem: The cortical neuron shown contains a poorly demarcated eosinophilic inclusion. Which stain is required to reliably detect these inclusions?
questions.explanation: Alpha-synuclein immunohistochemistry. Cortical Lewy bodies lack a halo and are easily missed on H&E; McKeith staging is synuclein based. Cortical Lewy bodies are easily missed on H&E and can be mistaken for reactive astrocytes; alpha-synuclein immunohistochemistry is required and is the basis of the McKeith neuropathologic staging (brainstem, limbic, neocortical). Neocortical Lewy pathology underlies DLB: fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, parkinsonism, neuroleptic sensitivity.
questions.imageAlt: H&E of cortex: neuron (arrow) with a poorly demarcated, homogeneous eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion lacking the halo of the brainstem form. (RITE Review deck, slide 142)

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant presents with hypotonia, poor suck, ptosis, and severe constipation. Repetitive nerve stimulation at 50 Hz demonstrates an incremental CMAP response. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Infantile botulism (Clostridium botulinum spore ingestion) results in presynaptic blockade of ACh release, presenting with constipation, descending paralysis, and facilitation/increment on 50-Hz stimulation. Treatment is human botulism immune globulin (BabyBIG).

questions.stem: A 45-year-old presents with thunderclap headache, diplopia and hypotension; imaging is shown. What is the most urgent intervention?
questions.explanation: Stress-dose hydrocortisone. Pituitary apoplexy causes acute adrenal insufficiency; steroids precede everything else. Sheehan syndrome is the postpartum ischemic equivalent. Hemorrhagic infarction of a pre-existing adenoma (often previously unknown); precipitants include anticoagulation, surgery, dopamine agonists, pregnancy. Thunderclap headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia (cavernous sinus, CN III most often), meningismus. The immediately life-threatening issue is adrenal insufficiency: give stress-dose hydrocortisone before anything else. Sheehan syndrome is the postpartum ischemic equivalent in a non-adenomatous gland.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal non-contrast and post-contrast T1 and sagittal post-contrast T1: enlarged sellar mass with a central non-enhancing (necrotic/hemorrhagic) component compressing the optic chiasm. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 129)

questions.stem: In internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) caused by a lesion of the right medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), what ocular motor deficit is observed during leftward horizontal conjugate gaze?

options.text: Inability to depress the right eye in adduction
Failure of the left eye to abduct, with normal right eye movement
Failure of the right eye to adduct, with dissociated horizontal nystagmus of the abducting left eye

questions.explanation: The right MLF carries conjugate gaze signals from the left abducens nucleus to the right oculomotor nucleus; its disruption prevents right eye adduction during leftward gaze, accompanied by abducting nystagmus in the left eye.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old male presents with acute vertigo, dysphagia, hoarseness, left Horner syndrome, left limb ataxia, and dissociated sensory loss (loss of pain/temperature on the left face and right arm/leg). What artery is occluded?

options.text: Left paramedian branch of the basilar artery
Left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or vertebral artery

questions.explanation: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome is caused by occlusion of PICA or, more often, the vertebral artery, injuring the nucleus ambiguus, spinal trigeminal nucleus, spinothalamic tract, inferior cerebellar peduncle, and descending sympathetics.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old has a 3-minute generalized convulsion during a fever of 39.5°C, with rapid return to baseline and normal examination. There is no history of prior seizures. What is the appropriate evaluation and counseling?

options.text: No routine imaging or EEG; evaluate the source of fever; counsel that recurrence is ~30% and epilepsy risk is only modestly elevated (~2%)
Emergent MRI and EEG; start levetiracetam

questions.explanation: Simple febrile seizures (generalized, <15 min, no recurrence in 24 h, age 6 mo–5 y) require no EEG, imaging, or ASM (AAP guideline). LP is considered under 12 months with incomplete immunization, meningeal signs, or pretreatment with antibiotics. Risk of later epilepsy rises with complex features, family history of epilepsy, and neurodevelopmental abnormality. Prolonged febrile seizures may be the first sign of Dravet or lead to mesial temporal sclerosis (FEBSTAT). Rectal diazepam or intranasal midazolam is prescribed for prolonged recurrences.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child presents with morning vomiting and ataxia. Posterior fossa MRI demonstrates a cystic lesion in the cerebellum with a hyperenhancing mural nodule. Pathology reveals bipolar astrocytes with hair-like processes and Rosenthal fibers. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma is the most common pediatric cerebellar neoplasm, classically a cyst with an enhancing mural nodule containing Rosenthal fibers; most harbor a KIAA1549::BRAF fusion.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with restless legs syndrome on pramipexole for 4 years reports symptoms now beginning in the afternoon and spreading to her arms. Ferritin is 40 ng/mL. What is the correct management?

options.text: Recognize augmentation; taper the dopamine agonist, transition to an alpha-2-delta ligand (gabapentin enacarbil or pregabalin), and replete iron to ferritin >75 ng/mL

questions.explanation: Augmentation (earlier onset, spread, shorter latency at rest) occurs in a majority of patients on long-term dopaminergic therapy, so alpha-2-delta ligands are now first-line pharmacotherapy (AASM 2024). Iron deficiency is central to pathophysiology (low CSF ferritin, dopaminergic dysregulation); oral or IV iron is indicated for ferritin <75 ng/mL. Antidopaminergics, antihistamines, and SSRIs exacerbate RLS. MEIS1 is the strongest genetic association.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 7-month-old girl has a 25-minute hemiclonic seizure during a fever, then a second prolonged febrile seizure on the opposite side 6 weeks later. By age 3 she has myoclonic, atypical absence, and focal seizures with developmental plateau. Genetic testing confirms a de novo truncating SCN1A variant. Which medication is most likely to worsen her seizures?
questions.explanation: Dravet syndrome results from haploinsufficiency of Nav1.1, which is preferentially expressed in inhibitory interneurons; sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine) aggravate seizures. Valproate and clobazam are first-line; stiripentol, fenfluramine, and cannabidiol have RCT support.

questions.stem: The lumbar MRI shown demonstrates multiple nerve-root masses, a capacious thecal sac and posterior vertebral scalloping. Which underlying diagnosis best accounts for all of these findings?
questions.explanation: Neurofibromatosis type 1. Dural ectasia occurs in Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos, but nerve-root tumors plus ectasia and scalloping in a young patient is NF1. Dural ectasia and posterior vertebral scalloping are mesodermal features of NF1 (also seen in Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos), distinct from the neurofibromas themselves. Other NF1 bone findings: sphenoid wing dysplasia, tibial pseudarthrosis, dystrophic scoliosis.
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal T2 lumbosacral spine: multiple rounded intradural/foraminal nerve-root masses along the cauda equina with a capacious thecal sac and posterior vertebral scalloping. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 23)

questions.stem: Noncontrast CT shows basal cistern and interhemispheric hyperdensity; a later image shows a stellate metallic artifact. What sequence of events is most likely?
questions.explanation: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage with subsequent clip artifact. Cisternal and interhemispheric blood followed by clip artifact indicates a clipped ACoA aneurysm.
questions.imageAlt: Noncontrast CT: hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns, anterior interhemispheric fissure, and gyrus rectus region with early ventricular prominence. Later image at the same level shows a stellate metallic streak artifact at the anterior interhemispheric location.
questions.salient: Modified Fisher grade predicts vasospasm; Rebleeding risk highest in the first 24 hours
questions.learning: Modified Fisher grade predicts vasospasm risk. Blood distribution predicts the aneurysm (interhemispheric: ACoA; sylvian: MCA; perimesencephalic: nonaneurysmal venous). Rebleeding risk is highest in the first 24 hours; secure the aneurysm early and give nimodipine for 21 days. Hydrocephalus in ~20%.
questions.note: Inferred from image and marginalia; no answer key in source. Hyperdensity could alternatively be read as contrast-enhanced mass; the later clip artifact favors SAH from a clipped aneurysm.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl with neurofibromatosis type 1 has a normal eye examination at diagnosis. What is the recommended screening for optic pathway glioma?

options.text: Annual ophthalmologic examination (acuity, color vision, fundoscopy) through at least age 8, with MRI only for abnormal findings
No screening; optic gliomas in NF1 are always symptomatic
Baseline MRI and repeat only for visual symptoms

questions.explanation: Annual ophthalmologic examination through age 8 (then every 2 years to 18) is the standard; screening MRI is not recommended because most NF1 optic pathway gliomas are asymptomatic, indolent, and never require treatment. Symptomatic or progressive tumors are treated with carboplatin/vincristine rather than radiation (secondary malignancy, moyamoya). Selumetinib (MEK inhibitor) is approved for inoperable symptomatic plexiform neurofibromas and is used off-label for progressive OPG.

questions.stem: Serial midsagittal T1 images from four related patients aged 15 to 33 show progressive cerebellar and pontine atrophy. Which hereditary ataxia is highest on the differential?
questions.explanation: Progressive cerebellar atrophy in a hereditary ataxia. Olivopontocerebellar atrophy with anticipation across a family typifies SCA2 (also SCA1, 3, 7); Friedreich spares the cerebellum and atrophies the cord; SCA6 is pure cerebellar.
questions.imageAlt: Midsagittal T1 in a normal control and four patients aged 15 to 33: progressive atrophy of the vermis and cerebellar hemispheres with flattening of the ventral pons in the older patients.
questions.salient: Pontine atrophy: SCA1/2/3/7, MSA-C; pure cerebellar: SCA6, AT; SCA2: slow saccades; SCA7: retinopathy; SCA3: most common
questions.learning: Pontine atrophy with cerebellar atrophy (olivopontocerebellar) favors SCA1, 2, 3, 7 and MSA-C; pure cerebellar atrophy favors SCA6, ataxia-telangiectasia, and late-onset cortical cerebellar atrophy. Friedreich ataxia shows cervical cord atrophy with relative cerebellar sparing.
questions.note: Specific SCA cannot be assigned from imaging.

questions.stem: Coronal section with symmetric cavitary necrosis of the putamina. Highest on the differential?
questions.explanation: Bilateral basal ganglia necrosis, gross. Bilateral putaminal necrosis is classic for methanol; CO targets the globus pallidus; kernicterus the pallidum in neonates.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal section with symmetric cavitary softening and discoloration of the bilateral putamina (and adjacent globus pallidus), with sparing of the cortex.
questions.salient: Methanol: formate, optic nerve injury, anion gap acidosis; fomepizole/dialysis; CO: pallidal necrosis, delayed leukoencephalopathy
questions.learning: Methanol: formic acid toxicity, putaminal hemorrhagic necrosis plus optic nerve injury (retinal ganglion cells), anion-gap metabolic acidosis; fomepizole and hemodialysis. CO: bilateral globus pallidus necrosis with delayed leukoencephalopathy. Cyanide: cortex and basal ganglia. Kernicterus: globus pallidus in neonates.
questions.note: Lesion location best fits putamen; no key supplied.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with bilateral painful vision loss and marked optic disc swelling. He recovers with IV steroids but relapses when prednisone is tapered below 10 mg. Serum AQP4-IgG is negative. What antibody test should be sent?

options.text: Anti-MOG IgG by live cell-based assay on serum

questions.explanation: MOG antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) favors children, bilateral anterior optic neuritis with disc edema, ADEM presentations, and conus-involving myelitis; it is highly steroid-responsive with relapse on rapid taper. Serum is the appropriate specimen; low titers on fixed assays lack specificity. Long-term therapy (IVIG, rituximab, mycophenolate) is for relapsing disease.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman recovering from optic neuritis has a normal-appearing fundus. Pattern-reversal visual evoked potentials show a well-formed P100 with prolonged latency in the affected eye. What does this indicate, and in what setting are somatosensory evoked potentials most decisive?

options.text: Retinal disease; SSEPs localize brainstem strokes
Cortical blindness; SSEPs assess sacral roots
Demyelination of the anterior visual pathway; bilaterally absent cortical N20 responses ≥24 hours after cardiac arrest reliably predict poor neurologic outcome
Axonal loss; SSEPs diagnose carpal tunnel syndrome

questions.explanation: Latency prolongation with preserved amplitude signals demyelination (VEPs may be the only evidence of a prior subclinical optic neuritis in MS work-up); axonal or retinal disease reduces amplitude. Bilateral absence of median N20 responses after cardiac arrest has a false-positive rate near zero for poor outcome when recorded off sedation and hypothermia; brainstem auditory evoked potentials are used for acoustic neuroma screening and intraoperative monitoring.

questions.stem: A brain biopsy of a frontal mass reveals sheets of round cells with perinuclear clear halos ("fried-egg" appearance) surrounded by delicate branching capillaries ("chicken-wire" pattern). What genetic alteration defines this tumor?

options.text: Combined whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion with IDH mutation

questions.explanation: Under the 2021 WHO classification, oligodendroglioma is defined molecularly by IDH1/2 mutation and complete whole-arm codeletion of 1p and 19q.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with a prior episode of optic neuritis has this axial FLAIR. The periventricular lesion morphology is most characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Dawson fingers on axial FLAIR. Ovoid lesions oriented perpendicular to the ventricles (Dawson fingers) follow medullary venules and are characteristic of MS.

questions.stem: Under the 2017 McDonald criteria, which additional finding would allow a diagnosis of MS at this single time point?

options.text: A second clinical attack is required

questions.explanation: CSF oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time when dissemination in space is met.
questions.imageAlt: Multiple ovoid periventricular hyperintensities oriented perpendicular to the lateral ventricles in the callososeptal interface, bilateral and symmetric.
questions.context: A 28-year-old woman with a prior episode of optic neuritis has this axial FLAIR. The periventricular lesion morphology is most characteristic of:
questions.salient: Dawson fingers: perivenular, perpendicular to ventricles, callososeptal interface; Central vein sign and paramagnetic rims increase specificity over small-vessel disease
questions.learning: McDonald dissemination in space: periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord. Central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions on SWI increase specificity versus small-vessel disease.

questions.stem: Cyst wall with ciliated columnar epithelium and proteinaceous content, from the anterior third ventricle. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Colloid cyst. Colloid cysts at the foramen of Monro have simple ciliated epithelium and mucoid content.
questions.imageAlt: Cyst wall of simple cuboidal to columnar, partly ciliated epithelium on a fibrous capsule containing dense proteinaceous material.
questions.salient: T1 bright/CT dense; positional headache and sudden death; Endoscopic resection when symptomatic or enlarging
questions.learning: Endodermal origin; anterior third ventricle at the foramen of Monro; intermittent obstructive hydrocephalus and sudden death. T1 bright and CT hyperdense from cholesterol/protein. Correlate with Exam 239/241 imaging.

questions.stem: The histology shown demonstrates a biphasic pattern with corkscrew eosinophilic fibers. Which of the following also contains these fibers?
questions.explanation: Alexander disease. Rosenthal fibers occur in pilocytic astrocytoma, Alexander disease and chronic gliosis; microvascular proliferation here does not imply high grade. Rosenthal fibers (alpha-B-crystallin/GFAP) and eosinophilic granular bodies are the diagnostic clues, but Rosenthal fibers also appear in Alexander disease, chronic gliosis around syrinx and craniopharyngioma. Microvascular proliferation here does not imply high grade, unlike in diffuse gliomas. MIB-1 is low.
questions.imageAlt: H&E: biphasic pattern of compact fibrillary areas alternating with loose microcystic areas; brightly eosinophilic corkscrew Rosenthal fibers (small arrows) and microvascular proliferation (large arrow). (RITE Review deck, slide 9)

questions.stem: The myelin-stained cord sections shown are from a patient who died of a progressive motor disorder. Which pathologic feature would be expected in addition to the tract pallor shown?

options.text: Onion bulbs in the ventral roots
Lewy bodies in the intermediolateral column
Loss of anterior horn cells with ubiquitin/TDP-43 inclusions

questions.explanation: Loss of anterior horn cells with ubiquitin/TDP-43 inclusions. ALS combines corticospinal tract pallor with lower motor neuron loss; dorsal columns are spared, unlike B12 deficiency or Friedreich ataxia. Combines upper motor neuron loss (CST pallor, Betz cell loss) with lower motor neuron loss (anterior horn cells, ventral root atrophy). Bunina bodies and ubiquitin/TDP-43 positive inclusions are the histologic hallmarks; SOD1 disease is TDP-43 negative. Dorsal column sparing distinguishes ALS from combined system disease (B12) and Friedreich ataxia.
questions.imageAlt: Myelin-stained transverse sections of spinal cord: symmetric pallor of the lateral corticospinal tracts (and the smaller anterior tracts), with preserved dorsal columns. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 58)

questions.stem: A patient with fever, cranial nerve VI palsy and lymphocytic CSF with very low glucose has the CT shown. Which complication results from arteritis in this condition?

options.text: Perforator infarcts of the basal ganglia

questions.explanation: Perforator infarcts of the basal ganglia. Tuberculous basilar meningitis: hydrocephalus, cranial neuropathies and lenticulostriate infarcts. Basal predominance is the hallmark of TB, fungal (cryptococcal, coccidioidal) and sarcoid meningitis, versus convexity predominance in bacterial meningitis. Complications: communicating hydrocephalus, cranial neuropathies (VI most common), and infarcts from arteritis of the lenticulostriate/perforator vessels. CSF: lymphocytic, very low glucose, high protein; AFB smear insensitive, PCR/culture and ADA help. Deck\'s contrast: intracranial hypotension gives smooth pachymeningeal (dural), not leptomeningeal, enhancement.
questions.imageAlt: Axial contrast CT: thick enhancement of the basal cisterns and leptomeninges overlying the cerebellar folia and vermis. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 136)

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male with chronic alcohol dependence presents with profound anterograde and retrograde amnesia and spontaneous confabulation, with preserved immediate recall. Where are the critical lesions?

options.text: Medial dorsal nuclei of the thalamus and mammillary bodies

questions.explanation: Korsakoff amnestic syndrome develops from untreated or chronic thiamine deficiency, damaging the diencephalic memory circuits (mammillary bodies and mediodorsal/anterior thalamic nuclei).

questions.stem: Biopsy from a 68-year-old with finger flexor and quadriceps weakness. Trichrome shows rimmed vacuoles. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Inclusion body myositis. Rimmed vacuoles with endomysial inflammation in this clinical pattern are IBM.
questions.imageAlt: H&E and modified Gomori trichrome: fibers containing rimmed vacuoles lined by basophilic granular material, with endomysial inflammation.
questions.salient: Congo red amyloid, p62/TDP-43, COX-negative fibers, 15 to 18 nm filaments; Anti-cN1A; refractory to immunosuppression
questions.learning: Rimmed vacuoles (Gomori), Congo red/thioflavin-positive amyloid, p62 and TDP-43 inclusions, COX-negative fibers, 15 to 18 nm tubulofilaments on EM. Clinically: finger flexor and quadriceps weakness over age 50, anti-cN1A antibodies, refractory to immunosuppression.

questions.stem: The CTA shown demonstrates a saccular aneurysm of the anterior cerebral artery below the genu. Which site is the most common location for intracranial aneurysms overall?
questions.explanation: Anterior communicating/ACA complex. About 90% are anterior circulation: ACom/ACA 30-40%, ICA/PCom \~30%, MCA 20-30%. Deck teaching point: the aneurysm sits on the distal ACA below the genu, so it is not a pericallosal-segment aneurysm. Distribution of intracranial aneurysms: \~90% anterior circulation (ACom/ACA 30-40%, supraclinoid ICA and PCom \~30%, MCA bifurcation 20-30%); \~10% posterior (basilar tip, SCA, PICA). Two or more affected first-degree relatives confers a roughly 30% chance of harboring an aneurysm; ADPKD, Ehlers-Danlos IV and coarctation are associations.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal and sagittal CTA reconstructions: rounded outpouching from the ACA anterior to the genu of the corpus callosum. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 70)

questions.stem: Quadriceps biopsy from a 5-year-old boy with Gowers sign and CK 15,000. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy, H&E. Fiber size variation, hypercontracted fibers, necrosis with phagocytosis, and endomysial fibrosis in this setting are dystrophinopathy.

questions.stem: The deletion involves exons 45 to 50. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Not a candidate for any exon-skipping therapy

questions.explanation: Exon 45-50 deletion is out of frame; skipping exon 51 restores the frame (eteplirsen).
questions.imageAlt: Transverse muscle section with marked fiber size variation, rounded fibers, hypercontracted (dark) hyaline fibers, scattered necrotic fibers with macrophage infiltration, and endomysial fibrosis. Marginal note: 5-year-old boy, Gowers sign, climbing difficulty, elevated CK, quadriceps.
questions.context: Quadriceps biopsy from a 5-year-old boy with Gowers sign and CK 15,000. Diagnosis?
questions.salient: Dystrophin absent (DMD) versus reduced/patchy (BMD); Reading-frame rule; corticosteroids prolong ambulation; cardiomyopathy surveillance
questions.learning: Dystrophin immunostaining absent (reduced/patchy in Becker). Fibrosis and fatty replacement progress with age; pseudohypertrophy of calves. Corticosteroids prolong ambulation; cardiomyopathy surveillance; exon skipping and micro-dystrophin gene therapy for eligible genotypes.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant presents with irritability, motor regression, hyperacusis (exaggerated acoustic startle), and a cherry-red macular spot. Hepatosplenomegaly is absent. What enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: Tay-Sachs disease (HEXA on chromosome 15) features GM2 ganglioside storage with cherry-red spots and hyperacusis, while organomegaly is absent.

questions.stem: Trichrome and H&E of leptomeningeal vessels in a 32-year-old with parietal hemorrhage: thick, irregular hyalinized walls of varying caliber. Highest on the differential?
questions.explanation: Hyalinized vascular malformation of the leptomeninges. Irregular thick-walled arterialized veins and arteries with hyalinization in a young patient with lobar hemorrhage indicate AVM; CAA is Congo red positive and occurs in the elderly.
questions.imageAlt: Trichrome and H&E: abnormally thick-walled, irregularly sized vessels with collagenous (blue on trichrome) hyalinized walls in the leptomeninges and superficial parenchyma. Marginal note: 32-year-old, leptomeningeal surface, parietal lobe.
questions.salient: AVM: intervening gliotic brain, hemosiderin, calcification; Cavernoma lacks intervening parenchyma
questions.learning: AVM histology: mixed arterial and venous channels with intervening gliotic brain, hemosiderin, and calcification. Amyloid angiopathy would show Congo red-positive, acellular eosinophilic wall thickening in an elderly patient, not a 32-year-old.

questions.stem: Handout panels grouped under Duchenne include a trichrome-type section with intrafiber red droplets. That panel is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Intrafiber lipid droplets indicate lipid storage myopathy (carnitine deficiency, MADD), not dystrophinopathy.
questions.imageAlt: H&E and trichrome: fiber size variation, rounded fibers, degenerating and regenerating fibers, increased endomysial connective tissue and fatty replacement. The third panel shows fibers packed with red lipid-type droplets on a trichrome-type stain.
questions.salient: Oil red O confirms lipid; MADD (ETFDH) is riboflavin-responsive; The other two panels show classic dystrophic change
questions.learning: Dystrophin immunostaining absent; utrophin upregulated; secondary reduction of sarcoglycans. Becker: reduced or truncated dystrophin, in-frame deletions. Female carriers may show mosaic dystrophin staining.
questions.note: The third panel (intrafiber lipid droplets) is more typical of a lipid storage myopathy (carnitine deficiency, multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency) than of dystrophinopathy; it is grouped under Duchenne in the source handout and is flagged here.

questions.stem: The silver stain shown demonstrates dense inclusions in nearly every granule cell of the dentate gyrus. Which disease is this?
questions.explanation: Pick disease. The dentate gyrus is the most reliable site for Pick bodies; AD tangles are flame-shaped and Gallyas positive. The dentate gyrus is the most reliable place to find Pick bodies. Contrast with AD tangles (flame-shaped, Gallyas positive) and with Lewy bodies (eosinophilic with halo, alpha-synuclein positive, not argyrophilic).
questions.imageAlt: Bielschowsky silver impregnation of hippocampal dentate gyrus: dense black spherical inclusions in nearly every granule cell. (RITE Review deck, slide 114)

questions.stem: A 62-year-old male smoker presents with right ptosis, miosis, and facial anhidrosis. Chest imaging reveals an apical mass invading the superior sulcus (Pancoast tumor). Where are the cell bodies of the second-order sympathetic neurons located?

options.text: Ciliospinal center of Budge (intermediolateral cell column of C8–T2)

questions.explanation: First-order neurons arise in the posterolateral hypothalamus and descend to the ciliospinal center of Budge (C8–T2); second-order preganglionic neurons travel over the lung apex to the superior cervical ganglion; third-order neurons follow the carotid. Facial anhidrosis implies a pre-ganglionic (first- or second-order) lesion.

questions.stem: Beta-amyloid immunostain of cortex. What two pathologies are shown?

options.text: Amyloid plaques and cerebral amyloid angiopathy

questions.explanation: Amyloid plaques and cerebral amyloid angiopathy, beta-amyloid immunostain. Parenchymal plaques plus intense vascular wall labeling of leptomeningeal and penetrating vessels indicate AD pathology with CAA.

questions.stem: This patient is APOE e4 homozygous and being considered for lecanemab. What is the key risk?
questions.explanation: ARIA-E/H risk is highest in e4 homozygotes; MRI surveillance required and anticoagulation is an exclusion.
questions.imageAlt: Beta-amyloid immunohistochemistry: intensely labeled leptomeningeal and penetrating cortical vessel walls, plus diffuse and cored parenchymal plaques in the cortex.
questions.context: Beta-amyloid immunostain of cortex. What two pathologies are shown?
questions.salient: Vascular amyloid is Abeta40-rich; plaques Abeta42-rich; APOE e4 raises CAA hemorrhage and ARIA risk
questions.learning: CAA accompanies AD in ~80% of cases but is independently a cause of lobar hemorrhage. Vascular amyloid is predominantly Abeta40; plaques are Abeta42-rich. Thal amyloid phases, Braak tau stages, CERAD neuritic plaque scores compose the NIA-AA ABC score. APOE e4 increases CAA-related hemorrhage and ARIA risk.

questions.stem: On the coronal T1 image shown, the left cavernous carotid lacks its normal signal void. What does this indicate?

options.text: Pituitary adenoma invading the cavernous sinus
Occlusion or very slow flow in the internal carotid artery

questions.explanation: Occlusion or very slow flow in the internal carotid artery. Flowing blood is black on spin-echo; loss of the flow void implies occlusion, to be confirmed with MRA/CTA. A vessel with flowing blood is black on spin-echo T1/T2; loss of the flow void means occlusion or slow flow (confirm with MRA or CTA). Deck\'s exclusions: not a sellar/suprasellar mass, optic glioma or mesial temporal sclerosis. A cavernous ICA occlusion can present with an ipsilateral MCA/ACA stroke or be silent with good circle of Willis collateral.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal T1 through the sella: the normal signal void of the left cavernous ICA is replaced by intermediate/hyperintense signal, while the right cavernous carotid retains its flow void. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 132)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with prior gastric bypass surgery and heavy use of zinc-containing denture cream develops progressive sensory ataxia, spasticity, and a mild neuropathy, with macrocytic anemia and neutropenia. Serum B12 is normal. What deficiency is most likely?
questions.explanation: Acquired copper deficiency (bariatric surgery, excess zinc inducing enterocyte metallothionein, malabsorption) produces a myeloneuropathy indistinguishable from subacute combined degeneration, with dorsal column T2 signal and cytopenias. Check serum copper and ceruloplasmin (also zinc); oral copper repletion halts but does not fully reverse deficits. Vitamin E deficiency (abetalipoproteinemia, AVED/TTPA) causes a similar sensory ataxia with retinopathy.

questions.stem: In myasthenia gravis, which electrodiagnostic finding on repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) at 3 Hz is diagnostic of a neuromuscular junction transmission defect?

options.text: Decremental response >10% between the 1st and 4th/5th CMAP

questions.explanation: Low-frequency (2–3 Hz) RNS depletes presynaptic ACh pools; in myasthenia gravis, reduced postsynaptic receptor density leads to failed transmission, producing a decrement of >10% by the fourth or fifth potential.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old female presents with severe headache, papilledema, and focal seizures. Unenhanced head CT reveals the "cord sign," and post-contrast MRI displays the "empty delta sign" within the superior sagittal sinus. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Dural sinus thrombosis prevents contrast filling within the lumen, producing the empty delta sign on contrast imaging and cord sign on noncontrast CT. Anticoagulation is indicated even with hemorrhagic venous infarction.

questions.stem: Felbamate is restricted to refractory epilepsy (particularly Lennox-Gastaut syndrome) because of what idiosyncratic toxicity?
questions.explanation: Felbamate carries boxed warnings for aplastic anemia (~1 in 4,000–5,000) and hepatic failure, usually within the first year, requiring informed consent and blood count/LFT monitoring. Pancreatitis is a valproate toxicity.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old develops sudden flaccid weakness of the right arm 5 days after a febrile respiratory illness during a late-summer enterovirus outbreak. Reflexes are absent in the arm, sensation is normal, and MRI shows T2 hyperintensity confined to the anterior horn gray matter of the cervical cord. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute flaccid myelitis. Asymmetric, proximal-predominant flaccid weakness with anterior horn (gray matter) T2 signal after a viral prodrome, most strongly associated with enterovirus D68 (also EV-A71), is AFM; CSF shows mild pleocytosis and the pathogen is usually found in respiratory rather than CSF samples. GBS is symmetric with sensory symptoms and normal cord MRI; transverse myelitis involves white matter with a sensory level and sphincter involvement. Treatment is supportive; IVIG is commonly given; recovery is often incomplete and nerve transfer surgery is used for persistent deficits.

questions.stem: An interictal EEG demonstrating generalized, paroxysmal, slow spike-and-wave discharges (<2.5 Hz) in a child with multiple refractory seizure types and intellectual disability is diagnostic of:
questions.explanation: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is defined by multiple seizure types (tonic, atonic, atypical absence), cognitive impairment, and slow (<2.5 Hz) generalized spike-and-wave complexes, with generalized paroxysmal fast activity in sleep.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with generalized AChR-antibody-positive myasthenia gravis without thymoma asks whether thymectomy is worthwhile. What did the MGTX trial demonstrate?

options.text: Benefit only in patients with thymoma
No benefit of thymectomy over prednisone alone
Thymectomy plus prednisone improved clinical status and reduced prednisone requirement and hospitalizations over 3 years

questions.explanation: MGTX (Wolfe 2016) randomized non-thymomatous AChR+ generalized MG patients aged 18–65 to extended transsternal thymectomy plus prednisone versus prednisone alone, showing better QMG scores and lower steroid exposure. Thymoma is an absolute surgical indication; thymectomy is not recommended for MuSK-MG. Newer targeted agents include FcRn antagonists (efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab) and complement inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab, zilucoplan).

questions.stem: Homogeneously enhancing periventricular lesion abutting the ependyma in a 65-year-old. Before biopsy, which step should be avoided?
questions.explanation: Primary CNS lymphoma. Steroids cause lymphoma to vanish transiently and lower biopsy yield.
questions.imageAlt: FLAIR: hyperintense periventricular lesion abutting the ependyma with surrounding vasogenic edema. T1 post-contrast: homogeneous, dense enhancement.
questions.salient: Diffusion restriction, CT hyperdense, periventricular; ring enhancement in AIDS (EBV); High-dose methotrexate; MYD88 L265P
questions.learning: Homogeneous enhancement, diffusion restriction (hypercellular), periventricular/callosal location, hyperdense on CT. Ring enhancement in AIDS-related (EBV-driven) cases. Avoid steroids before biopsy (vanishing tumor). High-dose methotrexate-based therapy; MYD88 L265P and CD79B mutations.

questions.stem: A healthy woman is found to carry the same pathogenic MECP2 variant as her severely affected daughter. What best explains her lack of symptoms?

options.text: Skewed X-chromosome inactivation favoring the normal allele
Reduced penetrance from a modifier gene

questions.explanation: Random XCI normally produces mosaic expression; skewing toward the wild-type allele can render carriers of X-linked dominant variants asymptomatic (also seen in CDKL5, PCDH19, X-ALD carriers, and DMD manifesting carriers when skewed adversely). Familial Rett is rare but classically involves an asymptomatic mother with favorable skewing. XCI assays on blood may not reflect brain.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy presents with progressive gait unsteadiness, absent lower extremity reflexes, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Sensory examination reveals severe loss of vibration and joint position sense. Nerve conduction studies demonstrate absent sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs) with preserved motor conduction velocities. What is the genetic cause of this condition?

options.text: GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the frataxin gene (FXN)
Point mutation in the PMP22 gene
CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in ATXN1

questions.explanation: Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive spinocerebellar degeneration caused by an unstable intronic GAA repeat expansion in FXN on chromosome 9. It selectively involves the dorsal root ganglia, resulting in absent SNAPs alongside normal motor conduction velocities.

questions.stem: A patient with HIV (CD4 40) has 2 weeks of confusion; multiple ring-enhancing lesions are shown. Best initial management?

options.text: Empiric pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine with reimaging at 2 weeks

questions.explanation: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions in an immunocompromised host. Multiple ring lesions with positive toxoplasma IgG warrant empiric treatment; response confirms the diagnosis.
questions.imageAlt: FLAIR: multiple supra- and infratentorial hyperintense lesions with edema. T1 without and with gadolinium: several ring-enhancing lesions in cortex, deep gray, and brainstem. Marginal note: cognitive impairment over 2 weeks, lymphoma or toxoplasmosis.
questions.salient: PCNSL: fewer, periventricular, EBV PCR, thallium avid, restricted diffusion; Biopsy if no response by 10 to 14 days
questions.learning: Toxoplasmosis: multiple, basal ganglia predilection, eccentric target sign, thallium-cold, responds to pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine within 2 weeks. PCNSL: fewer lesions, periventricular, EBV PCR in CSF, thallium/FDG avid, restricted diffusion. Empiric toxoplasma treatment first; biopsy if no response.

questions.stem: The silver-stained cortex shown demonstrates a plaque and tangles. Why is the amyloid core pale on this stain?

options.text: Silver stains neurites and tangles but not amyloid
The plaque is diffuse rather than neuritic

questions.explanation: Silver stains neurites and tangles but not amyloid. Amyloid requires Congo red, thioflavin or A-beta immunostaining; NIA-AA scoring combines Thal, Braak and CERAD. Silver stains (Bielschowsky, Palmgren, Gallyas) show tangles and plaque neurites but are insensitive to amyloid itself, which is shown with Congo red, thioflavin or A-beta immunostaining. Diagnostic criteria (NIA-AA 2012) combine A-beta plaque phase (Thal), Braak tangle stage and CERAD neuritic plaque score.
questions.imageAlt: Palmgren silver impregnation of cerebral cortex: a neuritic plaque (center, amyloid core appears as a pale yellow background) surrounded by dystrophic neurites, with flame-shaped neurofibrillary tangles in adjacent neurons. (RITE Review deck, slide 85)

questions.stem: The orbital and brain images shown demonstrate T2-hypointense masses that mold to the globe. Why should corticosteroids be withheld before biopsy?

options.text: Lymphoma may regress and yield a non-diagnostic biopsy
They cause hemorrhage into the lesion

questions.explanation: Lymphoma may regress and yield a non-diagnostic biopsy. T2-dark hypercellular lesions include lymphoma; steroids produce transient lysis and hide the diagnosis. Hypercellular tumors (lymphoma, medulloblastoma, PNET, germinoma) are T2 dark, hyperdense on CT and restrict diffusion. Primary CNS lymphoma is periventricular, homogeneously enhancing, and characteristically melts away with steroids, so hold steroids until biopsy. In HIV it is EBV-driven and ring-enhancing, mimicking toxoplasmosis. Treatment is high-dose methotrexate based, not resection.
questions.imageAlt: Axial and coronal T1 and T2 orbit and brain: homogeneous, T2-hypointense soft-tissue masses that mold around the globe and orbital wall rather than invading them, with enhancement. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 135)

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman on oral contraceptives presents with headache and seizure; imaging is shown. What is the appropriate treatment?

options.text: Withhold anticoagulation because of the hemorrhage

questions.explanation: Therapeutic anticoagulation despite the hemorrhage. Venous sinus thrombosis is anticoagulated even with hemorrhagic venous infarction; a parasagittal hemorrhage outside an arterial territory is the clue. Hemorrhagic infarct that does not respect an arterial territory, especially parasagittal or temporal-occipital (vein of Labbe), means think venous. Risk factors: OCP, pregnancy/puerperium, thrombophilia, dehydration, infection (mastoiditis in children), malignancy. Treat with anticoagulation even in the presence of hemorrhage; CT signs include the dense clot sign and empty delta sign on contrast CT.
questions.imageAlt: Axial CT (A): right posterior frontal parasagittal hemorrhage with edema. Axial FLAIR (B): cortical/subcortical edema in the same region. MRV (C): loss of flow in the superior sagittal and right transverse sinuses with reduced parasagittal cortical vein signal. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 78)

questions.stem: A 70-year-old male with severe left carotid stenosis presents after a hypotensive episode with non-fluent, effortful speech, but preserved auditory comprehension and intact repetition. What aphasia syndrome is this?
questions.explanation: Transcortical motor aphasia features non-fluent speech and intact comprehension, with preserved repetition (differentiating it from Broca aphasia) due to ACA–MCA watershed prefrontal injury sparing the perisylvian arcuate bundle.

questions.stem: Non-enhancing fourth ventricular mass found at autopsy of a 60-year-old; hypocellular fibrillary clusters. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Subependymoma. Paucicellular nuclear clusters in a dense glial matrix with microcysts are subependymoma (grade 1).
questions.imageAlt: Clusters of small uniform nuclei embedded in a dense, hypocellular fibrillary glial matrix with microcysts; adjacent higher-magnification panel shows the paucicellular background.
questions.salient: Adults, fourth or lateral ventricle, non-enhancing, often incidental; Lacks well-formed pseudorosettes of ependymoma
questions.learning: Fourth ventricle or lateral ventricle in adults; slow-growing, non-enhancing, often incidental at autopsy. Distinguished from ependymoma by low cellularity and lack of well-formed pseudorosettes.

questions.stem: On magnetic resonance imaging of an intracerebral hematoma, what hemoglobin degradation state is characterized by bright (hyperintense) signal on T1-weighted images and bright (hyperintense) signal on T2-weighted images?
questions.explanation: Late subacute hemorrhage (~1 week to 1 month) contains lysed red blood cells with extracellular methemoglobin, which is bright on both T1 and T2. Mnemonic by stage: hyperacute I-B, acute I-D, early subacute B-D, late subacute B-B, chronic D-D.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old has the post-contrast image shown. Which molecular feature predicts benefit from temozolomide?
questions.explanation: MGMT promoter methylation. Glioblastoma is IDH-wildtype by WHO 2021 definition; MGMT methylation predicts alkylator response. Enhancing rim = hypercellular, neovascular tumor; center = necrosis; T2 corona = vasogenic edema plus infiltrating cells, which is why gross total resection of the enhancing component still leaves disease. WHO 2021: glioblastoma is IDH-wildtype by definition (TERT promoter, EGFR amplification, +7/-10); IDH-mutant tumors with necrosis are now astrocytoma grade 4. MGMT promoter methylation predicts temozolomide benefit. Ring-enhancement differential: metastasis, abscess (DWI bright center), lymphoma in HIV, tumefactive demyelination (open ring).
questions.imageAlt: Axial post-contrast T1: left temporo-occipital mass with thick irregular rim enhancement around a non-enhancing necrotic center and surrounding low signal (edema and infiltrating tumor). (RITE Review deck, slide 19)

questions.stem: A patient presents with unilateral limb apraxia, alien hand phenomenon, cortical sensory loss (astereognosis), and asymmetric rigidity unresponsive to levodopa. What 4R tauopathy is this?
questions.explanation: Corticobasal degeneration is an asymmetric 4R tauopathy (astrocytic plaques, ballooned neurons) presenting with cortical signs (apraxia, alien limb, cortical sensory loss) alongside extrapyramidal rigidity. Corticobasal syndrome has heterogeneous pathology, including AD in ~25%.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man who injects drugs presents with fever, back pain and leg weakness; imaging is shown. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Empiric oral antibiotics and repeat MRI in 2 weeks
Urgent surgical decompression with intravenous antibiotics

questions.explanation: Urgent surgical decompression with intravenous antibiotics. Epidural abscess with neurologic deficit is a surgical emergency; LP through the collection is contraindicated and steroids alone do not treat the infection. Classic triad (fever, back pain, neurologic deficit) is present in a minority. Risk factors: IVDU, diabetes, alcohol, HIV, spinal procedures. Sources: contiguous discitis-osteomyelitis (anterior collections) or hematogenous seeding (posterior). S. aureus dominates. Emergent MRI with gadolinium (rim-enhancing collection) and surgical decompression plus 6+ wks antibiotics.
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal T1 (A) and axial (B) thoracic spine: loculated fluid collection in the posterior epidural space spanning several mid-thoracic levels, compressing the thecal sac. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 29)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with previously normal development has new myoclonic and atonic seizures, ataxia, and language regression; by age 5 she has lost vision, with retinal dystrophy on examination. Tripeptidyl peptidase 1 activity is absent in leukocytes. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

options.text: CLN2 (late-infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis); intracerebroventricular cerliponase alfa

questions.explanation: CLN2 disease (TPP1) is the most treatable NCL; biweekly intraventricular cerliponase alfa slows motor and language decline substantially (Schulz 2018). Early seizures with ataxia in a 2–4-year-old should prompt enzyme assay. CLN3 (CLN3, 1-kb deletion) presents with vision loss first at 4–7 years with vacuolated lymphocytes; CLN1 (PPT1) presents in infancy. Curvilinear inclusions on electron microscopy characterize CLN2.

questions.stem: In the blink reflex, stimulation of the right supraorbital nerve elicits a delayed ipsilateral R1 and delayed bilateral R2 responses; stimulation of the left supraorbital nerve yields normal R1 and R2 bilaterally. Where is the lesion?
questions.explanation: R1 (~10 ms) is an ipsilateral oligosynaptic pontine response; R2 (~30 ms) is bilateral and polysynaptic through the lateral medulla. A trigeminal (afferent) lesion delays all responses from stimulating that side, whereas a facial (efferent) lesion delays R1 and R2 recorded on the affected side regardless of which side is stimulated. The blink reflex is useful in Bell palsy prognosis, trigeminal neuropathy, and demyelinating polyneuropathies (delayed R1 in CIDP and GBS).

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male presents with an acute right-sided complete third cranial nerve palsy and contralateral left-sided hemiplegia with lower facial weakness. Where is the infarction localized?
questions.explanation: Weber syndrome results from ventromedial midbrain infarction interrupting the exiting oculomotor (CN III) fascicles and the adjacent descending corticospinal/corticobulbar tracts in the cerebral peduncle.

questions.stem: CT perfusion maps in acute left MCA stroke. Which combination defines salvageable penumbra?
questions.explanation: CT perfusion in acute ischemic stroke. Autoregulatory vasodilation preserves CBV in penumbra while transit time is prolonged; core shows CBV/CBF collapse.
questions.imageAlt: Three color-coded perfusion maps of the same level showing a wedge-shaped left MCA-territory abnormality; the marginal note labels one as the mean transit time map.
questions.salient: DEFUSE-3: core <70 mL, mismatch ratio ≥1.8, penumbra ≥15 mL; Core: CBF <30% of contralateral
questions.learning: Core: CBV or CBF <30% of contralateral. Penumbra: Tmax >6 s with preserved CBV. DEFUSE-3 mismatch criteria: core <70 mL, mismatch ratio ≥1.8, penumbra ≥15 mL. Autoregulation preserves CBV in penumbra until it fails.
questions.note: Individual map identities cannot be confirmed from the reproduction.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old developed a generalized seizure 3 days postpartum with BP 175/110. FLAIR and T2 are shown. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome in a postpartum patient. Symmetric posterior subcortical vasogenic edema in the setting of eclampsia is PRES.

questions.stem: Which finding would argue against PRES and for infarction?
questions.explanation: PRES edema is vasogenic with elevated ADC; restricted diffusion indicates cytotoxic injury.
questions.imageAlt: A: FLAIR bilateral parieto-occipital subcortical white matter and cortical hyperintensity. B: T2 posterior-predominant edema. Marginal note: 16-year-old postpartum seizure.
questions.context: A 16-year-old developed a generalized seizure 3 days postpartum with BP 175/110. FLAIR and T2 are shown. Diagnosis?
questions.salient: Vasogenic (elevated ADC), posterior predilection from sparse sympathetic innervation; Triggers: hypertension, eclampsia, calcineurin inhibitors; reversible with BP control and magnesium
questions.learning: Vasogenic edema (elevated ADC), posterior predilection from sparse sympathetic innervation of the posterior circulation. Triggers: hypertension, eclampsia, calcineurin inhibitors, chemotherapy, renal failure. Reversible with BP control and magnesium; hemorrhage or infarction in a minority.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with 2 days of fever, headache, aphasia, and a focal seizure. MRI shows left temporal T2/FLAIR hyperintensity with restricted diffusion and petechial hemorrhage. CSF has 120 WBC (lymphocytic), 80 RBC, protein 85, normal glucose. Initial CSF HSV PCR is negative. What is the correct next step?

options.text: Continue empiric IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours and repeat CSF HSV PCR in 3–7 days
Stop acyclovir since PCR is negative

questions.explanation: HSV-1 encephalitis PCR may be falsely negative within the first 72 hours; clinical-radiologic suspicion mandates continued acyclovir for 14–21 days with repeat testing. Untreated mortality exceeds 70%. Post-HSV anti-NMDAR encephalitis occurs in ~25% of children with relapse weeks later. Neonatal HSV-2 disease is treated with 21 days of high-dose acyclovir followed by oral suppression.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of generalized flaccid paralysis following heavy carbohydrate meals or rest after strenuous exercise. Serum potassium is 2.1 mEq/L during attacks. What channel is most commonly mutated?
questions.explanation: Hypokalemic periodic paralysis is most commonly caused by CACNA1S (~60%) or SCN4A variants; carbohydrate loads stimulate insulin release, driving potassium intracellularly. KCNJ2 causes Andersen-Tawil syndrome (periodic paralysis, dysmorphism, long QT).

questions.stem: A 4-month-old girl with infantile spasms has the coronal MRI shown. Which additional finding would confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chorioretinal lacunae. Aicardi syndrome: callosal agenesis, chorioretinal lacunae, infantile spasms; almost exclusively females. Classic triad: callosal agenesis, chorioretinal lacunae (pathognomonic on fundoscopy), infantile spasms. Seen almost exclusively in girls (and XXY males); presumed X-linked dominant with male lethality, though no gene is established. Other features: microphthalmia, costovertebral anomalies, choroid plexus papilloma, severe developmental impairment.
questions.imageAlt: Coronal T2: agenesis of the corpus callosum with parallel lateral ventricles and colpocephaly, polymicrogyria/heterotopia, and interhemispheric cysts. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 108)

questions.stem: A 3-day-old neonate presents with intractable multifocal clonic seizures unresponsive to phenobarbital and levetiracetam that stop within minutes of intravenous pyridoxine. Urine alpha-aminoadipic semialdehyde (alpha-AASA) and plasma pipecolic acid are markedly elevated. What gene is mutated?
questions.explanation: Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy is caused by biallelic ALDH7A1 variants in the lysine catabolic pathway; accumulating piperideine-6-carboxylate condenses with and inactivates PLP, depleting the cofactor for GAD and GABA synthesis. Treatment is lifelong pyridoxine plus lysine restriction and arginine supplementation. PNPO deficiency presents similarly but requires PLP rather than pyridoxine.

questions.stem: A macrocephalic toddler with mild delay has the MRI shown, with diffuse white matter swelling and anterior temporal subcortical cysts. Which gene is most commonly responsible?
questions.explanation: MLC1. MLC1 causes \~75% of megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts; ASPA is Canavan, GFAP Alexander, GCDH glutaric aciduria I, ATP7A Menkes. MLC1 (75%) or HEPACAM (GlialCAM) variants; astrocytic water/ion homeostasis defect. Macrocephaly in the first year, then surprisingly slow decline with ataxia, spasticity, seizures. Deck\'s macrocephaly-leukodystrophy list: Alexander, Canavan, MLC; also Menkes (X-linked copper transport, subdural effusions) and glutaric aciduria I (widened sylvian fissures, subdural collections).
questions.imageAlt: Axial T1 (two levels): diffuse swelling and low T1 signal of the cerebral white matter with anterior temporal subcortical cysts in a macrocephalic child. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 105)

questions.stem: According to the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial, what was the effect of treatment on acute demyelinating optic neuritis?

options.text: IV methylprednisolone improved final visual acuity at one year
IV methylprednisolone accelerated visual recovery without changing final acuity, while oral prednisone alone increased recurrent optic neuritis
Oral prednisone was equivalent to IV methylprednisolone
Steroids reduced conversion to MS at 15 years

questions.explanation: ONTT (Beck 1992) showed IV methylprednisolone hastened recovery and delayed (for 2 years) clinically definite MS in patients with MRI lesions, but did not alter 1-year visual outcome; standard-dose oral prednisone alone doubled recurrence and is therefore avoided. Baseline MRI lesion burden was the strongest predictor of MS conversion.

questions.stem: The photographs shown demonstrate posterior calf atrophy in a 22-year-old with a CK of 8,000. Which gene is most likely?
questions.explanation: DYSF. Miyoshi myopathy (dysferlin) affects the posterior compartment; GNE and MYH7 are anterior; TTN and TIA1 are late onset. Distal weakness pattern (MP2) sends you to the distal dystrophies, myotonic dystrophy, myofibrillar/desmin myopathy and Laing/Nonaka/Miyoshi. Posterior compartment (calf) predominance with very high CK in a young adult = Miyoshi myopathy (dysferlin, DYSF, allelic with LGMD R2); anterior compartment (tibialis anterior) = Nonaka (GNE, rimmed vacuoles, quadriceps sparing) and Laing (MYH7). Late-onset: Welander (TIA1) and Udd/Markesbery (titin).
questions.imageAlt: Clinical photographs of the lower limbs: distal tapering with atrophy of the posterior calf (gastrocnemius) compartment. (RITE Review deck, slide 208)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman 6 days postpartum presents with three recurrent thunderclap headaches over one week. CT and LP are unremarkable; CTA shows multifocal segmental "string of beads" narrowing of distal cerebral arteries. What is the diagnosis and expected course?

options.text: Giant cell arteritis; requires high-dose prednisone
Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome; angiographic resolution within 3 months, often treated with nimodipine

questions.explanation: RCVS is triggered by the postpartum state, vasoactive drugs (SSRIs, triptans, cannabis, decongestants), and sexual activity; recurrent thunderclap headache is the hallmark. Complications include convexity SAH, PRES, and infarcts. Glucocorticoids are associated with worse outcomes. Normal CSF distinguishes it from primary CNS vasculitis.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with progressive ataxia and dysarthria has central vision loss with a pigmentary macular degeneration; her father had ataxia and her child, aged 5, has recently developed ataxia and blindness. What spinocerebellar ataxia is this?
questions.explanation: SCA7 (ATXN7 CAG expansion) uniquely combines ataxia with cone-rod dystrophy and shows marked anticipation, particularly with paternal transmission. Other high-yield associations: SCA3 (most common worldwide; bulging eyes, neuropathy, parkinsonism), SCA2 (markedly slow saccades), SCA6 (CACNA1A late-onset pure ataxia with minimal anticipation), SCA1 (pyramidal signs), SCA17 (chorea/dementia, HD-like), DRPLA (myoclonus epilepsy, Japanese ancestry).

questions.stem: A newborn with high-output heart failure and a cranial bruit has the angiogram shown. What is the embryologic structure that forms the dilated venous sac?
questions.explanation: Median prosencephalic vein of Markowski. Vein of Galen aneurysmal malformation is a fistula into the persistent embryonic median prosencephalic vein; treated by staged embolization. Not a true aneurysm but an arteriovenous fistula into a persistent embryonic vein. Presents in the neonate with high-output congestive heart failure and a cranial bruit; infants present with macrocephaly and hydrocephalus (venous hypertension impairs CSF absorption); older children with developmental delay or hemorrhage. Staged transarterial embolization is standard; CHF at birth is a poor prognostic marker.
questions.imageAlt: Lateral angiogram: massively dilated midline venous sac (the embryonic median prosencephalic vein of Markowski) with multiple enlarged arterial feeders. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 68)

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy wakes at 4 a.m. with left facial twitching, drooling, gurgling sounds, and inability to speak, remaining fully aware. EEG shows high-amplitude right centrotemporal spikes with a horizontal dipole, markedly activated by drowsiness and sleep. Neurologic exam and development are normal. What is the expected outcome?

options.text: Spontaneous remission by mid-adolescence, often without treatment

questions.explanation: Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (SeLECTS, formerly benign rolandic epilepsy) is the most common childhood focal epilepsy; seizures are infrequent and nocturnal, and remission by age 15–16 is nearly universal. Treatment is optional; a minority evolve to the epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep (EE-SWAS/CSWS).

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman on atorvastatin develops progressive proximal weakness with CK 12,000 U/L that continues to worsen 3 months after the statin is stopped. Biopsy shows scattered necrotic and regenerating fibers with sparse lymphocytes and sarcolemmal MHC-I/C5b-9 deposition. What antibody is expected, and what is the treatment?

options.text: Anti-HMGCR; immunosuppression (steroids plus IVIG or methotrexate)

questions.explanation: Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy with anti-HMGCR antibodies is triggered by statin exposure in most adults but persists after withdrawal, distinguishing it from self-limited toxic statin myopathy; anti-SRP defines the other IMNM subtype with cardiac involvement. IVIG is particularly effective in anti-HMGCR disease. Anti-Jo-1 defines antisynthetase syndrome (ILD, mechanic's hands, arthritis).

questions.stem: The imaging shown demonstrates a cystic fourth ventricle with an enlarged posterior fossa and a small, rotated vermis. Which feature separates this malformation from mega cisterna magna?
questions.explanation: Vermian hypoplasia with upward rotation. Mega cisterna magna and Blake pouch cyst have a normal vermis; Dandy-Walker requires vermian hypoplasia, cystic fourth ventricle and enlarged posterior fossa. Requires all three: vermian hypoplasia with rotation, cystic fourth ventricle, enlarged posterior fossa (versus mega cisterna magna and Blake pouch cyst, which have a normal vermis). Hydrocephalus in most; associated callosal agenesis, occipital cephalocele, PHACE syndrome, FOXC1/ZIC1-ZIC4 deletions. Outcome tracks the associated supratentorial anomalies more than the cyst.
questions.imageAlt: Axial and sagittal T1: cystic dilatation of the fourth ventricle communicating with an enlarged posterior fossa, hypoplastic and upwardly rotated vermis, elevated torcula and tentorium. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 117)

questions.stem: A 32-year-old female presents with strictly unilateral, severe, periorbital headache attacks lasting 15 minutes occurring 8–12 times per day, accompanied by ipsilateral lacrimation and rhinorrhea. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Paroxysmal hemicrania is a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia characterized by multiple brief attacks (2–30 minutes, >5/day) that respond absolutely to indomethacin, which is diagnostic. Cluster attacks are longer (15–180 min) and less frequent; SUNCT attacks last seconds.

questions.stem: A young girl presents with developmental regression starting at 14 months of age, deceleration of head growth (acquired microcephaly), loss of purposeful hand movements, and midline hand-wringing stereotypies. What gene is mutated?
questions.explanation: Classic Rett syndrome is an X-linked disorder occurring almost exclusively in females, caused by typically de novo loss-of-function variants in methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2). Trofinetide was approved for Rett syndrome in 2023.

questions.stem: An immunocompromised patient with headache has the T2 image shown, with clustered non-enhancing cysts in the basal ganglia. Which test is most sensitive for the responsible organism?
questions.explanation: CSF cryptococcal antigen. Gelatinous pseudocysts in dilated perivascular spaces are cryptococcal; antigen testing outperforms India ink, and high opening pressure often requires serial LPs. Cryptococcus neoformans spreads along the Virchow-Robin spaces from the basal meninges, giving the soap-bubble appearance in the basal ganglia. Meningitis is the usual presentation; opening pressure is often very high and serial LPs are therapeutic. CSF cryptococcal antigen is more sensitive than India ink. Induction with liposomal amphotericin plus flucytosine, then fluconazole; watch for IRIS after ART initiation.
questions.imageAlt: Axial T2: multiple clustered, CSF-bright, non-enhancing cystic lesions in the bilateral basal ganglia (dilated perivascular spaces packed with organisms). (Neuroradiology deck, slide 93)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man who injects drugs presents with 5 days of severe back pain and fever, now with bilateral leg weakness and urinary retention. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?

options.text: Spinal epidural abscess (usually Staphylococcus aureus); emergent contrast MRI, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, and surgical decompression with drainage

questions.explanation: The classic triad (back pain, fever, neurologic deficit) is present in a minority at presentation, so risk factors (IV drug use, diabetes, immunosuppression, recent spinal procedure, bacteremia) should trigger MRI. Cord injury results from compression and venous infarction; outcomes depend on pre-operative deficit duration (<24–36 hours). Medical management alone is reserved for patients without deficit or with prohibitive surgical risk.

questions.stem: A previously normal 5-year-old loses the ability to understand spoken language over 3 months and is thought to be deaf, though audiometry is normal; he has had two brief nocturnal seizures. What EEG finding is expected?
questions.explanation: Landau-Kleffner syndrome (acquired epileptic aphasia): verbal auditory agnosia in a previously normal child with bilateral centrotemporal/posterior temporal spikes that become near-continuous in non-REM sleep (spike-wave activation in sleep, formerly ESES). Seizures are infrequent and easy to control; the language regression is the disability. Treatment: high-dose diazepam, corticosteroids/ACTH, valproate, ethosuximide, levetiracetam; avoid carbamazepine; multiple subpial transection for refractory cases. GRIN2A variants underlie a subset of the EE-SWAS spectrum.

questions.stem: Coronal sections from an infant with profound delay and spasms show a smooth cortical surface. Diagnosis and most common gene?
questions.explanation: Lissencephaly, gross. Agyria with a thick four-layer cortex is classic lissencephaly, most often LIS1 (Miller-Dieker with 17p13.3 deletion).
questions.imageAlt: Two coronal sections with a nearly smooth cortical surface lacking normal gyri, a markedly thickened cortical ribbon, thin white matter, and enlarged lateral ventricles.
questions.salient: DCX: anterior-predominant in boys, band heterotopia in girls; Cobblestone type: dystroglycanopathies with eye and muscle disease
questions.learning: Type 1 (classic): LIS1/PAFAH1B1 (posterior-predominant; Miller-Dieker with 17p13.3 deletion, facial dysmorphism), DCX (anterior-predominant in males; subcortical band heterotopia in females), TUBA1A. Type 2 (cobblestone): dystroglycanopathies (Walker-Warburg, muscle-eye-brain, Fukuyama) with eye and muscle involvement. Presentation: severe developmental delay, infantile spasms, hypotonia.
questions.note: Revised after review; earlier draft called this hydrocephalus. The smooth surface and thick cortex are unambiguous on the larger image.

questions.stem: The muscle biopsy shown demonstrates atrophy of fibers at the fascicle periphery. What is the mechanism?

options.text: CD8 T-cell invasion of non-necrotic fibers

questions.explanation: Complement-mediated capillary injury with ischemia. Perifascicular atrophy in dermatomyositis reflects membrane attack complex deposition on endomysial capillaries; PM/IBM show CD8 invasion. Perifascicular atrophy is nearly pathognomonic and reflects capillary dropout from complement (membrane attack complex) deposition on endomysial capillaries; infiltrate is CD4 T cells, B cells and plasmacytoid dendritic cells with a type I interferon signature (MxA staining). Contrast with polymyositis/IBM: endomysial CD8 T cells invading non-necrotic fibers expressing MHC-I.
questions.imageAlt: Muscle biopsy: perifascicular atrophy (small fibers at the fascicle periphery) with perivascular and perimysial inflammatory infiltrate. (RITE Review deck, slide 204)

questions.stem: A lesion confined to the right parietal optic radiations (Baum loop) produces which visual field defect?

options.text: Left homonymous superior quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky")
Left homonymous inferior quadrantanopia ("pie on the floor")

questions.explanation: Fibers traversing the parietal lobe (Baum loop) represent the inferior visual quadrant; lesions result in a contralateral homonymous inferior quadrantanopia.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man has several-per-hour brief episodes of unilateral arm and facial contraction lasting 1–2 seconds, followed over weeks by memory loss. Serum sodium is 124 mEq/L. MRI shows medial temporal T2 hyperintensity. What antibody is most likely?
questions.explanation: Faciobrachial dystonic seizures are pathognomonic for anti-LGI1 limbic encephalitis, which affects older men, produces hyponatremia, and responds to early immunotherapy (steroids/IVIG) better than to ASMs; tumor association is low (<10%). CASPR2 (also VGKC-complex) causes Morvan syndrome with neuromyotonia and is thymoma-associated. Anti-GABA-B causes refractory seizures with SCLC.

questions.stem: A patient receiving haloperidol develops acute neck twisting (spasmodic torticollis) and tongue protrusion within hours of dosing. What is the immediate treatment of choice?
questions.explanation: Acute dystonic reactions result from dopamine D2 receptor blockade with relative cholinergic excess; anticholinergic agents (diphenhydramine or benztropine) provide rapid resolution.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with alcohol use disorder presents confused and ataxic. DWI and T2 are shown. Best immediate treatment?

options.text: IV thiamine 500 mg three times daily before glucose

questions.explanation: Wernicke encephalopathy on DWI and T2. Symmetric medial thalamic signal is Wernicke encephalopathy; high-dose parenteral thiamine precedes glucose.

questions.stem: Which region is NOT typically involved in Wernicke encephalopathy?
questions.explanation: Putaminal necrosis points to methanol or Wilson disease, not thiamine deficiency.
questions.imageAlt: A: DWI symmetric bilateral medial thalamic hyperintensity. B: T2 bilateral paramedian thalamic hyperintensity. Marginal note: 52-year-old with encephalopathy and alcohol use; differential Wernicke vs basilar.
questions.context: A 52-year-old with alcohol use disorder presents confused and ataxic. DWI and T2 are shown. Best immediate treatment?
questions.salient: MRI only ~50% sensitive: treat empirically; Mimics: artery of Percheron infarct, deep venous thrombosis, CJD
questions.learning: MRI: medial thalami, mammillary bodies, periaqueductal gray, tectum; mammillary body enhancement in alcoholics. Sensitivity of MRI only ~50%, so treat empirically (thiamine 500 mg IV TID) before glucose. Artery of Percheron infarct is the key vascular mimic; bilateral thalamic venous infarct from deep venous thrombosis is another.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with fever, neck stiffness, and confusion. What is the appropriate empiric regimen, and when should dexamethasone be given?

options.text: Ceftriaxone alone; dexamethasone after CSF results
Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone; dexamethasone at 48 hours
Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone plus ampicillin; dexamethasone 10 mg IV given before or with the first antibiotic dose

questions.explanation: Adults >50, immunocompromised, or pregnant require ampicillin for Listeria; vancomycin covers resistant pneumococcus. Adjunctive dexamethasone (de Gans 2002) reduces mortality and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis when started before or with antibiotics and is continued only if pneumococcus is confirmed. Do not delay antibiotics for imaging or LP; obtain blood cultures first.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male presents with weakness and wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles.
