Routine nerve conduction studies show that stimulating the median nerve at the elbow yields a larger CMAP amplitude than stimulating at the wrist when recording from the abductor pollicis brevis. What anomaly accounts for this?
questions.explanation: Martin-Gruber anastomosis is a crossing branch from the median (usually anterior interosseous) nerve to the ulnar nerve in the forearm; proximal median stimulation activates crossed ulnar fibers, producing a larger CMAP amplitude at the elbow than at the wrist.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with orthostatic headache. Sagittal T1 and post-contrast axial and coronal images are shown. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Spontaneous intracranial hypotension. Smooth diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement with brainstem sagging indicates CSF hypovolemia.

questions.stem: Which enhancement pattern is expected here, and why does it differ from meningitis?

options.text: Pachymeningeal, spares sulci, from dural venous engorgement

questions.explanation: Dural venous engorgement gives smooth, sulcus-sparing pachymeningeal enhancement; infectious and carcinomatous meningitis enhance the pia and sulci.
questions.imageAlt: Exam 280: sagittal T1 with descent of the brainstem and cerebellar tonsils and effaced prepontine cistern; axial post-contrast T1 with smooth, diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement. Exam 300 coronal T1 post: thick continuous dural enhancement including the tentorium. Marginal notes: orthostatic headache with normal exam; headache after lumbar puncture that resolves lying flat.
questions.context: A 52-year-old with orthostatic headache. Sagittal T1 and post-contrast axial and coronal images are shown. Diagnosis?
questions.salient: Monro-Kellie compensation: SEEPS (subdurals, enhancement, engorged sinuses, pituitary hyperemia, sagging); Epidural blood patch first line; opening pressure may be normal
questions.learning: Monro-Kellie: CSF loss compensated by venous/dural engorgement (SEEPS: subdural collections, enhancement of pachymeninges, engorged venous sinuses, pituitary hyperemia, sagging brainstem). Opening pressure often but not always low. Epidural blood patch first line; CT/MR myelography to localize leaks; consider CSF-venous fistula.

questions.stem: A brain MRI reveals an extra-axial dural-based mass that uniformly enhances with gadolinium and exhibits a characteristic "dural tail." Histopathology shows concentric calcified psammoma bodies. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Meningiomas are slow-growing, generally benign extra-axial tumors originating from arachnoid cap cells, demonstrating avid homogeneous enhancement, a dural tail, and psammoma bodies.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old born at 29 weeks has bilateral leg-predominant spasticity with scissoring gait and normal cognition; MRI shows periventricular T2 hyperintensity with ventriculomegaly and thinning of the posterior corpus callosum. A second child, born at term with kernicterus, has generalized dystonia and upgaze palsy. Match the lesions.

options.text: Child 1: dyskinetic CP from thalamic injury; Child 2: spastic diplegia from PVL
Child 1: spastic diplegia from periventricular leukomalacia; Child 2: dyskinetic CP from globus pallidus injury
Both: basal ganglia injury from HIE

questions.explanation: PVL injures the periventricular corticospinal fibers to the legs in preterm oligodendrocyte-precursor-vulnerable white matter, producing spastic diplegia. Bilirubin toxicity targets the globus pallidus (with sensorineural hearing loss and upgaze palsy), while term HIE targets the putamen and thalamus; both cause dyskinetic CP. Cerebral palsy is a static motor disorder from early brain injury; regression should prompt a search for a genetic or metabolic mimic (e.g., dopa-responsive dystonia, hereditary spastic paraplegia).

questions.stem: The T1 image shown demonstrates a crescentic hyperintense extra-axial collection crossing suture lines. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Subacute subdural hematoma. T1-bright methemoglobin in a crescent that crosses sutures but not the falx; epidural is lenticular and bounded by sutures. T1 bright = methemoglobin, subacute. Subdural crosses sutures but not dural reflections (falx); epidural is lenticular, bounded by sutures, and can cross the midline. Deck\'s exclusions: hygroma (CSF signal), empyema (rim enhancement, DWI bright), en plaque meningioma (T1 iso/hypointense, enhances). In an elderly or anticoagulated patient a subacute SDH can present with isolated cognitive decline or fluctuating focal signs.
questions.imageAlt: Axial T1: crescentic, T1-hyperintense extra-axial collection over the left convexity that crosses suture lines and does not cross the midline, with sulcal effacement and mild midline shift. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 126)

questions.stem: Which hypothalamic nucleus serves as the primary master circadian pacemaker of the human body, receiving direct monosynaptic retinal input via the retinohypothalamic tract?
questions.explanation: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) coordinates endogenous circadian rhythms through rhythmic transcription of clock genes driven by melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cell afferents.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman on long-term metoclopramide has persistent oro-buccal-lingual stereotypies that continue after the drug is stopped. Which class of medication has FDA approval for this condition?

options.text: Increased dose of the causative D2 antagonist

questions.explanation: Tardive dyskinesia arises from chronic D2 blockade (postsynaptic supersensitivity, maladaptive plasticity), including from metoclopramide and prochlorperazine. Anticholinergics worsen classic TD (but help tardive dystonia). VMAT2 inhibitors deplete presynaptic dopamine and are approved; withdrawal of the offending agent is not reliably curative. Tetrabenazine carries depression/suicidality warnings.

questions.stem: The cervical MRI shown demonstrates a nidus of flow voids within the cord at C5-C6 with a large draining vein. Compared with a dural arteriovenous fistula, this lesion is more likely to present with:

options.text: Insidious congestive myelopathy in an older man
Acute hemorrhage in a young patient

questions.explanation: Acute hemorrhage in a young patient. Intramedullary (glomus) AVMs bleed; dural fistulas cause slow venous congestion. Type II (glomus) AVM: true nidus within the cord, younger patients, presents with acute hemorrhage rather than the slow congestive myelopathy of a dural fistula. Spinal AVMs/AVFs occur in HHT and in Cobb syndrome (cutaneomeningospinal angiomatosis).
questions.imageAlt: Sagittal T1 (A), T2 (B) and post-contrast T1 (C) cervical spine: cluster of intramedullary and extramedullary flow voids with a nidus at C5-C6 and a large posterior draining vein. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 41)

questions.stem: A 56-year-old fell 5 days before dying. Gross brain shown. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Organizing subdural hematoma, gross. A thick tan membrane-bound convexity collection is a subacute/chronic subdural hematoma.
questions.imageAlt: Lateral view of a hemisphere with a thick tan-yellow membrane-bound collection over the convexity. Marginal note: 56-year-old, falls, right parietal skull fracture, well for 5 days then deteriorated.
questions.salient: Bridging veins; lucid interval; isodense phase on CT is easily missed; Neomembrane neovascularity causes rebleeding
questions.learning: Bridging vein tear; elderly, alcoholics, anticoagulated patients. Neomembrane forms over 1 to 2 weeks; fragile neovascularity causes rebleeding and expansion. Lucid interval with delayed deterioration. CT density evolves hyper to iso to hypo over weeks; isodense phase easily missed.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman presents 3 hours and 45 minutes after onset of aphasia and right hemiparesis (NIHSS 12). Non-contrast CT shows no hemorrhage. She takes no anticoagulants and has no history of diabetes with prior stroke. What is the appropriate reperfusion treatment?

options.text: She is outside the thrombolysis window; antiplatelet therapy only
Intravenous alteplase (0.9 mg/kg) or tenecteplase (0.25 mg/kg) within the 4.5-hour window

questions.explanation: ECASS III extended IV thrombolysis to 4.5 hours; relative exclusions in the 3–4.5 h window (age >80, NIHSS >25, oral anticoagulation, diabetes with prior stroke) have been progressively relaxed in guidelines. Tenecteplase is now an accepted alternative (AcT, TRACE-2). Blood pressure must be <185/110 before lysis. Wake-up strokes with DWI-FLAIR mismatch may also be treated (WAKE-UP).

questions.stem: An arching, comb-shaped 8–10 Hz rhythm recorded over the central regions (C3, C4) that attenuates with contralateral hand movement or thought of movement, but is unaffected by eye opening, is termed:
questions.explanation: Mu rhythm is an 8–10 Hz central rhythm reflecting sensorimotor cortex idling that desynchronizes with limb movement or intention to move, remaining unaffected by eye opening.

questions.stem: The H&E shown demonstrates thick, glassy eosinophilic vessel walls. Which clinical presentation is most characteristic?

options.text: Recurrent lobar hemorrhage in an elderly patient

questions.explanation: Recurrent lobar hemorrhage in an elderly patient. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (A-beta 40): lobar bleeds, cortical superficial siderosis, amyloid spells; Boston 2.0 criteria. A-beta 40 deposition in media/adventitia of cortical and leptomeningeal vessels; Congo red with apple-green birefringence. Present in most AD brains but also independently. Clinically: recurrent lobar hemorrhages in the elderly, cortical superficial siderosis, transient focal neurologic episodes (amyloid spells), and CAA-related inflammation (steroid responsive). Boston criteria 2.0 use lobar microbleeds and cortical siderosis on SWI. APOE e2 (hemorrhage) and e4 (deposition) are risk alleles; ARIA with anti-amyloid antibodies is CAA-related.
questions.imageAlt: H&E: thick-walled cortical and leptomeningeal arterioles with homogeneous, glassy eosinophilic wall replacement. (RITE Review deck, slide 93)

questions.stem: Cystic cerebellar tumor with mural nodule in a child. Histology shows Rosenthal fibers. Which alteration is most common?
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma. Sporadic cerebellar pilocytic astrocytomas carry the KIAA1549::BRAF fusion.
questions.imageAlt: Biphasic pattern with compact bipolar (piloid) cells and loose microcystic areas; Rosenthal fibers (corkscrew eosinophilic hyaline bodies); smear shows long hair-like processes.
questions.salient: Biphasic compact/microcystic pattern, Rosenthal fibers, eosinophilic granular bodies; Optic pathway gliomas in NF1; Rosenthal fibers also in gliosis and Alexander disease
questions.learning: KIAA1549::BRAF fusion in most sporadic cerebellar cases; optic pathway gliomas in NF1. Rosenthal fibers and eosinophilic granular bodies are also seen in gliosis around slow lesions and in Alexander disease. Cyst with enhancing mural nodule; excellent prognosis after resection.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old with rapidly progressive dementia and myoclonus has the DWI shown. Which test is most specific?
questions.explanation: RT-QuIC on CSF. DWI cortical ribboning and striatal restriction is the most sensitive imaging sign; RT-QuIC is highly specific. vCJD shows the pulvinar sign. DWI is the most sensitive test (>90%), exceeding EEG (periodic sharp wave complexes) and CSF 14-3-3; RT-QuIC on CSF is highly specific. Rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus, ataxia, visual/cortical signs; median survival 4-6 months. Variant CJD shows the pulvinar sign (posterior thalami) and younger patients with psychiatric onset. Heidenhain variant is occipital; Brownell-Oppenheimer is ataxic; Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker and FFI are the inherited PRNP forms.
questions.imageAlt: Axial DWI, patient (top) versus control (bottom): restricted diffusion in the caudate heads and anterior putamina with asymmetric cortical ribboning. (Neuroradiology deck, slide 139)

questions.stem: A phenotypically normal man carries a 15q11-q13 deletion that he inherited from his mother, who is also normal. What is the risk that each of his children will have Prader-Willi syndrome, and what would be the risk for Angelman syndrome?
questions.explanation: Imprinting makes the deletion's effect depend on the transmitting parent's sex. Inherited from his mother, the deleted chromosome carries the maternal epigenotype and he expresses paternal genes normally. When he transmits it, the deletion is on the paternal chromosome, so each child inheriting it (50%) has PWS. Had a phenotypically normal woman inherited the deletion from her father, her children would face a 50% AS risk. Such inherited deletions are rare (most are de novo) but are the reason parental testing is recommended.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old patient presents with muscle stiffness that improves with repeated exercise (warm-up phenomenon) and prominent calf hypertrophy. Genetic testing confirms a heterozygous dominant-negative variant in CLCN1 inherited from an affected parent. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Myotonia congenita is caused by loss-of-function variants in the skeletal muscle chloride channel CLCN1; Thomsen disease is the autosomal dominant form, Becker the recessive (more severe, with transient weakness). Paramyotonia (SCN4A) worsens with exercise and cold.

questions.stem: Modified Gomori trichrome shows dark rod-shaped subsarcolemmal bodies. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Nemaline rod myopathy. Rods (Z-disc derived, alpha-actinin) define nemaline myopathy.
questions.imageAlt: Modified Gomori trichrome: clusters of dark red-purple rod-shaped bodies within the sarcoplasm, often subsarcolemmal.
questions.salient: NEB recessive most common; ACTA1 dominant severe; Facial weakness, high-arched palate, respiratory involvement; adult sporadic form with MGUS
questions.learning: Rods are Z-disc derived (alpha-actinin). Genes: NEB (most common, recessive), ACTA1 (dominant/de novo, severe), TPM2, TPM3, TNNT1 (Amish), KLHL40/41. Presentations from severe neonatal to adult sporadic late-onset (with MGUS). Facial weakness, high-arched palate, respiratory involvement.

questions.stem: A neonate presents with episodic tachypnea alternating with apnea, global hypotonia, and oculomotor apraxia. Axial brain MRI demonstrates thickening and horizontal orientation of the superior cerebellar peduncles with deep interpeduncular fossa excavation ("molar tooth sign"). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Joubert syndrome is a ciliopathy characterized by agenesis/hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis and the pathognomonic "molar tooth sign" on axial brainstem MRI.

questions.stem: Which pediatric posterior fossa brain tumor is hyperdense on unenhanced CT, arises within the roof of the fourth ventricle, and tends to drop-seed throughout the neuroaxis via the cerebrospinal fluid?
questions.explanation: Medulloblastomas are embryonal tumors arising in the cerebellar vermis/fourth ventricle that appear dense on CT due to high cellularity and frequently metastasize via CSF. Molecular groups (WNT, SHH, group 3, group 4) drive risk stratification.

questions.stem: The substantia nigra histology shown demonstrates eosinophilic inclusions with halos. Which gene is the most common cause of autosomal dominant Parkinson disease?
questions.explanation: LRRK2. LRRK2 is the commonest dominant cause; GBA the commonest risk gene; PRKN/PINK1 are recessive and often lack Lewy bodies. Alpha-synuclein (SNCA) and ubiquitin positive. Nigral Lewy bodies are identical in PD and DLB; distinction is clinical (one-year rule for dementia onset). Braak PD staging begins in the dorsal motor nucleus of X and olfactory bulb and ascends. SNCA duplication/triplication, LRRK2 (most common AD cause), GBA (most common risk gene), PRKN/PINK1 (AR, young onset, minimal Lewy pathology).
questions.imageAlt: H&E of substantia nigra: residual pigmented neurons containing round eosinophilic inclusions with a dense core and a pale halo (classic brainstem Lewy bodies); a pale body is also present. (RITE Review deck, slide 141)

questions.stem: A 62-year-old with infective endocarditis is found unresponsive after headache. Serial CT is shown. Mechanism of these hemorrhages?

options.text: Rupture of mycotic aneurysms / hemorrhagic septic emboli

questions.explanation: Multiple hemorrhages from septic emboli. Multiple simultaneous lobar and deep hemorrhages in endocarditis reflect septic emboli with mycotic aneurysm rupture or hemorrhagic transformation.
questions.imageAlt: Serial noncontrast CT: hyperdense hemorrhages in the left frontal lobe, right thalamus/basal ganglia with intraventricular extension, and bilateral occipital lobes. Marginal note: 62-year-old, unresponsive after headache, infective endocarditis.
questions.salient: Mycotic aneurysms are distal and fusiform; screen with angiography; Anticoagulation generally avoided; valve surgery timing controversial after hemorrhage
questions.learning: Mycotic aneurysms are distal (beyond the first MCA bifurcation) and fusiform; screen with CTA/catheter angiography. Anticoagulation is generally avoided in endocarditis with neurologic involvement; valve surgery timing is controversial after hemorrhage. Other causes of multiple simultaneous ICH: CAA, coagulopathy, venous thrombosis, hemorrhagic metastases, RCVS.

questions.stem: The histology shown demonstrates nucleus-free zones surrounding blood vessels. Which prognostic factor matters most for this tumor?
questions.explanation: Extent of surgical resection. Perivascular pseudorosettes define ependymoma; gross total resection is the dominant prognostic factor; WHO 2021 groups by molecular subtype (PF-A, PF-B, ZFTA). Perivascular pseudorosettes are present in nearly all ependymomas; true ependymal rosettes (cells around a central lumen) are more specific but less common. GFAP and EMA (dot-like) positive. Posterior fossa ependymomas in children arise from the fourth ventricle floor and extrude through the foramina of Luschka/Magendie (plastic ependymoma); WHO 2021 groups them molecularly (PF-A, PF-B, ZFTA-fusion supratentorial). Extent of resection is the dominant prognostic factor.
questions.imageAlt: H&E: tumor cells radially arranged around a blood vessel with a nucleus-free zone of fibrillary processes surrounding the vessel wall. (RITE Review deck, slide 34)

questions.stem: Young adult with longstanding focal seizures; cortical multicystic non-enhancing lesion without edema. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor. Soap-bubble cortical lesion without mass effect or enhancement is DNET.
questions.imageAlt: Axial T2 and FLAIR: cortically based, well-demarcated multicystic (soap bubble) lesion without surrounding edema or mass effect; T1 shows no enhancement.
questions.salient: Specific glioneuronal element with floating neurons; FGFR1; Scalloping of inner table; excellent outcome after resection
questions.learning: Children and young adults with long-standing focal epilepsy; temporal lobe most common. Histology: specific glioneuronal element with floating neurons in mucin-rich columns; FGFR1 alterations. Associated cortical dysplasia; scalloping of the inner table. Excellent outcome after resection.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has 3 months of rapidly progressive dementia, ataxia, and startle myoclonus; MRI shows cortical ribboning and striatal restricted diffusion. Which CSF test has the highest specificity for the diagnosis?

options.text: Real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) for prion seeding activity

questions.explanation: RT-QuIC has ~92% sensitivity and ~99% specificity for sporadic CJD and is now in CDC diagnostic criteria; 14-3-3 and tau are sensitive but nonspecific (positive in stroke, encephalitis). DWI is the most sensitive imaging sign (>90%). Codon 129 methionine homozygosity influences phenotype. Variant CJD shows the pulvinar sign and prion in lymphoid tissue.
